a-map-of-the-steer-the-beef-primals.context_blurb:
A butcher taking apart a whole steer works from a map. First he divides the carcass into a handful of big sections called primals, and then he trims each primal into steaks and roasts. One rule explains almost every price on that map: a muscle that worked hard all its life cooks up tough and cheap, and a muscle that barely moved cooks up tender and dear.

Start at the two ends of that rule. The chuck, the largest primal of all, is the shoulder and neck at the front of the animal, muscles that swing with every step and hold up a heavy head all day. So chuck is tough and cheap, best braised into pot roast or ground into burgers. The prized steaks come from the opposite kind of muscle. Ribeye and New York strip steaks are both cut from the centre of the back, right over the backbone, from one long muscle that mostly just rides along while the animal walks.

Why does work make meat tough? A muscle that labours all day builds up connective tissue, the chewy sheathing that binds its fibres, while a lazy muscle never builds much of it. That is why the round is a budget cut. The round, the second-biggest primal, is the back leg and rump, the muscles that push the steer forward all day long. Its meat is lean, with little fat streaked through it, and it goes dry and tough over high, fast heat, so it wants low, slow, moist cooking.

The long back muscle, the longissimus dorsi, gives two famous steaks: cut near the front, over the ribs, it is a ribeye, and cut further back, nearer the hind end of the loin, it is a strip. New York sells that strip under its own name and Kansas City under another, but it is one steak. Brisket comes from the lower chest, lying over the breastbone just above the front legs, and it is one of the hardest-working muscles a steer has. Cooked quickly, it is as tough as leather. Its secret is collagen, the main protein of connective tissue: held for many hours at low heat, collagen melts into gelatin, and gelatin is what makes slow-smoked Texas brisket silky, moist and ready to fall apart.

The softest steak hides where nobody can see it. The tenderloin, a slim muscle tucked beneath the spine in the lower back, close to the kidneys, does almost no work in a living steer, so it builds almost no connective tissue, and filet mignon is cut from it. The brisket lives the opposite life. A steer has no collarbone, the strut that braces our own shoulders, so its chest muscles must carry around 60 percent of its standing weight from the day it is born. That endless load packs the brisket with collagen. Even a single steak has its treasure. A thin, heavily marbled ribbon called the spinalis curls around the outer edge of every ribeye, and old butchers loved it so much that they nicknamed it the butcher's butter and kept it for their own suppers.

The short loin, midway along the back, is where two of the best muscles meet, so a slice across it with the bone left in carries strip loin on one side of a T-shaped bone and tenderloin on the other. That is why the porterhouse is called two steaks in one, and the T-bone is cut the same way. The porterhouse comes from the rear of the short loin, where the tenderloin swells, so ordering one instead of a T-bone buys you a much bigger piece of filet. American grading rules even require a porterhouse's tenderloin to measure at least an inch and a quarter across.

a-pineapple-is-dozens-of-fruits-fused-in.context_blurb:
The pineapple is a tropical plant from South America, and almost everything about it surprises people. Spanish and Portuguese sailors carried it to Europe in the 1500s, where it became a sign of welcome and luxury. Its tangy golden flesh is not even one fruit. It is dozens of tiny fruits joined around a central stalk.

Look closely at the rough skin and you will see diamond-shaped eyes spiralling around it. Every one of those eyes began as a single flower. Each flower left behind a small fruitlet, and the fruitlets swelled and merged side by side into one head.

No pineapple ever hung from a tree. The plant is a spiky rosette of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, only about waist to chest high, and from its centre it raises one fruit at a time, close to the ground. The plant is a bromeliad, which means it can start over from its own leftovers. Twist off the leafy crown on top, let it dry, root it in water and plant it, and in about two years it may give you a pineapple of your own.

A big helping of fresh pineapple makes your tongue sting because the fruit is digesting you back: raw pineapple is full of bromelain, an enzyme that splits proteins, and it starts breaking down the proteins of your own mouth much as a stomach would. The same enzyme makes fresh pineapple a natural meat tenderiser.

Heat ends the attack, because bromelain is fragile and stops working at about 71°C (160°F). That explains an old kitchen disaster. Stir fresh pineapple into Jell-O and the enzyme chews up the gelatin's protein, so the dessert stays a runny liquid. Canned pineapple lets the same jelly set firm, because it was heated during canning and the heat destroyed its enzyme.

One more thing never changes after harvest: the sweetness. A banana stores starch and keeps turning it into sugar after it is picked, but a pineapple stores no starch at all, so the sweetness it had on the plant is all it will ever have. That is why growers must pick pineapples fully ripe, and why parking one beside ripening bananas does nothing.

acquired-tastes-bitterness-as-a-poison-a.context_blurb:
Bitter is one of the five basic tastes, and it is the one people are born disliking. Children pull a face at their first sip of black coffee, and many adults remember gagging on a first stout or a bite of baking chocolate. Yet those same people often grow up to love all three. The story of why runs from a newborn's tongue to the bark of a South American tree.

Bitterness is the harsh taste that black coffee, dark beer and unsweetened chocolate share, and it is the classic acquired taste. Even babies a few days old screw up their faces at anything bitter, a reflex scientists think was wired in before birth as an alarm against poisonous plants, because most natural plant poisons taste bitter. A baby who spat out bitter leaves was less likely to swallow a deadly one.

So how does a father come to love the coffee his son spits into the sink? His tongue has not changed, and the coffee tastes every bit as bitter to him as it did the first time; what changed is his brain, which has learned to rate that bitterness as pleasant. Years of coffee do not wear out the taste buds. Scientists call the brain's verdict the drink's hedonic value, a measure of how pleasant a taste is judged to be.

The brain bothers to learn because each sip pays it back with a chemical reward: caffeine's lift in coffee and strong tea, alcohol's buzz in beer. That payoff ends up outweighing the bitterness. Without a payoff, nobody acquires the taste.

Some bitter things really are poisons we have learned to enjoy in small doses. Tonic water gets its bite from quinine, which comes from the bark of the cinchona, a tree of South America, and quinine is a genuine medicine against malaria. It is also toxic in large amounts, so American law caps how much a bottle of tonic may hold. Other plants hide cyanide in their cells and release it when teeth crush the tissue. Cassava root, bitter almonds and lima beans all carry these cyanide-releasing compounds, and the faint bitterness they give off is the old alarm telling us not to eat too much.

afternoon-tea-and-the-high-tea-myth.context_blurb:
Afternoon tea is a small British meal of hot black tea and dainty bites, eaten in the long gap between lunch and a late dinner. It began around 1840 with Anna Russell, Duchess of Bedford, who felt faint with hunger every afternoon because fashionable dinner came at eight. She had tea and little cakes brought at four, began inviting friends, and the habit spread through Queen Victoria's court and then across England.

The star of the tea tray became the scone, a warm round of quick bread split open and heaped with clotted cream and jam, served beside thin sandwiches and small iced cakes.

Posh hotels now sell that dainty spread as 'high tea', and the name sounds grander than anything. It is borrowed. In the 1800s a real high tea was the hearty hot meal a working family ate in the early evening, after the factory shift: bread, butter and tea, filled out with fried fish or meat, ham, cheese and pie. Many Britons still call their evening meal 'tea'.

Neither 'high' nor 'low' ever described rank; they described furniture, because high tea was eaten sitting up at the tall dining table, while low tea, the ladies' afternoon tea, was taken from the low tables beside the parlour sofas.

Even the scone has its quarrels. In Cornwall the jam goes onto the warm scone first and the clotted cream sits on top, because cream spread straight onto a warm scone would melt into it and leave it soggy. Over the border in Devon, cooks spread the cream first like butter and crown it with jam, and Queen Elizabeth II was said to take the Cornish side.

aged-beef-dry-vs-wet-and-why-age-it-at-a.context_blurb:
Meat straight off the animal is not the best meat. Butchers have known for centuries that beef improves if it rests in the cold for days or weeks, and steakhouses still boast about how long theirs has aged. The reasons lie in the muscle's own chemistry, which keeps working long after the animal has died.

The first change makes things worse. Within about a day of slaughter, the soft muscle stiffens on its own into a rigid block. This is rigor mortis: two muscle proteins, actin and myosin, lock together for good. Cooked in that state, beef is chewy and unpleasant, so it must rest before anyone eats it.

Rest is where the improvement happens. Hung for days or weeks in a chilled room, beef turns tender all by itself. The muscle's own natural enzymes, mainly ones called calpains, slowly snip apart the proteins that make it tough, so the beef in effect digests its own toughness. Most supermarket beef gets a quieter version of the same treatment. Sealed in vacuum plastic, it ages in its own juices during the two or three weeks it spends being shipped and distributed. This is wet-aging: nothing dries out, no weight is lost, and the flavour stays mild.

Dry-aging, in open air, goes further. As the enzymes break down muscle protein, they free amino acids, above all glutamate, the savoury umami compound that is sold by the jar as MSG powder. That is why a dry-aged steak tastes seasoned even though no one sprinkled anything on it.

Time keeps changing the taste. Around 30 days, dry-aged beef turns nutty, and by 45 days and beyond it takes on a deep funk that chefs compare to blue cheese, built by the same slow aging that makes strong cheese strong. The price is steep. Fans blowing cold, dry air over the meat for weeks pull moisture out of every surface, until the outside turns into a hard, dark crust like jerky, called the bark, which the butcher shaves off and throws away. Between the water lost and the bark trimmed, a quarter or more of the starting weight is gone, which is part of why dry-aged steak costs so much more.

al-pastor-a-shawarma-spit-that-became-a-.context_blurb:
Tacos al pastor are one of the great food meetings of the last century: a Middle Eastern way of cooking dressed in Mexican flavours. Lebanese immigrants carried spit-roasted shawarma to Mexico, Mexican cooks remade it with their own ingredients, and by the 1960s the result had become a favourite of the taquerías of Mexico City.

Most taco fillings cook flat on a griddle. Al pastor meat is stacked into a tall cone on an upright spit, the trompo, named for the spinning top it resembles, and as the cone turns beside the flame the taquero shaves thin, crisp ribbons off the browned outside straight onto a tortilla. A shawarma cook works in just the same way.

Two swaps made the dish Mexican. Shawarma is lamb, but in Mexico lamb was hard to come by and costly, so cooks switched to pork, a meat Mexicans already raised and loved. The swap came easily, since the Lebanese newcomers were mostly Christians, with no rule against eating pork. On top of the cone the cooks set a whole pineapple, whose juice drips down to baste the meat as it turns, and a charred sliver of it lands on every taco. How the pineapple got up there is still a delicious mystery.

The spit itself is no ancient Aztec idea; it came with immigrants from Lebanon, who began arriving in the late 1800s and settled around Puebla, where they cooked lamb shawarma as they had at home. The marinade, though, is Mexican through and through: dried red chillies, garlic, cumin, clove and vinegar. Its glowing red-orange colour is deepened by achiote, also called annatto, a brick-red seed from the Yucatán ground to a paste, which Maya cooks were already using to colour their food.

Puebla still keeps an older cousin of the dish. Since the 1930s its taquerías have served tacos arabes: the same spit-roasted meat, wrapped not in a corn tortilla but in pan arabe, a soft wheat flatbread the Lebanese brought from home. The restaurant La Oriental, open since 1933, calls itself the birthplace of the Arab taco.

Even the name looks back to the old country. In Spanish, al pastor means 'shepherd style', after the herdsman's old open-fire spit roast, and fittingly so, since the whole story began with lamb turning on a spit. The English word pastor, a shepherd of a congregation, grows from the same root.

alice-waters-and-farm-to-table.context_blurb:
Alice Waters is an American chef who in 1971 opened Chez Panisse, a restaurant in Berkeley, California. Diners expected fancy French cooking. What they found was an argument about ingredients, and it helped launch America's farm-to-table movement. Waters did not invent cooking with local, seasonal food, but she became its great champion.

Her rule was that a perfect, ripe fruit or vegetable is the star of the plate, so the cook should serve it simply, or hardly cook it at all, and season it only to bring out what it already is. The best ingredients, she said, let you cook very plainly, and the food is extraordinary because it tastes of itself.

Chez Panisse has no long menu: each night brings one set meal with no choices, and it changes every evening, because it is built from whatever nearby farms have picked at the peak of ripeness that week. To keep that promise, Waters built direct ties with local farmers, ranchers and dairies, some of whom still supply the restaurant.

In 1995 she took the idea to school. At a Berkeley middle school named for Martin Luther King, she and the students turned a weedy, trash-strewn acre into the Edible Schoolyard, an organic garden with a kitchen classroom, where the students raise vegetables, gather them and cook them into their own meals. The idea spread, and it helped inspire Michelle Obama's vegetable garden at the White House.

allspice-the-new-world-berry-that-tastes.context_blurb:
Allspice is a spice of the New World, from the islands of the Caribbean, with a flavour so rich that it fooled the people who named it. Jamaica still grows most of the world's supply, and Jamaicans call it pimento. It warms jerk chicken, Christmas cakes and spiced winter drinks.

When English cooks of the 1600s first smelled it, they caught cinnamon, nutmeg and clove all at once, and they took it for a mixture of the three, so around 1621 they called it allspice. The name describes the flavour, not the ingredients: allspice is a single dried berry, picked unripe from one kind of tree, Pimenta dioica.

Columbus's crews had met it first, in the 1490s, while hunting for the pepper of the Indies. The little brown berries were dead ringers for peppercorns, so Europeans named the spice Jamaica pepper, after the island that grew it. It is one of the very few major spices native to the Americas rather than Asia.

For centuries the tree refused to leave home. Growers shipped its seeds to other tropical lands, only to see them refuse to sprout. The seeds, it turned out, germinate reliably only after a trip through a bird's gut, which wakes them up. Without birds to eat the berries and scatter the seeds, new plantations struggled to take root.

anatomy-of-a-chefs-knife-every-part-has-.context_blurb:
A chef's knife looks like one simple blade, but a cook who knows it sees half a dozen tools. Each part, from the point to the steel hidden inside the handle, has its own job. Learn the map and you work faster and more safely, because you stop forcing one spot on the blade to do everything.

Start at the front. The tip is the narrow point where the edge and the back of the blade sweep together, and it is the knife's precision instrument for scoring pork skin, peeling silverskin off a tenderloin, or nicking meat to see whether it is done. The flat is the broad side of the blade: lay it over a garlic clove and thump it with your palm to burst the clove, then use the same flat side as a scoop to carry the bits to the pan. Crush with the flat, never with the edge.

At the back of the edge, nearest the handle, sits the heel, the widest and thickest stretch of the cutting edge, so it takes the most force and is the part to drive down through hard jobs like the woody neck of a squash, raw carrots or small bones. Above the edge runs the spine. The spine is the blunt back of the blade, left thick on purpose, and because it is dull a cook can rest a finger or palm on it and bear down hard for more power and control.

The edge is not straight. Its curved middle section is the belly, and that curve is what lets a knife rock: keep the point on the board and pump the handle up and down to mince herbs or garlic. A dead-flat edge, like that of many Japanese knives, cannot rock at all. Right at the base of the blade, beside the handle, there is a small scooped notch, the choil, which cradles the fingers in the pinch grip, where a cook squeezes the bottom of the blade between thumb and first finger for far more control than the handle alone can give.

Many Western knives carry a bolster, a heavy steel collar where blade meets handle, which adds weight and balance and also works as a finger guard, a raised barrier that keeps a wet, slippery hand from slipping forward onto the edge. Not every knife has one; many Japanese knives skip it.

The last part is invisible. The tang is the part of the blade's steel that continues inside the handle. In a well-made Western chef's knife it fills the whole handle as one solid piece, a full tang, which makes the knife strong and shifts its weight back toward the hand that holds it, so it feels planted rather than tip-heavy. A traditional Japanese knife does the opposite. Its steel narrows to a thin spike buried inside a wooden handle, a hidden tang, so the knife is light and balanced toward the point, suited to slicing on a long forward stroke.

ancestral-eating-keto-paleo-carnivore.context_blurb:
Keto, paleo and carnivore are three modern diets that look backward for their rules. Each argues that a diet heavy in grain and sugar has made modern people sick, and that eating more like our ancestors can help. They disagree with one another, and with mainstream advice, about what belongs on the plate.

Keto surprises people because it does not cut fat: it cuts carbohydrates almost to nothing and replaces them with plenty of fat, from fatty meat, eggs, cheese and butter to avocado and olive oil. Fat becomes the main fuel, around three-quarters of the day's calories.

With so little carbohydrate, the body cannot run on blood sugar as usual. The liver steps in as a fuel factory, breaking stored fat into ketones, a fuel the body can burn in place of glucose. That state is ketosis, the engine the diet is named for. The most surprising customer is the brain, which doctors long taught could live on almost nothing but glucose, yet ketones cross into it and take over much of its fuel supply.

Keto did not begin as a weight-loss plan. In 1921, at the Mayo Clinic, the physician Russell Wilder named and built the ketogenic diet to control epileptic seizures in children, and it worked. In a large Johns Hopkins study, more than half of nearly a thousand children became completely free of seizures, and doctors still prescribe keto for epilepsy that drugs cannot control.

Wilder was improving on a harsher cure: around 1912 the doctor Hugh Conklin had treated epileptic patients by making them go without food for weeks, because fasting often stopped their seizures. Fasting works by pushing the body into ketosis, but no one can starve for long. Wilder's insight was that a diet very high in fat could copy the chemistry of fasting while the patient kept eating.

Paleo, popularised by Loren Cordain's 2002 book The Paleo Diet, starts from a different idea: our genes are still tuned to the Stone Age, before anyone farmed. So paleo allows fish, meat, eggs, fruit and vegetables, but no bread, dairy, beans or refined sugar, because every one of them came into the human diet only with farming or with modern industry, too late for the body to adapt. Carnivore goes further still: animal foods only, no plants at all. Its strictest form, the 'lion diet', which Jordan Peterson, a psychologist, and his daughter Mikhaila have followed, cuts the menu to beef, salt and water.

Can a person really live on meat? The Arctic explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson ate nothing but meat for a full year, with doctors watching, and stayed free of scurvy. He also described 'rabbit starvation': living on very lean meat such as rabbit, with almost no fat, he fell ill within days, and the sickness vanished once fat went back on his plate. Dietary fat is not optional; the body needs it.

The ancestors themselves did not share one diet. Anthropologists who recorded the meals of hunter-gatherers, from Inuit seal hunters to Hadza foragers in Tanzania, found every pattern from mostly meat to mostly plants, with animal food making up anywhere from about a quarter of the calories to nearly all of them. Paleo is a useful rule of thumb, not a photograph of one true Stone Age menu.

And carnivore, with all its online fans? Its followers report relief from autoimmune trouble, joint pain and low mood, while critics warn that a diet without plants cannot be healthy for long. Mainstream medical reviewers who read the studies found too little evidence so far to show that the diet delivers any of the benefits its fans report, and the long-term data does not yet exist. It has no fibre and can raise LDL cholesterol; whether it does lasting good or harm is still an open question.

anchovy-and-fish-sauce-the-umami-bomb.context_blurb:
The anchovy is a small, oily fish, salted and packed in jars and tins, and plenty of people who would never eat one whole love what it does to a dish. Cooks around the world use it, and the sauces fermented from it, as a hidden source of deep savoury flavour. That flavour has a name, umami, and it is one of the five basic tastes.

Slip a single oil-packed fillet into a pan of tomato sauce and within a minute it melts away, leaving the sauce richer and more savoury but not the least bit fishy. That is why cooks hide a secret anchovy in stews and pasta sauces, where nobody ever spots it.

That savoury depth was first pinned down in Japan. The chemist Kikunae Ikeda of Tokyo wondered why a plain broth called dashi tasted so satisfying, and found the answer in what it was simmered from: kombu, sheets of kelp seaweed. In 1908 he named its savoury taste umami and set it beside sweet, sour, salty and bitter as a fifth basic taste.

The anchovy can hide even when a recipe leaves it out. Caesar Cardini, who invented the Caesar salad in Tijuana in 1924, found whole anchovy fillets too harsh for his salad. His dressing still tasted of the sea, thanks to Worcestershire sauce, which is itself made from anchovies fermented in salt for about two years.

Why does a cured fish taste meaty? Raw protein is nearly tasteless. Salting, fermenting and aging break protein down and set free glutamate, the amino acid that triggers the savoury taste. That is how a mild fish becomes a punchy anchovy, and how a bland curd of cheese, aged for many months, becomes Parmesan.

The Romans built a whole cuisine around a fermented fish sauce they called garum, and it never quite died. In Cetara, a fishing village on the Italian coast, anchovies still ferment under salt in little chestnut barrels, and the amber juice that seeps out is bottled as colatura di alici, a name that means 'a dripping'. Half a world away, cooks in Thailand and Vietnam ferment anchovies with salt for months into nam pla and nuoc mam, sauces strikingly like garum. It is tempting to think one side copied the other, but historians have found no link, chemical or historical, and believe each tradition most likely arose on its own: the same good idea, born twice.

apperts-sealed-jars-canning-before-anyon.context_blurb:
Around 1800, France was at war across Europe, and its armies kept running out of food that would not rot on the march. The government offered a prize of 12,000 francs to anyone who could keep food good for months. The winner was a Paris cook named Nicolas Appert. His invention, canning, still feeds the world, though he never understood why it worked.

Appert was no scientist: before he ever sealed a meal, he had made his name in Paris as a pastry chef and confectioner. His method was a cook's method, too, because he packed cooked food into glass jars, corked them, sealed the corks with wax and boiled the jars for hours. The food kept for months, and around 1810 the prize was his. He died poor all the same, in 1841.

Appert had the right method for the wrong reason. Nobody yet knew about microbes, so he believed his seal worked simply by keeping out air. Decades later Louis Pasteur showed the truth: the heat kills the tiny living spoilers, and the seal keeps new ones out. Glass had another flaw, since it shattered on rough army wagons. Peter Durand, an Englishman, took out a patent of his own in 1810 on a sturdier container, the tin can, and by 1813 a London factory was filling cans for the British Army and Navy.

For about fifty years nobody invented a can opener, so soldiers simply stabbed and levered their rations open with bayonets and knives. Shop labels told buyers to cut round the top of the can with a hammer and chisel. Home canning came later. In 1858 the tinsmith John Landis Mason patented his jar, with a threaded glass mouth and a metal lid that screwed down onto a rubber ring, so any family could seal a jar airtight in its own kitchen and use it again every harvest.

Canning has a deadly enemy, though. Botulism, the deadly poison that can breed in a badly boiled jar, takes its name from botulus, the Latin word for sausage, because in the early 1800s the German doctor and poet Justinus Kerner traced a run of fatal poisonings to spoiled sausages. Done right, canning keeps food almost forever. A tin of roast veal, packed for William Parry's Arctic voyage of 1824, came home unopened and sat in a museum, and when it was at last opened in 1938, the story goes, the veal inside was still pink and in perfect condition.

Acid is the home canner's friend. Tomatoes, fruit and pickles are acidic enough to stop botulism spores from making their toxin, so a pot of boiling water is enough to can them. Low-acid foods such as green beans, corn and meat lack that protection, and their spores survive ordinary boiling at 212°F. Those foods go into a pressure canner, which traps steam under pressure and pushes the jars to about 240°F, hotter than open boiling water can ever get and hot enough to kill the spores.

are-seed-oils-bad-the-honest-fat-debate.context_blurb:
Soybean, corn, canola, sunflower and cottonseed oils fill supermarket shelves, cheap and slow to spoil. Critics lump them together as 'seed oils' and call them a hidden driver of modern disease; defenders say the evidence points the other way. The honest debate turns on how the oils are made, which fats they carry, and what the body actually does with them.

People have pressed olives and churned butter since ancient times, because both can be done by hand. Nobody can squeeze oil out of a corn kernel or a soybean that way, because wringing oil from such tiny seeds takes powerful industrial presses and chemical solvents, which is why bottled seed oils are barely a century old.

Today the soybeans are crushed into flakes and bathed in hexane, a solvent distilled from petroleum that dissolves fat and pulls out nearly every drop of oil. Critics point to that petroleum step; defenders note that only traces remain in the finished oil.

The first great seed-oil product was a solid. In 1911 the soap maker Procter & Gamble launched Crisco, a snow-white shortening made by hardening cottonseed oil, and its name is short for crystallized cottonseed oil. To push lard and butter out of American kitchens, it gave away millions of free cookbooks in which every recipe called for Crisco. Canola has a story of its own, because no plant is called canola. Canadian scientists, led by Baldur Stefansson, used ordinary cross-breeding to take the bitter, harmful erucic acid out of rapeseed oil, and in 1978 the new oil got a made-up name, canola, from Canadian Oil, Low Acid.

Fresh from the seed, the oil is still crude. Refiners finish it in three steps the industry calls RBD: refined, then bleached through clay filters to strip the colour, then deodorized with high heat and steam to drive off the smell and taste. Critics see heavy industrial processing; defenders see oil made stable and usable. Cold-pressed olive oil skips it all. The critics' central claim is about balance: for most of history, they estimate, people ate about as much omega-3 fat as omega-6, but seed oils have pushed the modern ratio toward twenty to one, and they argue that this flood of omega-6 tilts the body toward chronic inflammation. It is a real hypothesis, though the biology behind it is disputed.

Defenders answer with large studies. One study gathered over 68,000 people from 13 countries and checked their blood for linoleic acid, the chief fat of seed oils, and the people with the highest levels went on to suffer less heart disease and fewer strokes. Controlled trials also show linoleic acid lowers LDL cholesterol. The critics' chain reaction, in which linoleic acid becomes arachidonic acid and stokes inflammation, mostly breaks at its first link. When researchers traced it, only a tiny fraction converted, about 0.2 percent of the omega-6 people eat, and raising linoleic acid in trials did not change the blood markers of inflammation.

The critics' strongest evidence came out of storage. In the Minnesota Coronary Experiment, begun in 1968, thousands of hospital patients replaced butter with seed-oil fats and their cholesterol fell, yet when the researcher Christopher Ramsden recovered the lost data from forty-year-old tapes, the deaths had not fallen at all. The oil-fed patients died at equal or even higher rates. Lower cholesterol had not bought longer life.

On one point both sides agree: the deep-fryer. The omega-6 fats in corn and sunflower oil are fragile at high heat, and reusing them for frying day after day, as fast-food kitchens do, breeds toxic aldehydes, harmful breakdown products that build up with every reuse and far faster than in olive oil. Seed oils look worst as the backbone of reused fryer oil, while butter, olive oil and tallow remain time-tested choices, and a little seed oil used gently at home is far less of a worry.

arepas-the-other-corn-cake-masarepa-not-.context_blurb:
The arepa is the daily bread of Venezuela and Colombia: a thick, round cake of corn dough, browned on a griddle until it is crisp outside and soft within. People in this corner of South America have cooked corn cakes like it for nearly three thousand years.

What makes an arepa is its flour. Mexican tortilla dough begins with corn steeped in limewater, an ancient process called nixtamalization. Arepa flour, masarepa, never meets lime at all. Its corn is boiled in plain water, then dried and milled, so the flour is already cooked before it reaches the kitchen.

In Venezuela the cake is cooked first and filled afterwards. The cook slices the hot arepa through its edge, opening it into a pocket the way you would open a bread roll, and packs it with pulled chicken, beans or soft white cheese. The best-loved filling, the reina pepiada, is chicken mashed with avocado.

Colombia goes its own way. Colombian arepas are usually thinner and seldom opened up. When a Colombian cook wants a cheesy arepa, the cheese is worked into the dough by hand before the cake is shaped: the arepa de queso.

For generations, Venezuelan breakfasts cost a morning of labour called la piladera: beating soaked kernels with a heavy pestle in a waist-high wooden mortar, the pilón. In 1954 the engineer Luis Caballero Mejías patented a precooked corn flour, and in 1960 it reached the shops as Harina P.A.N., sold with a slogan that cheered the end of the pounding.

Along Colombia's Caribbean shore, street cooks found one more trick. They half-fry a cake, cut a slit along its edge, slide a whole raw egg inside and drop it back into the oil. The cake puffs, and the egg cooks sealed in its heart: the arepa de huevo.

asado-and-chimichurri-argentine-fire-and.context_blurb:
The asado is Argentina's great weekend ritual: a long, slow outdoor feast of beef, cooked on a wood-fired grill while friends and family gather round for hours. It comes down from the gauchos, the cowboys of the grassy pampas, and it runs on fire, salt, patience and a strict sense of who is in charge.

The grill is the parrilla, and its golden rule is that meat cooks over embers, not flames. The cook burns hardwood down to a bed of glowing coals, sets the meat above them, and controls the heat by raising or lowering the grate, never by feeding the fire.

Visitors often expect a secret marinade, but there is none. Good grass-fed beef gets one seasoning, salt, rubbed on before the meat goes over the coals or while it cooks, and the meat, the wood and the fire do the rest. One person makes every call, the asador, the grill-master, who judges the fire, decides when each cut goes on and comes off, and what is served first, while the guests stand back with their wine.

The beef's partner is chimichurri, a bright green sauce of parsley, garlic, oregano, vinegar, oil and a pinch of chilli. Nothing in it is ever cooked: the cook simply mixes it raw, lets it rest so the flavours blend, and spoons it over the grilled meat at the table. Showpieces get special treatment. For asado a la cruz, a whole lamb is spread on a tall iron frame shaped like a cross, tilted toward the coals, where the heat from the side roasts it for about four hours.

An asado also has an order, and newcomers get it wrong by reaching for the steak. The prime cuts come near the end. The meal opens with quick bites while the guests are still arriving: sausages such as chorizo and morcilla, the blood sausage, along with sweetbreads, often dressed with chimichurri.

The finest charcoal for an asado is made from quebracho, among the hardest woods in South America. Its coals hold a fierce, even heat for three or four hours and leave very little ash. Its name is a warning, for quebracho comes from quiebra hacha, the axe-breaker, a wood hard enough to snap an axe.

authentic-ragu-alla-bolognese.context_blurb:
Bologna, a rich old city in northern Italy, gave the world its most copied meat sauce, the ragù alla bolognese. Abroad it is usually ladled over spaghetti and swimming in tomato. At home in Bologna it is something else: a slow-simmered sauce of meat, built step by careful step, which the city guards so closely that it keeps an official recipe, last updated in 2023.

Start with the pasta. Bologna serves its ragù on tagliatelle, long flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta, or layers it into lasagne, but never puts it on spaghetti. Fresh egg ribbons have a slightly rough surface that grips the heavy meat sauce, while on smooth, round spaghetti the sauce slides off and pools at the bottom of the bowl.

The sauce begins with a soffritto of onion, carrot and celery, minced fine by hand and softened slowly in butter and oil before any meat goes in. So where did spaghetti bolognese come from? The oldest known recipe under that name turned up in America, in a 1917 cookbook sold to help the families of Italian soldiers in the First World War. Spaghetti won abroad because America had no tradition of fresh egg pasta, and delicate fresh ribbons did not travel well.

Two ingredients surprise outsiders. Deep into the long simmer, a small glassful of whole milk goes in, a little at a time, to soften the tomato's sharpness, tenderise the meat and mellow the whole pot. The 2023 recipe calls the milk advisable rather than required. The wine, splashed in once the beef has browned to lift the brown bits from the pot, is dry white wine, not red. The tomato itself is only a modest spoonful, because this is a meat sauce, not a tomato sauce.

The deepest flavour goes in first. Before any beef, the cook melts small cubes of pancetta, Italy's salt-cured, unsmoked pork belly, until the fat runs and the pork turns golden, and the beef then browns in that rendered fat, so the whole sauce tastes richer. The dish's roots reach back before Bologna wrote down its own recipe. The earliest recorded ragù served over pasta was cooked in the 1790s in Imola, near Bologna, by Alberto Alvisi, the private cook of Barnaba Chiaramonti, who in 1800 was elected Pope Pius VII.

b12-the-animal-only-vitamin-and-why-vega.context_blurb:
Vitamin B12 is one of the strangest nutrients in your food. An adult needs only a speck of it each day, about 2.4 micrograms, yet without it the body falls seriously ill. It comes almost entirely from animal foods, and that one fact makes it the nutrient every vegan has to plan around.

B12 has two jobs the body cannot skip: it keeps your nerve cells healthy, and it helps the body make the oxygen-carrying red cells of the blood. You get it from meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and essentially not from plants.

Liver is the richest source of all, with a small serving of beef liver holding around thirty times an adult's daily need. Next come shellfish: a three-ounce serving of clams carries several days' worth, leaving salmon and tuna far behind. Liver's power was proved before anyone knew B12 existed. In the 1920s a disease called pernicious anaemia slowly wasted a patient's blood away, and it killed. Then in 1926 the American doctors George Minot and William Murphy fed their patients about half a pound of raw beef liver a day, and within weeks the patients' blood recovered. The cure won them a share of a Nobel Prize.

Here is the twist: no animal makes B12, because every bit of it is built by bacteria and a few related microbes. Cows, fish and clams only store what those microbes make, which is why the vitamin ends up in animal tissue and not in plants. The body stores it too. The liver keeps a reserve that can last three to five years, so someone who stops eating every animal food, with no pills to make up for it, can go about three years before the deficiency appears. Most other B vitamins wash out within days and have to be replaced all the time.

Eating B12 is not the same as absorbing it. The stomach must also make a protein called intrinsic factor, which escorts the vitamin across the far end of the gut, and if the body's own defences destroy that protein, absorption stops no matter how much B12 is on the plate. That is the true cause of pernicious anaemia, which is why it is treated with B12 injections rather than food. For vegans the honest answer is fair to both sides. A well-planned vegan diet can be healthy, but its B12 has to come from a supplement or from fortified foods, because whole plants cannot supply it. Vegans who take their B12 often have better levels than meat-eaters do, but it is the one gap a plants-only diet cannot close by itself.

baklava-and-phyllo-dough-stretched-thin-.context_blurb:
Baklava is the great pastry of the lands once ruled by the Ottoman Empire, from Turkey and Greece to Lebanon and Syria. Its maker layers sheet upon sheet of see-through dough, each brushed with butter, bakes the tray until it crackles, then floods it with sweet syrup. Every bite is crisp and sticky at the same time.

Between the sheets lies a thick layer of finely chopped nuts, and the tray is cut into diamonds before it bakes so that every piece can drink in the honey or sugar syrup.

The dough is the marvel. Phyllo dough, named from the Greek word for 'leaf', is pulled out over a wide table until light shines through it, and dozens of these sheets, each brushed with melted butter, go into one tray. Turkish bakers call it yufka.

Gaziantep, in southeastern Turkey, makes a baklava many Turks call the finest anywhere, filled with pistachios grown on the trees of the surrounding hills, and in 2013 it became the first Turkish food to win Europe's protected-origin status. The syrup obeys a strict rule: cold syrup on hot baklava, or hot syrup on cold, but never hot on hot. The gap in temperature lets the layers soak up syrup slowly and stay crisp. Pour hot syrup onto hot pastry and the phyllo gulps down too much, too fast, and goes soggy.

Baklava was also a reward of state. Each year in the middle of Ramadan, by Ottoman court custom, the Sultan presented trays of baklava to the Janissary soldiers, the elite infantry of the palace, who carried them back through the streets in the Baklava Procession. Istanbul's bakers had a test of their own. By guild tradition, a cook was made a master only if his phyllo was so fine that a coin let fall from about 69 centimetres up pierced every layer of a finished baklava.

balut-the-egg-with-the-embryo.context_blurb:
Balut is one of the Philippines' best-loved street snacks and one of the most startling foods a visitor can meet. In Manila and other cities, vendors walk the evening streets calling out its name and sell warm boiled duck eggs from buckets of hot water. From the outside, a balut looks like any hard-boiled egg.

The surprise is inside. A balut is a fertilised duck egg left to develop before it is boiled, so a curled, half-formed duckling lies within the shell. To millions of Filipinos it is a cheap and ordinary comfort food, often eaten late at night with friends.

Regulars know how to open one. First crack a little opening at the top and drink the warm broth from around the duckling straight out of the shell, and only then peel the rest. The yolk and the chick are eaten next, seasoned with a little salt and vinegar, or with chilli and garlic.

Timing is everything. The young Filipino version, balut sa puti, is kept warm for about 17 days, stopped before the chick grows a beak, feathers or claws. Old-style makers use no machine at all, for the eggs lie under warm sand or heaps of rice husks for those 17 days until they are ready to boil. Vietnam's version is kept warm for up to three weeks, until the duckling is plainly a duckling.

banh-mi-a-french-baguette-that-became-vi.context_blurb:
Banh mi, the crackly sandwich sold at street stalls the length of the country, is the most famous sandwich in Vietnam. It is a child of colonial history. France ruled Vietnam from the 1860s and brought its bread along, and Vietnamese cooks turned that bread into something entirely their own.

The sandwich is built in a baguette, slit along its length and packed with fillings, and locals first called that strange French loaf banh tay, 'Western bread'. Vietnamese bakers soon changed it. They blended rice flour, a cheap local staple, into the wheat dough, often as much as half, which made the loaf lighter, airier and crisper than the chewy French original, as well as cheaper and better suited to a hot, wet climate.

The loaded sandwich the world knows is younger than it looks. Under French rule a banh mi was often just bread with a thin smear of pâté. After the French left, family shops in Saigon, today's Ho Chi Minh City, began stuffing the bread with meats, and one of the first, Hoa Ma, opened there in 1958.

The fillings join two kitchens. French pâté and mayonnaise sit beside Vietnamese cold cuts. One favourite is cha lua, a smooth pork paste rolled up in banana leaf and steamed until firm, then cut into pale rounds; the leaf gives it a faint fragrance and its neat round shape.

All that richness needs a sharp edge, and do chua provides it: shredded carrot and daikon, a mild white radish, pickled in sweet-and-sour vinegar. With fresh coriander leaves and hot chilli, its acid and crunch cut straight through the fat.

The bread's last secret is rough handling. French bakers fold their dough gently to keep the crumb tender. Vietnamese bakers instead beat the dough hard in a mixer, slap the loaves quickly into shape and bake them with steam, and that rough treatment gives the airy, poofy crumb inside a thin, crackly crust.

beef-wellington.context_blurb:
Beef Wellington is the grand showpiece of British roasts: a whole beef tenderloin, coated in mushrooms and wrapped in golden pastry, baked and carried to the table to be cut into thick rounds. Every slice shows rings of pastry, mushroom and rosy beef. It is famous for being difficult to get right, and its name hides a mystery.

The beef bakes sealed inside a jacket of puff pastry, which makes the Wellington the most lavish meat-in-a-blanket of them all.

Between beef and pastry lies duxelles, mushrooms chopped very fine with shallots and herbs and cooked down to a dark, dry paste. The French chef François Pierre La Varenne created it in the 1600s and named it for his employer, the Marquis d'Uxelles. Its job is to keep the pastry crisp. The dish has one dreaded failure, the soggy bottom, when juice from the meat and water from the mushrooms soak into the base and leave it pale and mushy. On television baking contests, that verdict has sunk many a cook whose beef was a perfect pink.

Chefs add a second guard. Before the pastry goes on, the seared fillet is first wrapped in prosciutto, a thin, salty, dry-cured ham that soaks up escaping juice like a sponge. Ham and duxelles, sometimes laid over a thin crêpe, form the moisture barrier that is the real secret of a good Wellington.

The name is the deepest puzzle. The dish is said to honour Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington, the general who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo, but nobody can prove it. Historians who found the menu of the grand banquet the Duke himself gave in 1839 to celebrate his victory discovered that the dish was not on it anywhere. The food writer Leah Hyslop suspects the name was a patriotic relabelling of a fashionable French dish, filet de bœuf en croûte, beef fillet in a crust.

beer-and-bread-grew-up-together-mesopota.context_blurb:
Some fifty centuries back, the first great cities rose in Sumer, the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates in the south of modern Iraq. The Sumerians grew barley, and from the same grain they made both their daily bread and a thick, bubbling beer. The two foods grew up side by side, so closely that one began inside the other.

Beer was so central that it served as wages, because coins had not been invented, and labourers on temple and palace lands were paid partly in a daily ration of beer, about a litre. A clay tablet from the city of Uruk, often called the oldest known payslip, records the handout; its picture-signs show a pointed beer jar beside a head eating from a bowl.

The Sumerians even honoured a goddess of brewing, Ninkasi, who was believed to watch over every batch. Her name meant something like 'lady who fills the mouth', a cheerful boast about what beer does. Brewing began in the oven: Sumerian brewers first baked a twice-baked loaf of barley bread called bappir, then crumbled it with malted grain into water to ferment, so the bakery and the brewery were cousins.

Sumerian beer was unfiltered, and a crust of floating hulls and yeast covered the top of the jar, so drinkers sat around one big shared jar and sipped through long reed straws, some over a metre long, that reached past the crust to the clean beer underneath. The scene is carved on Queen Pu-abi's cylinder seal from the royal tombs at Ur.

The oldest full beer recipe hides in a sacred hymn: the Hymn to Ninkasi, written down around 1800 BCE, praises the goddess while walking through every step of brewing. Its steady rhythm helped brewers memorise the process at a time when few could read. In 1989 California's Anchor Brewing Company, working with a scholar of Sumer, brewed a beer straight from the hymn, barley bread and all, and it came out as smooth and bubbly as champagne, with a faint smell of dates.

beluga-caviar-roe-from-a-fish-older-than.context_blurb:
Caviar is among the most expensive foods on Earth. In a top restaurant one tiny tin may sell for thousands of dollars, and diners eat the glistening dark beads one careful spoonful at a time. The most prized of all is beluga caviar, from an armoured giant of a fish whose family outlived the dinosaurs.

For all the fuss, caviar is a simple natural food: salted fish eggs, the raw roe of the sturgeon, lightly salted and nothing more.

Beluga caviar comes from the beluga sturgeon, a fish, and not from the beluga whale, a mammal that only shares the name. The sturgeon looks prehistoric, with rows of bony plates for armour, and it lives in the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea, swimming up their rivers to spawn. It can grow monstrous. The record fish, a female landed on the Volga in 1827, measured about 7.2 metres, roughly as long as a small van, and weighed over a tonne and a half.

The eggs cost a fortune because the fish grows up so slowly: a female beluga needs up to twenty years to mature and make eggs worth harvesting, so a spoonful of caviar can come from a fish older than the person eating it. That slow life made it easy to wipe out. Over a hundred years and more, the nets took belugas faster than they could breed, and the species is now critically endangered, with most trade in wild eggs banned. Nearly all legal beluga caviar today comes from farmed sturgeon, raised in tanks and ponds.

Eating it has its own ritual. Caviar is served with a little spoon made of horn, bone or mother-of-pearl, never metal, because metal reacts with the salts and fats in the roe and leaves an unpleasant, tinny taste.

best-by-vs-use-by-vs-sell-by.context_blurb:
Grocery packages are stamped with confusing dates: 'best if used by', 'sell by', 'use by'. Most shoppers treat them as safety deadlines, and most of them are nothing of the kind. Manufacturers set them as guesses about quality, and misreading them is one reason Americans throw away mountains of perfectly good food every year.

A 'Best if Used By' date is a promise about flavour, not safety: it marks the last day the maker expects the food to be at its peak of freshness. Afterwards the food is still safe to eat, though it may taste a little less lively, so a yogurt one day past its best-by is usually fine.

A 'Sell-By' date is not meant for shoppers, because it tells the store how long to keep the product on its shelves, so that older stock goes out first. Milk kept cold is usually good for about a week past it.

Only one food in the United States carries a date the law truly requires. That food is infant formula, and past its use-by date the maker no longer promises that the formula still holds the full amount of every nutrient on the label. Every other date, in some fifty different phrasings, is the maker's own call. Eggs show the gap plainly. On a graded American egg carton the sell-by date may fall no more than 30 days after packing, yet eggs kept cold at home stay safe to eat for weeks after that date has come and gone. The pack date hides in a three-digit code on the carton, the day of the year from 001 to 365.

So how do you know when food has really gone bad? Spoilage bacteria are the ones that make food smell sour and feel slimy, and they seldom cause illness. The germs that put people in hospital, Salmonella and Listeria, cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, so food carrying them usually looks, smells and tastes perfectly normal. 'It seems fine' is no test of safety. Go by safe storage times instead, and remember that Listeria keeps growing even in the fridge.

birdseye-and-flash-freezing-the-inuit-se.context_blurb:
Around 1915 a young American named Clarence Birdseye was trading furs on the frozen coast of Labrador and fishing beside the Inuit. What he saw on the ice changed the way the world eats. The frozen food of that era was a grey, mushy disappointment; within a few years he had built machines that made it taste fresh.

The Inuit fished through holes in the ice in wind far below zero, and every trout they pulled out froze rock-solid within seconds of leaving the water. Weeks later Birdseye thawed and cooked some of that fish, and it tasted as fresh as if it had just come out of the water. Frozen food back home never did.

Birdseye always said he had not invented freezing, since people had frozen food for centuries. His breakthrough was seeing that one thing decides between fresh and ruined, and that thing is speed: the faster the freeze, the better the food. He humbly said he had simply taken Inuit knowledge and the scientists' theories and adapted them to mass production. In 1953 the company that still carries his name, Birds Eye, tried breaded sticks of every kind, but only the fish stick lasted, and the rest of the line flopped.

Why does speed matter? Water inside food turns to ice as it freezes. Fast freezing makes tiny crystals that leave the cells whole, but slow freezing grows big crystals that puncture the cell walls, so when the food thaws its juice leaks out and it goes limp. That is why a strawberry frozen slowly at home thaws into mush, while blast-frozen peas stay firm.

Speed also explains a fishmonger's secret: frozen fish is often fresher than the 'fresh' fillet on ice. Fish frozen at sea is gutted and frozen within hours of the catch, before it starts to break down, while a fillet on the counter may have spent up to two weeks on ice since it left the water. Vegetables tell the same story. Peas go into the freezer within about two and a half hours of picking, but fresh-picked peas can lose around half their vitamin C in a single day, so a bag of frozen peas may beat the 'fresh' ones from the produce bin.

biryani-and-dum-cooked-by-trapping-its-o.context_blurb:
Biryani is one of the great rice dishes of South Asia, cooked across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh in dozens of regional styles. Long-grain basmati rice and richly spiced meat go into one heavy pot, and the pot is sealed so the dish finishes in its own steam. Every region argues about the details, but all of them agree on how the pot is built.

A biryani is never stirred together: the cook builds alternating layers of half-cooked rice and spiced meat, so each stays distinct as they steam side by side instead of blending into porridge.

The dish was born in royal kitchens. The Mughal emperors, who ruled much of India from the 1500s, came down from Central Asia with the Persian pilaf, rice cooked in a well-seasoned meat broth, and in their kitchens it met India's spices and became biryani. The historian Lizzie Collingham places its birth in the kitchens of the emperor Akbar, and the name comes from a Persian word meaning to fry or roast. One famous branch grew in exile: when the British drove Awadh's last king, Wajid Ali Shah, to a suburb of Calcutta in 1856, his royal cooks created Kolkata biryani, which is marked by a soft-cooked potato that the grander court versions never held.

The last stage is dum, from a Persian word for breathing or steaming. The pot sits over the lowest flame while the food finishes in its own trapped steam, so the lid must let nothing escape. Old cooks sealed the heavy clay pot by pressing a rope of dough around its rim beneath the lid, a seal called the pardah, or veil, which bakes into a crust as the biryani cooks.

Kacchi biryani is the hardest test of all, because raw marinated meat goes in with rice that is only half cooked and both must finish at the same moment, so a small mistake in heat or timing leaves the meat tough while the rice has already turned to mush. The safer pakki style cooks the meat and the rice separately before they are layered.

Saffron, steeped in warm milk and trickled between the layers, gives biryani its gold streaks and its perfume, and saffron is the dried, thread-like stigma of the crocus flower, picked by hand, three to a blossom. It takes around 150 flowers to make a single gram, which is why saffron costs more, ounce for ounce, than gold.

bivalves-the-filter-feeders-that-clean-t.context_blurb:
Oysters, mussels, clams and scallops are bivalves, soft animals that live inside two hinged shells. They have no jaws and never chase a meal. Instead each one is a living pump that draws seawater through its body and strains out food. That filtering makes them delicious, makes them powerful cleaners of the sea, and, when the water turns bad, makes them dangerous.

A grown oyster pumps dozens of gallons of water a day across its gills, which serve as both lungs and net: the same hair-covered filaments that take oxygen from the water also catch drifting algae and sweep them along to the mouth.

Because a living bivalve clamps its shell shut when it senses danger, cooks use a simple test. Tap a gaping mussel or clam on the counter: a live one snaps shut, but one that stays open is already dead, and dead shellfish breed dangerous bacteria, so it goes straight in the bin.

Filtering on a grand scale cleans whole bays. Two centuries ago Chesapeake Bay held so many oysters that they could strain all of its water in about a week, but a century of over-harvesting made the oyster population collapse, and the few left today need more than a year for the same job. Oysters are a bay's living kidneys.

The same pump can turn deadly. When toxic algae bloom along a coast in a red tide, they release nerve poisons such as saxitoxin, and filter-feeders pile the poison up in their flesh to levels far higher than in the sea around them. The blue mussel soaks up the toxin faster than any other shellfish, so monitoring programmes test it first, as a sentinel that warns of danger early. The illness it warns of, paralytic shellfish poisoning, has no antidote, and its first sign, usually inside two hours of eating, is a tingling and numbness in the lips; severe cases can stop a person's breathing within a day.

The old rule that oysters should be eaten only in months with an R in their names is folklore, but it points at a real danger, because the R-less months from May to August bring warm water, and warm water feeds toxic algae blooms and makes shellfish spoil fast. California quarantines its wild mussels every year from May until the end of October.

black-pepper-the-king-of-spices-vine.context_blurb:
No spice is traded more than black pepper, yet few of the people who shake it onto their food have ever seen where it grows. The plant is tropical, at home in hot, rainy forest, and on the plant pepper looks nothing like the black grains in a grinder. Every colour of peppercorn, and much of the history of the spice trade, starts on one vine.

Pepper grows on a woody climbing vine, Piper nigrum, which twines up trees, poles or trellises to about four metres, its stems hung with long spikes of fruit. A peppercorn looks like a seed you could plant, but botanically it is a tiny dried berry, a true little fruit, so ground pepper is really crushed dried fruit.

The vine is native to the Malabar Coast of south-west India, where wild pepper still grows in the rainforest of the Western Ghats, and that shore became the heart of the spice trade, pulling in traders from Arabia, Portugal and the Netherlands. The black, white and green peppercorns in a spice shop are not three spices from three plants, for all of them are berries from that same vine, treated in different ways.

For black pepper, the farmer picks the berries while they are still unripe and green, dips them briefly in hot water, and dries them in the sun for days, until the skin shrinks and wrinkles into a dark shell. Green peppercorns are unripe berries too, but they are kept fresh instead of dried, often packed in jars of salty brine, so they hold their bright colour and a softer flavour. White pepper takes extra work: the berries are left on the vine to ripen fully, then soaked in water for about a week until the dark outer skin rots and rubs away, leaving only the pale seed inside. It is milder, and cooks use it in pale sauces where dark specks would show.

In the first century, Roman ships made the long voyage to India for pepper, and it was so valuable that merchants weighed and counted peppercorns out like coins. Pliny the Elder complained that Romans were throwing fortunes at a wrinkled berry that fed nobody.

Chilli peppers share the name and the burn but are no relatives at all: they grow on the Capsicum bush, native to Central and South America, and chillies reached India only after Europeans carried them across the ocean, after 1492.

black-pepper-the-king-of-spices.context_blurb:
Black pepper has been one of the world's most precious spices for more than two thousand years. It travelled from one stretch of Indian coast to the tables of Rome, Venice and Lisbon, and on the way it was weighed out like treasure, demanded as ransom and even used as money. Its story is the story of the spice trade itself.

Every peppercorn in a mill began as a berry, a small round fruit, one of dozens hanging in a bunch from a climbing vine, Piper nigrum. The vine's homeland is the Malabar coast in the south-west of India, where it was grown for thousands of years, long before Greeks or Romans had ever heard of it.

Black, white and green peppercorns do not come from three different plants; all three are the very same berry, picked at different stages of ripeness and cured in different ways. Black is the unripe berry, briefly cooked and dried in the sun until it wrinkles; white is the ripe berry soaked until its outer flesh rubs away; green is the unripe berry kept fresh.

In medieval Europe pepper was so precious that merchants weighed the berries out one by one and people paid wages and debts with them, so the spice earned the name black gold. The custom survives in English law as the peppercorn rent, a token payment that makes a lease binding, and in Bermuda a Masonic lodge has paid its yearly rent to the Governor with a single peppercorn, carried in procession on a velvet cushion, ever since 1816.

Pepper could even be a prize of war. In 408 the Visigoth king Alaric besieged Rome and demanded a ransom of gold, silver and silk, plus three thousand pounds of pepper, and when Rome's envoys asked him what the citizens would have left, he answered: their lives. Pepper also named another spice by mistake. When Columbus tasted the fiery red pods of the Caribbean in 1492, the only thing he knew that burned like them was the peppercorn, so he called them peppers, but chilli and black pepper are unrelated plants from opposite sides of the world, a New World pod and an Old World vine.

Venice had long made fortunes reselling pepper to the rest of Europe, until Vasco da Gama of Portugal sailed round Africa to India in 1498; once ships could buy pepper at its source, its price in Europe collapsed, and in Lisbon it sold for less than a fifth of the Venice price. Pepper's bite comes from piperine, which plays the same trick as chilli's capsaicin, fooling the tongue's heat sensor into reporting warmth, though the two molecules are entirely different.

The trade is older than anyone guessed. Embalmers preparing Ramesses II, the great pharaoh who died in 1213 BCE, packed Indian peppercorns into his nostrils, proof that pepper had crossed half the world over three thousand years ago.

blue-zones-the-longevity-places-and-the-.context_blurb:
The Blue Zones are five places where people are said to reach the age of 100 unusually often: Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, Ikaria in Greece, Nicoya in Costa Rica and Loma Linda in California. For decades their diets were held up as a recipe for a long life, and the writer Dan Buettner made them world-famous. More recently, a researcher has questioned the age records behind the whole idea.

The name has a humble origin: around 2000 the demographers Michel Poulain and Gianni Pes circled long-lived villages on a map of Sardinia in blue ink, reportedly because a blue felt-tip was the only pen on the desk, and the colour stuck. Okinawa's volcanic soil was poor ground for rice, so the older generation there lived largely on the purple sweet potato, which supplied roughly 60 percent of their calories over their lifetimes.

Across all five places, researchers found the same cheap staple turning up daily, about a cupful: beans, from black beans in Nicoya to fava beans and chickpeas in Sardinia and Ikaria and soybeans in Okinawa, and Buettner calls them the world's greatest longevity food. Okinawans also follow an old Confucian rule at meals, hara hachi bu, which means stopping when you are about 80 percent full. It works partly because the brain needs about twenty minutes to notice that the stomach is full.

Loma Linda's centenarians are mostly Seventh-day Adventists, who live about ten years longer than most Americans, and those who ate a handful of nuts most days had roughly half the risk of heart disease. They also avoid smoking and drinking, a reminder that a whole way of life is at work, not one magic food.

Then came the doubts. Saul Newman, a demographer, received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2024 after arguing that the biggest driver of these places' striking numbers of very old people is sloppy record-keeping and pension fraud, not diet. He pointed out that most claimed supercentenarians have no birth certificate, and that in 2010 Japan found more than 230,000 listed centenarians missing, some long dead while relatives collected the pensions. Buettner rejects the critique as an unpublished opinion paper and says careful checks in Okinawa found almost no missing centenarians. The plain food lessons, more beans and vegetables and less junk, may still hold; it is the magic age claims that are in dispute.

bread-and-circuses-the-roman-grain-dole.context_blurb:
By the second century AD, Rome had swollen into a city of about a million people, and its rulers had learned that a hungry crowd is a dangerous one. So the state fed its citizens. The grain dole, called the annona, was the biggest free food scheme of antiquity, and it shaped Roman politics for centuries.

The handout was wheat, given free each month to some 200,000 adult male citizens, and the whole supply operation had a name of its own, the cura annonae, the care of the grain supply.

Through the Republic and the early Empire the dole was raw grain, not bread, so each man carried home about 33 kilograms of wheat a month, and his own household had to grind it, knead it and bake it. To keep the distribution halls on the Campus Martius from turning into a crush, each citizen brought a token, a small claim-piece called a tessera, which proved he was on the rolls and held his place in line.

Italy's own farms could never feed a million mouths, so after Augustus seized Egypt in 30 BC, the wheat of the Nile valley became Rome's breadbasket, carried north each year by great grain fleets.

Only in the third century did the dole become real bread. The emperor Aurelian is usually credited with handing out free baked loaves, and with adding pork, olive oil and salt to the ration, so that it became close to a full meal. Long before that, around AD 100, the poet Juvenal mocked his fellow Romans in his tenth Satire: a people who once gave out army commands and high office now hungered anxiously for only two things, bread and circuses, panem et circenses. The phrase still means a government that buys quiet with food and shows.

bread-rises-the-gas-trapped-in-the-loaf.context_blurb:
Bread is one of the oldest foods people make, and one of the cleverest. Flour, water and a pinch of something alive become a loaf that is more air than dough. Bakers mastered the trick thousands of years before anyone understood it. The secret is a gas, a living fungus that makes it, and a stretchy net that holds it in.

The gas is carbon dioxide, the same gas that fizzes out of a can of soda and that you breathe out with every breath. As the dough rises, carbon dioxide blows thousands of tiny bubbles inside it, and the heat of the oven firms the dough around them, so every hole in a slice of bread is a bubble of gas caught as the loaf baked.

The maker of that gas is yeast, and the sandy grains in the packet are not dead powder, for yeast is a living fungus, a microscopic single-celled creature that eats the sugars in dough and gives off carbon dioxide, a process called fermentation. Bakers share it with brewers, because baker's yeast and brewer's yeast are the very same species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which people have used to brew beer for sixty centuries or more.

Gas alone would leak away. When a baker kneads wheat flour and water, the flour's proteins link into gluten, a stretchy network that wraps every bubble like the skin of a balloon and holds the gas in so the dough can rise. That is why bread flour is sold as 'strong': it carries more protein than the 'weak' flour meant for cakes, so it builds more gluten, traps more gas and gives a taller, chewier loaf.

Yeast makes a little alcohol alongside its gas, the same alcohol found in beer and wine, but the heat of the oven drives the alcohol off, leaving only the smell of fresh bread. The oven also gives one last lift, called oven spring: in the first minutes of baking, the gas trapped inside the dough heats up and expands, puffing the loaf upward, even while the rising heat is killing the yeast. Then the crust sets and the shape is fixed. Around 3000 BCE, Egyptian bakers made the first bread that truly rose, most likely by accident, when dough left out in the warm air caught wild yeast that drifted in and puffed up on its own. The Egyptians were already brewing beer with such yeast.

Not every rise needs yeast. Pancakes and muffins puff up in minutes because baking soda and baking powder are chemical leaveners, in which an acid and a base react and fizz out carbon dioxide the moment the batter gets wet, with no living microbe and no waiting. And some bread is meant never to rise at all. Jewish families eat flat matzah at Passover because, as the Book of Exodus tells it, the Israelites had to flee Egypt in such haste that their dough had no time to rise, so it baked flat.

brillat-savarin-the-first-food-writer.context_blurb:
Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin, a Frenchman born in 1755 who died in 1826, was a lawyer and judge, not a cook. Yet his love of eating made him one of the most quoted food writers who ever lived. His 1825 book, The Physiology of Taste, is still read today, and French cooks have named both a cake and a cheese in his honour.

The cheese is the Brillat-Savarin, a soft, buttery triple-cream cheese of cow's milk with a white bloomy rind, which a Paris cheese-selling family renamed for him in the 1930s, about a hundred years after he died, though he never made a cheese in his life. His own adventures took him far from France: fleeing the Reign of Terror in 1793, he lived nearly three years in America, where he shot a wild turkey in the woods of Connecticut, praised the bird warmly, and by one account asked Thomas Jefferson how best to cook it.

In 1844 the Julien brothers, Paris pastry chefs, honoured him with the savarin, a yeast cake baked in a ring and drenched in rum syrup, a cousin of the rum baba without its raisins. Because it is baked in a ring mould, the cake comes out with a hollow in the middle, and pastry chefs traditionally fill that well at the table with whipped Chantilly cream, or sometimes with pastry cream or fresh fruit.

The Physiology of Taste was the first book to treat eating and flavour as a serious art, worth studying as carefully as music or science. It is the source of the famous saying that what you eat reveals who you are, and of another line claiming that a new dish does more for human happiness than the discovery of a star.

Brillat-Savarin also had his own explanation for weight gain: after three decades of fighting his own waistline and listening to more than 500 dinner conversations with overweight friends, he blamed starchy, floury foods, bread, flour and sugar, and told heavy people to cut them out. His advice is often called an ancestor of today's low-carbohydrate diets, though it was one man's opinion in 1825, not settled science.

broccoli-kale-and-cabbage-are-the-same-p.context_blurb:
Head cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi sit in separate bins at the grocery store, each with its own name and price. They look like six different vegetables. They are not. Over many centuries farmers took one scruffy wild plant and bred it in different directions, swelling a different part of it each time, and the result fills half the produce aisle.

Botanists count all of them as one and the same species, Brassica oleracea, a single wild plant pushed in different directions by breeding.

The wild ancestor, wild cabbage, still grows on the chalk and limestone cliffs on both sides of the English Channel, including the White Cliffs of Dover, because it shrugs off salt spray and lime but cannot stand being crowded by grass and shrubs. Out on those cliffs it looks nothing like a neat supermarket vegetable, for it is a leggy, scrubby, grey-green weed with loose, fleshy leaves, rather like an overgrown kale. Breeders swelled different parts of that one plant. A Brussels sprout is a giant side bud, and dozens of them grow in rows up a single tall, thick stalk, not one to a plant.

Broccoli and cauliflower are flower heads picked early, so each tiny bead on a broccoli floret is an unopened flower bud, and a cauliflower left in the garden will eventually bloom. The round bulb of kohlrabi is the plant's swollen stem, grown above the ground, not a root, even though its German name means 'cabbage-turnip'.

Because every form is one species, they cross freely: let broccoli and kale flower side by side and bees carry pollen between them, so the seed a gardener saves grows into a mongrel mix that looks like neither parent. Seed savers keep each type far apart, up to a mile, or bag the flowers. The whole family shares a sharp, sulphurous, slightly bitter bite from compounds called glucosinolates, which the plant makes on purpose as a chemical defence, because they taste nasty to the animals that would eat it.

Not every look-alike belongs to the family's single species, for the turnip, like bok choy, is a separate species, Brassica rapa, a close cousin of broccoli but not the same plant. At Cirencester's agricultural college, about 1860, breeders coaxed broccoli and other cabbage forms out of wild cabbage from the coast, and the feat delighted Charles Darwin, who had published On the Origin of Species the year before, because it showed selection reshaping a plant. The family's sharp compounds are also its healthy ones, and in one study steaming kept almost all of them in cabbage, while stir-frying destroyed up to 70 percent and boiling washed them out into the water.

butter-margarine-and-the-fat-wars.context_blurb:
Butter has been churned from cream for thousands of years. Margarine was invented in 1869 as a cheap factory substitute, and for most of the twentieth century the two fought a war over the kitchen table, with health advice switching sides as the science changed. Some battles in that war are settled now; others are still being fought.

In 1869 Napoleon III offered a prize for a cheap butter substitute to feed soldiers and poor families, and the chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès won it. The first margarine contained no plant oil whatsoever, because Mège-Mouriès churned beef fat, called oleo oil, with skimmed milk into a spread he named oleomargarine. Dairy farmers fought back, and some American states forced margarine to be sold colourless or even dyed pink, so that no shopper could mistake it for butter. Wisconsin kept its anti-margarine rules until 1967.

Vegetable oil is liquid at room temperature, so to turn it into a firm stick, factories force hydrogen into the oil, using a metal catalyst under heat and pressure, until its melting point rises and it sets solid. The process is called hydrogenation, and by about 1950 it had replaced beef fat in margarine. Partial hydrogenation, though, bends some fat molecules into a shape almost never found in nature, creating trans fats, and the evidence against them is now firm: by the 1990s studies had linked them clearly to heart disease.

In the 1950s the American scientist Ancel Keys blamed the saturated fat of butter and lard for much of the heart disease in the country, which turned margarine into the doctors' favourite for decades. Several modern reviews have re-examined that evidence and found the link between saturated fat and heart disease weaker than people once thought, and critics argue that Keys picked which countries' data to include; the question is still not fully settled. The irony is that the 'heart-healthy' stick margarines of that era were full of trans fats.

The newest front is seed oils, and for now that dispute is genuinely unsettled. Critics in the Make America Healthy Again movement have branded eight common oils the 'hateful eight', arguing that omega-6 fat drives inflammation. Defenders point to trials in which these oils looked harmless or even helpful, and to the finding that only about 0.2 percent of the omega-6 people eat turns into the compound the critics worry about. Confident claims in either direction deserve a sceptical eye.
