cooking-dried-beans-soak-and-the-hard-bo.context_blurb:
Dried beans are cheaper than canned ones and, many cooks say, tastier, but they ask for more care. A bag of dried beans needs a long soak and a proper boil before it is ready to eat, and with one popular bean, the red kidney bean, skipping that boil can make people genuinely sick.

Dried beans are stored bone-dry and hard. Given hours in a bowl of cold water, they drink the water back in and swell to roughly twice their size, so when they reach the pot the heat can travel to the very centre and cook them evenly, with no chalky core. Most cooks soak beans for at least five hours, often overnight.

The soaking water turns cloudy for a reason. Beans hold a group of sugars called oligosaccharides that humans have no enzyme to digest, so the sugars pass whole into the gut, where bacteria feast on them and make gas. Those gassy sugars dissolve in water and leach out during the soak, so a cook who pours the cloudy water away and cooks the beans in a fresh pot sends much of the gas down the drain.

The red kidney bean, the bean that gives a pot of chili its body, hides something worse than gas. Raw, it carries a natural toxin called phytohaemagglutinin, a kind of lectin, and eating just four or five raw beans can bring on nausea and vomiting within one to three hours, though most people recover quickly. Canned kidney beans carry no such risk, because the cannery has already cooked them under pressure before the can is sealed. They can go straight from the tin onto a cold salad; the danger lies only in dried beans that someone cooks, or undercooks, at home.

Dangerous as it is, the toxin falls apart quickly in real heat: at a hard, rolling boil of 100°C, just ten minutes wipes it out completely. Thirty minutes is the safe, belt-and-braces rule, and a proper boil cuts the beans' toxin from about 70,000 lab units to a few hundred.

Gentle heat is the trap. A slow cooker on its Low setting warms beans to about 80°C, and at that heat the toxin is activated faster than it is destroyed, so the beans can end up roughly five times as toxic as raw ones. Half-cooked kidney beans are worse than raw beans; only a true, hard boil makes them safe.

cooking-made-us-human-the-fire-hypothesi.context_blurb:
Humans are the only animals that cook. The Harvard anthropologist Richard Wrangham argues that cooking made our ancestors human: by unlocking far more energy from the same food, fire paid for a bigger brain. His critics answer that stone tools did much of that work first.

Gym folklore calls raw egg the purest protein. In a 1998 experiment, volunteers swallowed egg protein marked with traceable atoms, and the body absorbed about 91 percent of it from cooked egg but only about half from raw, thanks to denaturation, the heat uncoiling each tightly folded protein. A protein is a string of amino acids, folded into a tight bundle. As an egg white sets at about 60 to 70°C, the heat uncurls that bundle, but the string itself stays whole, with not one link broken. Enzymes can only cut the bonds they can reach, so a cooked protein is an opened parcel, not a broken one.

A wild chimpanzee spends about half its waking day grinding through fruit, leaves and raw meat; a human spends less than an hour chewing. Wrangham argues that cooked food handed those hours back to our ancestors along with a flood of extra calories, and that the extra calories fed the growth of bigger brains. When Victoria Wobber and Wrangham offered captive chimpanzees, which have never used fire, raw or cooked carrot, sweet potato and beef, the chimps chose the cooked version of all three.

When volunteers ate potato, green banana, plantain, oats and wheat both raw and cooked, cooking raised the starch they absorbed by 28 to 109 percent, because heat lets water into the tough, tightly packed starch crystals until they collapse into a loose mush that enzymes digest easily. When Rachel Carmody fed mice meat, sweet potato and peanuts, the mice on raw food lost weight while the mice on cooked food kept theirs. The cooked-meat mice even ate less, about 54 grams over four days against 65.

Katherine Zink and Daniel Lieberman tested the rival idea, that tools came first, by feeding volunteers tough raw goat meat with sensors on their jaw muscles. Unsliced, the meat chewed like gum. Once it was cut with a stone flake and the plants were pounded, with no fire at all, both the effort of every chew and the number of chews in a day dropped by nearly 20 percent.

Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler found that across the primates, body size predicts gut size, since apes living on leaves and rough fruit need a large fermenting gut. By that rule a 65-kilogram primate should carry nearly 1.9 kilograms of gut, yet a human of that weight carries only about 1.1, roughly 60 percent of the prediction. Our oversized brain costs about 9.5 extra watts, but when the pair weighed heart, liver, kidneys, gut and brain together, a 65-kilogram human's total came to about 4.3 kilograms, exactly what any primate of that size carries. The small gut pays for the big brain.

A German team followed 513 raw-food eaters for nearly four years, with supermarkets all around them. Besides heavy weight loss, about 30 percent of the women under 45 stopped having menstrual periods, a sign of a body so short of energy that it shuts down reproduction, and the researchers said the diet could not be recommended for the long term.

The theory's weak point is the fire itself, because Wrangham's timeline needs cooking by roughly 1.8 million years ago, when the teeth shrink and the brain grows. The oldest sure sign of fire kept in one place, wood ash, burnt bone and sediment baked past 300°C in South Africa's Wonderwerk Cave, is about one million years old, some 800,000 years after Wrangham's date. He inferred his date from bones and teeth, not ash, so it remains a hypothesis.

In another mouse trial, Carmody pitted cooking against pounding with a rock: cooking improved a diet of pounded food, but pounding added nothing to a diet that was already cooked. Lieberman still reads the story differently. At Tanzania's Olduvai Gorge, cut-marked bones and stone tools date back 2.6 million years, far older than any ash, and he and Zink argue that slicing and pounding alone could explain our smaller teeth and jaws. In Lieberman's account fire still helped, but it came second, making a meal that stone tools had already made chewable easier still. The two camps are still arguing.

coriander-cumin-and-the-umbel-seed-famil.context_blurb:
Coriander, cumin and caraway are three of the world's great seed spices: tiny ridged seeds that season food from India to Mexico. They are cousins, members of one big plant family, and cooks mix them up all the time. Each has a story, from a soapy-tasting leaf to a name with an insect hidden in it.

Start with a single herb, Coriandrum sativum. Americans call its fresh green leaf cilantro and its dried round seed coriander, but the leaf and the seed grow on the very same plant. British cooks simply call the leaf coriander as well.

The leaf and the seed taste nothing alike. The fresh leaf is bright and lemon-lime, thanks to compounds called aldehydes, while the toasted, crushed seed is warm and nutty with a faint taste of orange, thanks to a compound called linalool. That leafy brightness causes a famous quarrel. To some people cilantro tastes like soap, and it is not fussiness: a smell-receptor gene called OR6A2 is finely tuned to the aldehydes in the leaf, the same family of chemicals found in soaps. The trait runs in families, and it varies by ancestry: about 21 percent of East Asians dislike the leaf, but only 3 to 7 percent of South Asian, Hispanic and Middle Eastern people do.

The ancient Greeks disliked the smell too. Their name for the herb, koriandron, may come from koris, the Greek word for the bedbug, because bruised coriander leaves were thought to give off a fetid, buggy stink.

The family's earthiest member is cumin, Cuminum cyminum, a small, ridged, yellow-brown seed that cooks toast in a dry pan and grind into a warm powder. American chili powder leans on it more than on any other spice, and most curry mixes and Indian garam masala depend on it too. The ancient Egyptians prized it as a spice and used it in mummification, and Indian and Pakistani cooks pair it with coriander seed in a blend called dhana jeera: dhana is coriander, jeera is cumin.

Cumin has a lookalike that fools cooks constantly. Caraway, Carum carvi, has the same small ridged boat shape but a sharper bite, and it is the seed baked into seeded rye bread, its flavour coming mostly from an oil called carvone. The two are so alike that even their names got tangled: caraway's name traces back through Latin cuminum and Greek karon, words that first meant cumin.

All of these seeds are cousins in one big plant family, the Apiaceae, also called umbellifers, and the produce aisle is full of their relatives, because carrots, parsley and celery belong to the same family. The family is named for its flowers. Tiny blossoms sit on spokes that fan out from one point like a little umbrella, a cluster called an umbel, from the Latin umbella, a parasol.

couscous-the-grain-thats-steamed-never-b.context_blurb:
Couscous is a staple of North Africa, from Morocco through Algeria to Tunisia: a heap of tiny golden beads that cooks there traditionally steam rather than boil. It looks exactly like a grain that grew in a field, which is why so many eaters are surprised to learn that every bead was made by hand.

Couscous is really the world's tiniest pasta, wheat flour rolled into little balls and dried, made from the same kind of wheat as dried Italian pasta. That wheat is durum, the hardest wheat grown, whose name is Latin for "hard", the root of the word "durable". Millers grind durum into semolina, a coarse, gritty, golden flour quite unlike soft white bread flour, and every couscous bead is rolled from it.

Making couscous by hand is a skill passed down by watching and copying. The cook dampens the semolina in a wide bowl with a light shower of water. Then she rubs handfuls of the moist flour between her palms, over and over, until it rolls into tiny pellets. She sifts them, sends the bits that are too small back to be rolled again, and keeps going until every bead is even.

The dish is very old. Some of the earliest couscous recipes anyone knows appear in Arabic cookbooks from al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled Spain of the thirteenth century, more than 700 years ago, and they treat it as an ordinary, settled dish. Cooking tools found in older North African tombs hint that couscous may be older still.

cream-transformed-whipped-and-frozen.context_blurb:
A carton of cream is the raw material for some of the world's favourite treats. Whip it and it stands in peaks; churn it in the cold and it becomes ice cream; whip it too far and it turns into something else entirely. Each change depends on the tiny globules of fat in the cream.

Whipped cream is a foam. Beating drives countless tiny air bubbles into the cream, and the fat globules crowd around each bubble and cling together into a soft scaffold that holds its shape. That only works with plenty of fat: whipping cream is 30 to 36 percent milk fat and heavy cream 36 percent or more, while skim milk has almost no fat, so it froths for a moment and collapses.

Keep beating past stiff peaks and the fat globules stop half-joining and clump together completely, so the foam falls apart into pale yellow lumps of butterfat in thin buttermilk: the cook has started making butter by accident.

Ice cream needs different motion. Left alone in the freezer, sweet cream sets into a hard, icy brick. An ice cream maker never stops churning as the mix turns cold, and inside it a blade called the dasher scrapes freezing crystals off the cold wall and breaks them up. The water sets into countless tiny crystals, too small to feel, instead of a few big, gritty ones.

Even in the freezer a tub of ice cream never sets rock solid, because the sugar dissolved in its water drags down the point at which that water freezes. This is called freezing-point depression: at freezer temperature some of the water stays as a thick, unfrozen syrup, and that syrup is what lets a scoop slide through.

Ice cream also holds a hidden ingredient, air, which the factory whips in as the mix freezes, so one gallon of mix can fill two gallons of tubs. Ice cream makers call that extra volume overrun. Cheap brands run near 100 percent overrun, which makes the tub roughly half air, while premium pints hold far less air and more butterfat, so they feel heavier in the hand.

creme-brulee-and-the-custard.context_blurb:
Crème brûlée is a classic French dessert: a chilled, silky custard in a small dish under a thin sheet of hard caramel. Its name means "burnt cream", and eating it begins with a small, satisfying act of destruction that has made it a favourite in bistros everywhere.

The ritual comes first: the diner taps the spoon down to crack the hard, glassy top, and that delicate snap as the crust gives way is the whole point of the dessert. Only one part of crème brûlée is actually burnt, and it is the sugar. Just before serving, the cook scatters sugar over the custard and melts it under the flame of a little torch until it caramelizes into brown glass, while the custard underneath stays pale and smooth.

Before kitchen blowtorches, cooks burnt the sugar with an iron plate on a long handle, heated red-hot in the fire and called a salamander, after the lizard of old legend that people believed could live inside flames unharmed. Beneath the crust, the custard is cream set with egg yolks, sugar and vanilla, heated gently. Modern recipes leave out flour entirely, which keeps the custard silky and trembling instead of firm like a pie filling, and the yolks carry natural emulsifiers that keep the cream and egg from separating.

Eggs are touchy. Custard starts to set at around 70°C and turns grainy past about 80°C. So pastry cooks bake crème brûlée in a water bath, a bain-marie, where the little dishes stand in a pan of hot water that slows the heat and sets the eggs into a smooth gel instead of scrambled curds.

Crème brûlée's cousin, crème caramel or flan, begins with the same custard but finishes the opposite way: the cook pours liquid caramel into the bottom of a plain mould, adds the custard on top, and after baking turns the whole thing out upside down, so the caramel runs down its sides as a soft sauce. The French call it renversée, "turned over". One dessert wears its caramel as a hard lid; the other wears it as a glossy cloak.

croissant-lamination-and-viennoiserie.context_blurb:
The croissant is the flaky crescent of the French breakfast table, but its flakes are built, not born. Tear one open and it peels into dozens of thin, crackly sheets, each made with patience, cold butter and a rolling pin. Its story runs from Vienna to Paris, with a famous legend along the way.

A croissant gets its flakes from lamination: the baker folds cold butter into the dough again and again, building paper-thin layers of dough and butter all the way through, so no special flour is needed. The French pastry mille-feuille wears the trick in its name, which means "a thousand leaves", because a feuille is a leaf or sheet. North Americans call that stack of puff pastry and cream a Napoleon.

Lamination begins with what bakers call the lock-in. The baker seals a single flat block of cold butter inside a sheet of dough, like a parcel, then rolls it out and folds it, so that one block spreads into thinner and thinner sheets with every turn. Each turn is a letter fold, the dough folded in three the way a letter is folded to fit a business envelope, and every fold nearly triples the layers, so a few folds turn one block of butter into dozens of sheets.

Temperature is everything. The butter must stay cool and clay-like, bendable but never soft, so the dough goes back into the fridge between folds. If the butter warms up, it melts into the dough, the separate layers merge, and the croissant bakes up heavy and greasy instead of flaky. Too cold, and the butter shatters into lumps.

The oven does the rest, because butter is not pure fat: it is roughly a sixth water, and in the heat that hidden water turns instantly to steam, which pries the layers of butter and dough apart into airy pockets.

The French call the croissant's family viennoiserie, "things in the style of Vienna": yeast-raised doughs, rich with butter and eggs, that sit between bread and pastry, so a croissant gets a double lift, from yeast and from laminated butter. The name points to where the croissant came from. Its ancestor was the kipferl, a crescent-shaped roll from Austria, which an Austrian officer, August Zang, sold at his Viennese bakery in Paris in the late 1830s before French bakers copied it. The buttery, laminated croissant we know is a French refinement of the early 1900s.

A popular tale claims that Viennese bakers created the croissant in 1683, in the shape of the Ottoman crescent, to mark their city's escape from a Turkish army. Historians call it a legend, spread in the twentieth century by the writer Alfred Gottschalk with no records from the time behind it. The evidence that sinks it is older bread: Vienna's records mention a crescent roll called the chipfen as early as 1227, more than four centuries before the battle it is supposed to celebrate.

cross-contamination-how-outbreaks-actual.context_blurb:
Most big outbreaks of food poisoning do not start with meat that was fully cooked. They start with germs hitching a ride from raw meat to other food, on a board, a knife, a hand, a plate or a sponge. Cooks call that invisible journey cross-contamination, and stopping it is the heart of a safe kitchen.

The danger is easiest to see with a single board: chicken sliced on it is headed for a hot pan, and the heat will kill its germs, but lettuce chopped on the same unwashed board is eaten raw, so nothing ever kills the bacteria it picked up. That is why raw meat and ready-to-eat food should never share a board or a knife. The separation starts in the shop. Raw meat, poultry and seafood leak juices that carry their germs, so the raw meats should go into bags of their own at the checkout, apart from the fruit and lettuce.

Busy restaurant kitchens make the board mistake almost impossible with colour-coded boards, so that every kind of food has its own: red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, green for fruit and vegetables, blue for raw fish, white for dairy. At home, one board can be made safe again in two steps. Hot soapy water washes off the visible scraps, and then a diluted bleach solution, about a tablespoon of unscented bleach to a gallon of water, left a few minutes and rinsed off, kills the germs that washing leaves behind.

The fridge has rules too, and gravity writes them. Juices drip downward, so raw meat goes in a sealed dish on a lower shelf, beneath anything eaten as it is, like salad or cut melon. Professional cooks go further and rank their raw meats by how hot each must be cooked, with ready-to-eat food on top and raw chicken and turkey on the very bottom shelf, because poultry needs the highest cooking temperature of all, so any drip from above lands on food that will get even hotter.

The same thinking applies at the grill, where a platter that carried raw burger patties is coated in their juices, so the cooked burgers go back inside on a fresh, clean platter, never on the one that held them raw. A marinade that has soaked raw chicken is full of raw-meat bacteria too, so before it can be brushed on as a sauce it must be boiled hard for a few minutes; the other safe choice is to set some aside before it ever touches the meat.

The worst offender may be the humble sponge. In 2017 scientists at Germany's Furtwangen University examined used dish sponges and found 362 kinds of bacteria living in them, as many as 54 billion cells crammed into each cubic centimetre, a density to rival human waste, because a sponge is damp, warm and full of food scraps. Worse, the sponges their owners cleaned regularly held no fewer bacteria than sponges nobody ever cleaned, and the cleaning may even have left tougher germs behind. The surest fix is simply to replace a sponge about once a week, since wiping counters with an old one only smears germs around.

crustaceans-on-the-plate-shrimp-crab-lob.context_blurb:
Shrimp, crabs and lobsters are crustaceans, armoured sea creatures that look nothing like fish. Cooks crack, peel and clean them, and diners pay high prices for their sweet meat, yet lobster was once so cheap that New Englanders had no use for most of it. Their strange bodies explain both how we eat them and why they spoil so fast.

A crustacean wears its skeleton on the outside: the hard shell a diner cracks open is the animal's whole frame, armour and skeleton at once, with no bones inside, which is why eating one means cracking and peeling to reach the muscle. The dark line that recipes tell you to pull from a shrimp's back is no vein at all, because it is the shrimp's gut, the tube that carries its waste out. Cooks remove it because it can taste gritty and a little bitter, not because it is dangerous, since cooking kills any bacteria in it.

Prawns, crayfish, shrimp, lobsters and crabs all belong to the decapods, Greek for "ten feet" after their ten walking legs, and of the nearly 15,000 decapod species, crabs alone make up almost half.

A lobster in danger escapes with a tail-flip: it clenches the muscles on the underside of its body, snaps its fan-shaped tail down and under, and shoots backward through the water, away from a seal or an octopus. That hard-working escape muscle is exactly the firm, sweet tail meat that diners prize.

Lobster was not always a luxury. In colonial New England, early accounts say, storms heaped lobsters on the beaches up to two feet deep, and people scorned them as food for servants, apprentices and children and used them as bait. Farmers even spread the surplus lobsters over their fields to fertilize the crops. Because lobster rots quickly, it could not be shipped beyond the coast, so it stayed cheap for about two centuries. The change came on rails: in the mid-1800s railroads, along with canning, carried lobster far inland, and by the 1880s it had become a fashionable dish for wealthy diners in Boston and New York, with prices to match.

A favourite tale holds that jailed colonists got lobster at so many meals that they revolted. When the food historian Sandy Oliver went looking, she found no colonial account of prisoners eating lobster at all, and the tale itself only turns up in the 1900s. The earliest version of the complaint she could find, from the 1800s, was about salmon, not lobster.

Crustaceans are sold alive in tanks, or with their heads on and packed in ice, for a reason: the moment one dies, powerful digestive enzymes stored in a gland called the hepatopancreas leak out and start digesting the animal's own muscle, a process called autolysis, turning firm, sweet meat mushy within minutes. Fast-growing bacteria speed the spoiling, so the animal is best kept alive until it is cooked.

curing-salt-as-a-preservation-machine.context_blurb:
Long before refrigerators, a farm family that slaughtered a pig in late autumn had to make the meat last through winter and spring. Salt was the answer. Curing slows the microbes that rot meat, and it changes the meat's texture, colour and flavour too, which is why we still cure ham, bacon and prosciutto today.

For most of history, packing meat in salt was the main way to keep it from rotting, and salt-curing stayed the chief method until mechanical refrigeration replaced it in the late 1800s. Sailors lived on salted meat. On voyages lasting months, crews, most famously those of Britain's Royal Navy, ate salt beef and salt pork from wooden barrels along with rock-hard ship's biscuit. The Finnish tall ship Moshulu was still serving it in 1938, on grain voyages from Australia that took more than three months. Corned beef, the salty pink beef of Saint Patrick's Day, has nothing to do with maize, because in older English a "corn" was any small grain or pellet, and the corns that named the dish were the coarse grains of salt rubbed into the meat.

Salt is not a poison to bacteria, so how does it protect meat? It works by osmosis: heavy salt pulls water out of the meat and out of every microbe cell, so the bacteria dry up and cannot grow, starved of water rather than poisoned. A salt level near 20 percent reliably stops spoilage bacteria. One killer shrugs off ordinary salt, Clostridium botulinum, which can thrive in the airless heart of a sausage or ham and makes the toxin behind botulism, so curers add a pinch of a second salt, nitrite, which blocks it. In the past, nitrite came from saltpeter, potassium nitrate, which bacteria in the cure turn into nitrite.

The disease is named for the food. In the 1800s the German doctor Justinus Kerner studied outbreaks of a deadly poisoning that numbed its victims and then stopped them swallowing and breathing. He named it botulism from botulus, the Latin word for sausage, because badly preserved sausages and hams were behind the outbreaks. Too much nitrite is itself poisonous, so curers buy it already diluted, as pink curing salt, only about 6 percent sodium nitrite mixed into ordinary salt, and the makers dye it bright pink so that no cook ever mistakes it for table salt. Nitrite does a second job, too. It releases nitric oxide, which binds to the meat's own red pigment, myoglobin, and cooking sets that pigment into a stable pink, so ham, hot dogs and bacon stay pink after cooking while a beef roast turns grey-brown.

Prosciutto di Parma, the silky raw ham of the hills around Parma, is never cooked at all: it is made with nothing but sea salt and time, hanging in cool air for at least 14 months and up to three years, until salt and slow drying pull the water so low that nothing can grow. Its rules even forbid nitrite. Before a ham may carry the five-pointed Ducal Crown of Parma, an inspector pierces it in several places with a slim needle carved from horse bone and sniffs the needle for any trace of hidden rot. Hams that fail are sold as ordinary ham.

curry-is-a-british-word-and-curry-powder.context_blurb:
India has no dish called curry. The word is an English catch-all, stretched by British visitors over hundreds of very different regional dishes, and the yellow curry powder of Western pantries is a British invention that a traditional Indian kitchen never needed.

English speakers arriving in the 1600s borrowed kari, a word from Tamil, the language of southern India, where it meant one kind of dish: a spiced sauce or relish of meat, fish or vegetables, eaten over boiled rice. British colonizers stretched it into "curry", a label for almost anything spiced.

Curry powder was a shortcut, created so British households could fake Indian flavours from a single tin without fresh whole spices. In 1784 the first curry powder sold in shops was advertised in London, not by a grocer but by Sorlie's Perfumery Warehouse on Piccadilly, a perfumer's shop.

Indian cooks dry-toast whole seeds in a hot pan and pound them in a mortar just before cooking, because spices lose their flavour once they are ground and left to sit. They keep separate blends for separate dishes, such as rasam or pav bhaji, instead of one jar for everything. Even garam masala, Hindi for "warm spice mix", carries no chili fire, because the warmth in its name comes from the old Ayurvedic idea that spices such as cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and pepper warm the body from within.

dal-why-lentils-rice-is-a-nutritional-po.context_blurb:
Dal, spiced lentils ladled over rice, is an everyday meal across India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal. It is cheap, quick and comforting, and it is also a small feat of nutrition, because lentils and rice each fill gaps that the other leaves.

In Nepal the plate is called dal bhat, dal for the lentil stew and bhat for the steamed rice, and it is the national dish, eaten by many families at least once a day. Himalayan porters, who haul heavy loads up mountain trails, cheer on tired hikers with a rhyming chant that promises dal bhat power around the clock.

Dal is the word for dried pulses that have been split in half, such as red lentils, split peas and split chickpeas, and splitting each one down the middle lays its soft inside bare, so dal cooks through in under an hour with no overnight soak. The word itself comes from a Sanskrit root meaning "to split". In a country where vast numbers of people eat almost no meat, dal is how they stay well fed, because pulses are India's cheapest plant source of protein. Moong dal carries about 24 grams of protein in every 100 grams, and India grows more pulses than any other country.

Rice and lentils each lack a different piece of the protein puzzle: pulses are rich in the amino acid lysine but low in methionine, while rice is the mirror image, so eaten together each supplies what the other is missing and the plate delivers every essential amino acid. The same grain-and-legume pairing turns up worldwide, in beans with tortillas and hummus with pita.

Plain dal tastes flat, so the cook finishes it with a flourish called tadka. Whole spices such as cumin and mustard seeds, dried chillies and a pinch of asafoetida sizzle in hot ghee until fragrant, and the crackling fat goes over the dal just before it is served. Most spice aromas dissolve in fat rather than water, so blooming them in ghee pulls out far more flavour than the watery dal ever could.

Lentils, like all seeds, store phytic acid to lock up minerals for a future plant, and in the gut it grabs iron and zinc and keeps the body from absorbing them. Letting the lentils sprout for a day or two before cooking brings the seed to life and breaks down much of its phytic acid, about 60 percent, so far more iron and zinc reach the body.

dashi-and-the-discovery-of-umami.context_blurb:
Dashi is the clear golden broth under miso soup, noodle bowls and simmered dishes, the quiet foundation of Japanese cooking. It takes only two ingredients and a few minutes, yet in 1908 it led a Tokyo chemist to a taste that science had missed.

Dashi needs just two things: kombu, a broad dried kelp from Japan's cold northern coasts, warmed gently in water, and shavings of dried bonito fish. It is prized less for its own flavour than for the way it lifts every other ingredient. A spoonful tastes deeply savoury, yet not sweet, sour, salty or bitter, and that savouriness is umami, now counted as the fifth basic taste beside the other four. The kelp carries the taste in one compound, glutamate, an amino acid, one of the building blocks of protein. In 2000, researchers at the University of Miami found the tongue's own umami receptor, proof that umami is a true basic taste with a sensor of its own.

The man who named it was Kikunae Ikeda, a chemist at Tokyo Imperial University. In 1908 he noticed the savoury depth of his wife's kombu soup, pulled brown crystals of glutamate out of a batch of kombu broth, and named the taste. He built "umami" from mi, "taste", and umai, the ordinary Japanese word for delicious, so the name means roughly "delicious taste". Ikeda did not invent the taste; he gave a name to something that had always been there.

The same glutamate fills foods far from Japan, above all the tomato, a fruit that grows on a vine: a fully ripe tomato holds about ten times the free glutamate of a green one, which is why it turns more savoury as it ripens. Ikeda believed our love of umami is a built-in protein detector, because glutamate is itself a building block of protein, so a food rich in it usually carries protein too, just as sweetness flags sugar.

Each half of dashi tastes mild on its own, yet together they taste powerfully savoury, because the bonito brings a second umami molecule, inosinate, and glutamate and inosinate multiply each other's strength instead of simply adding up. Ikeda's student Shintaro Kodama found inosinate in dried bonito in 1913.

After weeks of smoking and months of curing with mould in the sun, that bonito becomes katsuobushi, a block as hard as wood; Guinness lists it as the hardest food on Earth. To use it, the cook shaves the block into curls as thin as paper with a blade set in a box, the way a carpenter planes a board. In 1909 Ikeda patented a way to make glutamate in bulk as a white powder, monosodium glutamate, or MSG, and it is the very same glutamate found in kombu, tomatoes, parmesan and cured ham, simply isolated as a salt. Its bad name traces back to a single 1968 letter blaming headaches on Chinese restaurant food, and controlled studies never confirmed the scare.

deep-frying-why-hot-oil-cooks-dry-not-gr.context_blurb:
Deep-frying looks like the greasiest way to cook, yet a good fryer turns out food that is crisp and barely oily. The secret is a battle at the food's surface between hot oil and the water inside the food, and the cook who understands that battle never serves a soggy, oil-logged fry.

The first rule is heat: food dropped into oil hot enough, about 177 to 191°C, comes out crisp and barely greasy, while the same food in oil that is too cool comes out pale, soggy and soaked. Hotter oil means less grease, not more.

The roar of bubbles when raw potato hits the oil is not the oil boiling, because frying oil sits at roughly twice the boiling point of water, so the water just under the food's surface flashes into steam the instant it goes in and blasts outward. That bubbling doubles as a timer: as the food fries, its water runs out, the storm of bubbles calms to a few big, slow ones, and a cook who sees that quieting knows the fritters or fries are nearly done.

The escaping steam does a second job, because its outward rush pushes the oil back and keeps it from soaking in, which is why food that sits in oil the whole time can still come out dry. The shield only works while the food stays hot enough to steam hard; let the oil cool and the steam weakens, the shield fails, and the oil creeps in.

While the surface is wet, the evaporating water pins it at about 100°C, too cool to brown. As soon as the outer layer has dried, the surface temperature shoots up toward the heat of the oil, and only then does the crust brown and turn golden, through the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars, while the inside stays moist.

Most of the oil in fried food actually gets in after the frying is over. As a fry cools, the steam inside it condenses back into water, and the shrinking vapour sucks the oil clinging to its surface in through the pores. In one study of tortilla chips, only about a fifth of the final oil entered during frying, and about two-thirds came in during cooling, which is why fries are best eaten at once, after a quick drain on paper towels.

dont-crowd-the-pan-brown-vs-steam.context_blurb:
A golden crust on seared meat or sautéed mushrooms depends on one rule that busy cooks love to break: give the food room. A crowded pan does not save time. It turns a sear into a steam bath and leaves the food pale and sad.

Pile a whole basket of mushrooms into one skillet and they come out grey, pale and limp instead of brown and crisp, because the food is stewing rather than searing. The puddle that collects around them came out of the mushrooms themselves: heat drives their own water out, and in a packed pan that water has nowhere to escape, so the food cooks in a cloud of its own moisture.

The physics sets a hard limit: while liquid water is present and boiling, the food's surface cannot rise above 100°C, water's boiling point, because the incoming heat goes into turning that water to steam instead of heating the food. Browning, the Maillard reaction, only really takes off around 150°C, so a wet, crowded pan is stuck far below it however high the burner goes.

That is why restaurant cooks pat a steak dry with paper towels before it touches the hot pan, since removing the surface water lets the meat climb straight past the boiling point and start browning in the first minute instead of wasting the pan's heat on boiling off moisture.

For a big beef stew, a patient cook sears the cubes a few at a time and browns every batch before any broth goes in, because that browning cooks a deep, savoury flavour into the meat that the whole stew depends on. Crowd the pot with all the cubes at once and they turn grey and steam, and that flavour never forms.

dont-rinse-raw-chicken.context_blurb:
Many home cooks rinse raw chicken under the tap before cooking it, because it feels clean and careful. Food-safety scientists now ask them to stop, because the habit spreads germs around the kitchen and removes almost none from the bird.

The advice from the United States Department of Agriculture is simple: do not wash raw chicken at all, but put it straight into the pan and cook it as it is. In 2019 the agency ran a whole public campaign, "Washing Raw Poultry: Our Science, Your Choice", to break the old habit.

When water from the tap strikes soft raw meat, it flings a fine mist of droplets loaded with bacteria such as salmonella and campylobacter, and that spray lands on counters, hands, clothes and any salad sitting nearby, as far as two or three feet around the sink. Scientists call the effect aerosolization.

Rinsing also fails at its own goal, because bacteria cling fast to the surface of the meat, so even when the water runs clear almost none of them has washed away. Rinsing, soaking or brining in vinegar, lemon juice or salt water does not destroy bacteria; only cooking the chicken to 74°C inside kills them. For a crisper sear, pat the chicken dry with a paper towel instead, which helps the crust without splashing germs, though it does not clean the meat.

dried-pasta-and-its-sicilian-arab-roots.context_blurb:
Dried pasta is one of the great preserving inventions: strands of dough that keep for a year on a shelf. Many people believe Marco Polo brought it to Italy from China, but that is a myth. The story of dried pasta runs through Arab Sicily, and its secret lies in a very hard wheat.

Boxed dry pasta, pasta secca, is only semolina and water, while fresh pasta adds egg, which makes it richer but brings moisture and spoils fast, so fresh egg pasta must be eaten within days and the eggless dried strands keep for months. The semolina is coarsely milled durum wheat, and its warm golden colour comes from carotenoid pigments that grow naturally in the durum grain, the same family of pigments that colours carrots, so no egg or dye is needed.

Durum is Latin for "hard", and durum is the hardest wheat of all and richer in protein than bread wheat, and that protein forms a strong, stretchy web of gluten that traps the starch and holds each strand together in boiling water. That is what keeps good spaghetti al dente, "to the tooth", instead of collapsing into mush.

The oldest record of a dried-pasta trade comes from Sicily, where in 1154 the Arab geographer al-Idrisi, writing for the island's Norman king Roger II, described huge buildings at Trabia turning out dried pasta in shiploads and sending it to Calabria and to Muslim and Christian lands. The strands even kept an Arabic name, itriyya. That was about 140 years before Marco Polo came home to Venice.

The Marco Polo myth was invented as advertising: in 1929 The Macaroni Journal, the magazine of American pasta makers, printed a tale about one of Marco Polo's sailors, conveniently named Spaghetti, who watched a Chinese woman roll out noodles and copied her. Marco Polo's own writings show he already knew pasta when he saw it in China.

Today the town of Gragnano, near Naples, makes some of the most prized dried pasta, and its protected-origin rules allow only bronze dies, the moulds the dough is pressed through to shape each strand. Bronze leaves the surface of the pasta slightly rough and chalky, unlike the slick dies of most modern factories, and that rough surface is what lets sauce grip instead of sliding off.

dry-heat-vs-wet-heat-matching-the-method.context_blurb:
Every cut of meat comes with a cooking method built in. Tender cuts want fast, dry heat, like grilling, searing and roasting. Tough cuts want slow, wet heat, like braising and stewing. Choose wrong and you ruin an expensive steak or waste a cheap cut that could have been glorious, and the reason lies in how hard each muscle worked.

The tenderloin, which runs along the spine, is the softest cut on the animal because that muscle barely moves while the animal is alive, so its fibres stay thin and soft, while hard-working muscles like the shoulder and legs grow thick and tough. Hard-working cuts such as beef shank, brisket and chuck are also packed with collagen, the connective tissue that makes meat chewy, while a lean, idle cut like the tenderloin has very little of it.

So a chuck roast from the shoulder needs to be braised, simmered gently in liquid, covered, for hours, until its collagen melts and the cheap cut turns fall-apart tender. Throw a raw brisket on a blazing grill for a few minutes a side, the way you would a rib-eye, and it comes out tougher, drier and chewier than ever, because fast, dry heat gives the collagen neither the time nor the moisture to melt while the meat fibres dry out.

The mistake works the other way too: a filet mignon braised for hours has almost no collagen to melt and very little fat, so the long simmer has nothing to soften and simply leaves a dried-out steak, grey and dull. A tender cut wants seconds of fierce heat, not hours in liquid. Braises and stews are close cousins. A braise is one big piece of meat, like a pot roast, sitting only partly in its liquid in a covered pot. In a stew, small, even chunks of meat lie completely under the liquid.

Neither one browns in the pot, because water cannot climb much past its boiling point of 100°C, while the Maillard browning that gives meat its deep crust only really takes off at around 140 to 150°C. So a cook who wants both a crust and tenderness browns the raw meat first in a very hot, dry pan and only then adds the wine and stock for the long simmer, since once the meat is wet it can never get hot enough to brown.

foods-that-take-years-time-as-the-ingred.context_blurb:
Some of the world's most prized foods have a secret ingredient that no shop sells: time. A few cheap raw materials, grape juice, milk, a leg of pork, are left to wait for months or years, and the waiting turns them into foods worth a fortune. Three Mediterranean classics show how it works.

In Modena, in northern Italy, makers of traditional balsamic vinegar leave cooked grape syrup to mature for a dozen years or more, passing it along a row of little barrels made of cherry, chestnut and oak until it turns thick, dark and sweet-sour. It is so precious that a cook spends it a drop at a time, over strawberries or ice cream. The oldest grade, extravecchio, waits 25 years or more. Real balsamic never begins as wine: the fresh juice of white Trebbiano grapes is first boiled down into a thick syrup called mosto cotto, cooked must, and nothing else is ever added, so the dark colour and deep flavour come from the barrels and the years. A cheap supermarket "balsamic vinegar of Modena" may reach the shelf only two months after it is made, bulked out with wine vinegar and often darkened with caramel colouring to look as glossy as the real thing.

Parmigiano-Reggiano, the hard, pale-gold grating cheese from the country around Parma and Reggio Emilia, must age at least twelve months before it may carry its name, and the best wheels wait two or three years; each 38-kilogram wheel takes about 550 litres of milk. The tiny white crystals that crunch in a well-aged wedge are tyrosine, an amino acid set free as the cheese's proteins slowly break down, so they are a trusted sign that a wheel has truly matured.

Spain's most prized ham, jamón ibérico, comes from black Iberian pigs and is never cooked: the legs are packed in salt for about two weeks, then hung to dry for one to four years, until salt, air and time alone have cured them for carving into slices thin enough to see light through. The finest grade, jamón ibérico de bellota, comes from pigs turned loose in the autumn season called the montanera to roam the oak forests and fatten on fallen acorns, about five kilograms a day; bellota is Spanish for acorn.

Nothing is added to any of these foods to make them taste so deep. During the long wait, natural enzymes slowly chop large, fairly bland molecules such as proteins and starches into small, intensely flavoured ones, like the savoury amino acids in cured ham and the crunchy tyrosine in old cheese.

durian-the-fruit-banned-from-trains-and-.context_blurb:
The durian is a spiky, football-sized fruit of Southeast Asia's rainforests, from Borneo and Sumatra to the Malay Peninsula, with soft, creamy flesh inside a thorny husk. Millions of people in Southeast Asia adore it, and many more cannot stand to be in the same room with it. It is banned from trains, planes and hotels, all for the same reason.

Since 1988, Singapore's underground trains have banned durian, which has its own picture on the no-entry signs, because its overpowering smell lingers in the closed, air-conditioned cars long after the fruit has gone. It is the only item on those signs with no fine printed beside it, just a red slash. Across Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand its fans adore it so much that they call it the king of fruits. It is often confused with the jackfruit, a milder green cousin and the largest fruit that grows on any tree, up to about 35 kilograms, its skin knobbly with blunt bumps rather than thorns, and smelling sweetly of mango and pineapple.

The durian's stink is not rot: the ripe fruit makes it on purpose, from compounds built around sulfur, the same chemical family behind the smells of onion, garlic and rotten eggs. In 2017 the cancer researcher Bin Tean Teh and his team read the durian's genes and found a set that switches on hard as the fruit ripens to pump out those sulfur compounds. One April day in 2018, some 500 people at a university library in Melbourne were evacuated over a suspected gas leak, and firefighters in hazmat suits traced the smell to a rotting durian in a cupboard, its odour spread through the building by the air conditioning.

Yet the taste stuns those who get past the nose: in 1856 the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace described durian flesh as a rich, sweet custard strongly flavoured with almonds and said it was worth a voyage to the East. Biologists think the far-reaching smell, which can carry over a kilometre on a still night, evolved to call in animals such as orangutans, elephants, tigers and wild boars, which eat the soft flesh and carry the big seeds away to sprout somewhere new.

The smell is made of tiny, volatile molecules that evaporate into the air and seep out through any gap, even from fruit wrapped in plastic and sealed in a cooler, and then hang in closed, air-conditioned spaces. That is why budget airlines such as Scoot and AirAsia ban durian outright and many Southeast Asian hotels forbid it.

Village elders across the region warn that eating durian with beer or whiskey can kill, but no such death has ever been confirmed in scientific journals, so the warning remains a folk belief. There is a grain of chemistry behind it: a University of Tsukuba study found that durian can block an enzyme the body uses to clear alcohol, which could cause a nasty, hangover-like reaction.

e-coli-burgers-greens-and-the-outbreak-t.context_blurb:
E. coli O157:H7 is a germ that lives in cattle and can kill. It makes a poison called Shiga toxin, the leading cause of sudden kidney failure in American children under five. In the early 1990s it killed four children who had eaten undercooked hamburgers, and the outbreak changed how every American kitchen cooks a burger.

The only thing that makes a burger safe is heat: the patty must cook right through, until even its middle is steaming hot, at least 71°C, so the inside of a burger should never stay pink. Cold never kills the germ, which survives both the fridge and the freezer.

Beef is not the only danger. Leafy greens such as romaine, spinach and sprouts rival ground beef as a source of E. coli O157, and because a salad goes from the field to the bowl raw, with nothing ever hot enough to kill the germ, a bowl of greens can carry more risk than a fully cooked burger. Many leafy-green farms sit near cattle feedlots, and runoff tainted with manure seeps into the canals and wells that water the crops, so when that irrigation water is sprayed over the fields, it lands the germ straight onto leaves headed for a salad. Even raw cookie dough with no egg in it is risky, because flour is a raw farm product: the grain picks up E. coli in the field, and grinding and bleaching do not kill it, so only baking makes the dough safe.

The outbreak that changed the rules came from Jack in the Box, the fast-food chain, in 1992 and 1993: its undercooked burgers sickened 732 people in California, Washington, Idaho and Nevada and killed four young children. Afterward, kitchens lived by a split rule, steak rare if you like, but burgers well done, even when both come from the same cow. A whole steak carries its germs only on the outside, where a hot pan sears them away in seconds, but the grinder chops up those dirty outer surfaces and folds them all through the meat, so E. coli that was once skin-deep ends up in the middle of every patty. That is why in 1994 the American government declared O157:H7 illegal in raw ground beef, and why the 71°C rule targets burgers, not steaks.

eat-food-mostly-plants-the-whole-food-id.context_blurb:
Michael Pollan is an American journalist who spent years tracing where food really comes from, through cornfields, cattle feedlots and the factories where snacks are designed. His books argue that people eat best by choosing real, whole food over products engineered in laboratories, and he packed that whole argument into a rule short enough to remember for life.

In Defense of Food, Pollan's 2008 book, begins with a seven-word rule in three short parts: eat real food, don't eat too much of it, and let most of it be plants. He calls it his whole philosophy of eating, and he says the trick hides in the first part, because by "food" he means real, whole food, not the engineered products that fill the middle aisles. Pollan calls those products "edible foodlike substances": things made by food science to look like yogurt or cereal that are, in his words, no longer the products of nature.

His rules for the shop are easy to use. Imagine your great-grandmother pushing the cart beside you, Pollan says, and buy nothing she would not recognise as food, since she never cooked with guar gum, carrageenan or soy lecithin. He also warns shoppers to be most suspicious of a package that boasts about its health benefits, because in his view a health claim on the box is a good sign the product is not really food, while the fresh vegetables, which make no claims, sit silent.

Pollan borrowed the word nutritionism from the sociologist Gyorgy Scrinis to name the habit of judging food by its separate nutrients, fat-free or vitamin-added, instead of as a whole food, which Pollan argues is more than the sum of its parts. It is a way of thinking about eating rather than a proven laboratory result. His book opens with a paradox: for decades Americans followed nutrition science more closely than ever, counting fats and chasing vitamins, and yet, Pollan argues, their health got worse instead of better. Some agricultural scientists have pushed back on parts of his case.

An orange shows the idea at work: a whole orange and a glass of its juice hold about the same sugar, but the whole fruit also keeps about three grams of fibre, pectin locked in its cell walls, which slows the sugar down and fills you up. That is why one orange is plenty while the juice of four goes down in seconds. Without that fibre the juice spikes blood sugar far faster, close to a cola.

eating-for-energy-vs-growth-vs-recovery.context_blurb:
A runner training for a marathon, a teenager in a growth spurt and an athlete recovering from a hard workout all need different things from food. Carbohydrates, protein and fats each do a different job in the body, and the right mix depends on what the body is being asked to do.

Muscles draw on two main fuels, shifting between them as the work gets harder. Body fat is the steady, all-day fuel, burned most at rest and during easy effort, and even a lean runner carries many hours of it in reserve. As the effort climbs, carbohydrate takes over: above about 60 percent of top effort it supplies more than half the energy, and an all-out sprint runs almost entirely on it.

That fast fuel is stored carbohydrate, called glycogen, packed into the muscles and liver, and an untrained runner holds less than two hours' worth, so around mile 20 of a marathon the tank can run dry and the legs turn to concrete, the moment runners call hitting the wall. To push the wall back, marathoners carb-load for days before a race. Every gram of glycogen the muscles store holds about three grams of water with it, so the extra kilogram or two on the scale on race morning is almost all water, not fat.

Growing bodies have other needs: during a growth spurt, teenagers need about 1,300 milligrams of calcium a day, roughly four cups of milk, and they need vitamin D alongside it, because without vitamin D the body cannot absorb that calcium or lock it into bone. The teen years are the biggest window of life for building bone.

After a hard workout, a recovery snack such as chocolate milk pairs protein, which repairs the muscle fibres the exercise damaged, with carbohydrate, which refills the glycogen the muscles burned so they are fuelled for next time. Eating fairly soon helps, though the famous thirty-minute window is mostly gym lore, since the real window spans hours.

A nutritionist feeding a marathoner, a growing teenager and a desk worker can serve similar foods to all three and change mainly the balance between carbohydrate and protein. The runner tips toward carbohydrate to fill the fuel tank, the growing teen needs extra protein and calories to build tissue, and the desk worker, who burns little glycogen, needs fewer carbohydrates.

emulsion-and-hollandaise.context_blurb:
Hollandaise is the warm, silky, golden sauce of French cooking, and one of the most famous sauces to go wrong. It is made of fat and a sour, watery liquid that do not want to stay together, so the whole art of the sauce lies in keeping the peace between them.

Shake oil and vinegar in a jar and the dressing looks smooth for a minute, then splits back into layers, because oil and water refuse to blend: vinegar is mostly water, and fat and water simply will not stay combined on their own. Shaking only makes a short-lived emulsion, a mixture of tiny droplets of one liquid suspended in another.

The best-known home of hollandaise is eggs Benedict, the brunch dish of a poached egg and Canadian bacon on a toasted English muffin, finished with the warm, golden hollandaise made from egg yolk, melted butter and lemon. What holds it together is the egg yolk, the emulsifier: its lecithin molecules have one end that grabs water and one end that grabs oil, so they wrap around each droplet of fat and keep the droplets from merging again.

The name means "Dutch sauce", yet the sauce is French, and an older name, sauce Isigny, honours Isigny in Normandy, a town famous across France for its butter, the main fat of the sauce. Hollandaise also has a cold cousin in almost every fridge: mayonnaise, the same trick of egg yolk, fat and acid held together by lecithin, made with oil instead of melted butter.

The usual way to ruin a hollandaise is heat: egg-yolk proteins thicken and then clump solid at about 65 to 70°C, and once they seize they can no longer hold the fat, so the sauce breaks into a greasy, grainy puddle. Pouring in the butter too fast can break it too, because each yolk can only coat so much fat at a time. A good cook rescues a broken sauce by putting a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl and whisking the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time, so that the new yolk's lecithin gathers up the loose fat and pulls the sauce back together.

Swap the lemon for a sharp reduction of tarragon, shallot and wine vinegar and the same yolk-and-butter emulsion becomes béarnaise, the classic sauce for a grilled steak. Legend says it was first served around 1836 at a restaurant near Paris in the former home of King Henri IV, who was born in the province of Béarn, so the sauce is named for the king's homeland.

Beurre blanc, "white butter", proves that the yolk is not the only way: it binds butter into a reduction of white wine and shallots with no egg at all, held together by the butter's own milk solids and hard whisking off the heat. Legend says the cook Clémence Lefeuvre invented it by accident near Nantes around 1900, when she set out to make béarnaise and forgot the egg yolks.

emulsions-fat-and-water-made-to-hold-han.context_blurb:
Oil and water are the odd couple of the kitchen. They refuse to mix, yet many of cooking's best sauces, from mayonnaise to hollandaise to a good salad dressing, are made of both. The trick is an emulsion: one liquid shattered into tiny droplets and held inside the other, with a little help from a go-between.

Stir oil into a glass of water as hard as you like and it breaks into a cloud of droplets, but a few seconds after the spoon stops, the oil has risen back into a layer on top, because oil is lighter than water, about 0.9 grams per millilitre against water's 1.0. A vinaigrette, classically three parts oil to one part vinegar, behaves the same way: shaken hard it looks blended, but it is only a temporary emulsion, and within a minute it has split again, the oil floating over the vinegar. That is why cooks shake it again just before pouring.

To make the two stay together, a cook needs an emulsifier. An emulsifier molecule has two faces, because one end grips water and the other grips oil, so it buries its oily end in a tiny droplet of oil while its watery end sticks out, wrapping each droplet in a coat that stops it from joining its neighbours. In mayonnaise the emulsifier is the egg yolk, rich in a natural emulsifier called lecithin, which holds the oil and the vinegar together for weeks in the jar. For a salad dressing, a spoonful of mustard does the same job: emulsifying chemicals in the coating of the mustard seed wrap the droplets and slow their merging, so the dressing holds together and coats the salad.

A single yolk can only coat so much oil at a time, so the oil must go in as a thin, slow trickle while the cook whisks, letting the yolk keep up with every drop; tip it in all at once and the oil floats free and the sauce never forms. Finished mayonnaise is about 80 percent oil, yet the oil is the part broken into droplets, and the small amount of watery vinegar and yolk forms the continuous background that holds them, an arrangement chemists call an oil-in-water emulsion. According to the food writer Harold McGee, beating a single tablespoon of oil into mayonnaise can shatter it into about 30 billion droplets.

Hollandaise is the warm member of the family: butter, lemon and egg yolk whisked over gentle heat into the golden sauce of eggs Benedict, and one of the five mother sauces of French cooking.

When an emulsion breaks, as when mayonnaise suddenly turns thin and greasy, its droplets have bumped into each other and merged into bigger and bigger blobs, a process called coalescence, until the oil and water separate. Pouring the oil too fast causes it, and in a warm egg-and-butter sauce so does too much heat. A broken sauce can usually be saved: the cook puts a fresh egg yolk, or even half a teaspoon of water, in a clean bowl and whisks the broken sauce into it a few drops at a time, giving the loose fat a fresh coat of emulsifier. Only a sauce whose eggs have curdled from heat is beyond rescue and must be started again.

emulsions-making-oil-and-water-get-along.context_blurb:
Mayonnaise is a small miracle in a jar: a thick, creamy spread made mostly from a liquid that should never stay mixed with the rest. Its oil and its vinegar or lemon juice refuse to blend on their own, and one ingredient in the recipe makes peace between them.

Whisk oil and vinegar together, three parts to one, and the dressing turns cloudy for a moment, but leave it a few minutes and it has separated into two layers again, because oil and water are immiscible: they refuse to stay mixed. A sauce that does stay blended, like mayonnaise, is called an emulsion.

The surprise is how much oil a jar holds: mayonnaise is about 80 percent oil by weight, with only about 7 or 8 percent water and about 6 percent egg yolk, the oil smashed into microscopic droplets floating in that little bit of water. The egg yolk does the holding, because it is packed with lecithin, molecules with one end that loves water and one end that loves oil, so each wraps an oil droplet and keeps the droplets from rejoining. No yolk, no mayonnaise, and the same yolk trick powers hollandaise and Caesar dressing.

Mayonnaise most often fails when the cook rushes the oil. The yolk cannot wrap each new droplet in time, so the loose oil clumps back together and the sauce breaks into a greasy, separated slick. The cure is to whisk the broken sauce slowly into a fresh yolk in a clean bowl until it thickens again.

A plain vinaigrette needs help too, and mustard gives it, because a spoonful of mustard acts as an emulsifier, binding oil and vinegar so the dressing separates far more slowly. Emulsions hide all over the kitchen: milk and cream are droplets of fat in water, while butter is the reverse, tiny drops of water trapped in fat.

Italian cooks save their pasta water for the same reason: the cloudy water is full of dissolved starch, which keeps droplets of fat or melted cheese suspended, turning a greasy puddle into a smooth, glossy sauce. Physicists studying cacio e pepe found that the sauce holds best with about equal weights of grated pecorino and hot pasta water.

enzymatic-browning-why-cut-apples-and-av.context_blurb:
Slice an apple and within hours its cut face is brown, though it never went near a stove. Avocados, bananas and potatoes do the same. The browning is chemistry, not decay, and the very reaction that spoils a fruit salad also gives the world a favourite drink.

The fruit's own enzyme, called polyphenol oxidase, causes it: the instant a knife exposes the flesh, the enzyme meets oxygen from the air and starts building brown pigment, which is why a sliced apple browns even in the fridge. A bruise browns for the same reason, because when an apple hits the floor, the blow bursts the cells open at the point of impact, mixing the enzyme with the fruit's colourless phenols and letting oxygen in. That one spot goes brown even though the skin never broke.

A squeeze of lemon stops the browning, because lemon's acid, helped by its vitamin C, makes the juice too sour for the enzyme to work, which is why guacamole gets lime juice and apple slices get a dip in lemon water. A few fruits barely brown at all, and pineapple is the champion: its juice is so rich in acid and vitamin C that a dip in it keeps sliced apple from darkening.

Cold only slows the enzyme, so peeled potatoes chilled in water still brown once they thaw, but a brief plunge into boiling water, called blanching, destroys the enzyme for good, because heat above about 70 to 90°C denatures it so it can never restart. Apples blanched for four or five minutes have almost no browning enzyme left.

The brown is not rot or mould: the enzyme turns the fruit's colourless phenols into compounds called quinones, which link up into melanin, the same family of pigment that colours human skin and hair and makes a suntan. A browned apple is pigmented, not spoiled.

Black tea uses the same enzyme on purpose: fresh green tea leaves are crushed and left to oxidize, and the enzyme turns their pale catechins into the dark compounds that make black tea black, while green tea skips the step. Cocoa makers use the reaction too. Biotech scientists finally built an apple that stays white without help, the Arctic apple, by genetically switching off the gene for its browning enzyme, so its slices make almost no brown pigment. It was one of the first genetically engineered fruits sold whole and fresh.

escoffier-and-the-kitchen-brigade.context_blurb:
Before Auguste Escoffier, a big restaurant kitchen was a hot, shouting, often drunken scramble. In the late 1800s this French chef, cooking for the grandest hotels of London and Paris, turned it into a disciplined team with ranks, stations and rules, and big restaurants still run his way. Along the way he created a famous dessert and a famous toast for an opera star.

Escoffier called his system the brigade de cuisine: he divided the kitchen into more than 20 specialised stations, such as a poissonnier who cooks only fish and a pâtissier who makes only desserts, so each cook mastered one job and every plate gathered its parts station by station. The model was the army, where Escoffier had spent nearly seven years as a cook, rising to chef de cuisine of the Rhine Army in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, and he carried its ranks and chain of command straight into the kitchen. He also laid down rules the old kitchens had never known, with no shouting, no smoking and no drinking on duty, so cooks who had long kept a bottle at their station now worked sober, in a clean and nearly silent line. In the dining room he helped make courses arrive one at a time, hot and plated, replacing the older French style of service, in which every dish was set on the table at once and most went cold before the diners reached them.

Each station had its own head cook, a chef de partie. The most powerful of them was the saucier, who made every sauce and sautéed dish and stood second only to the sous-chef among the cooks. The garde-manger, the "keeper of the food", ran the cold station, making salads, pâtés, charcuterie and cold soups without ever touching the stove.

Escoffier also changed what was cooked. A generation earlier, the great chef Marie-Antoine Carême had turned French grande cuisine into towering, ornate showpieces. Escoffier cleared away that clutter, trimming the garnish for a simpler, quicker style called cuisine classique, in which the food and the technique carried the plate. He wrote the whole system down in Le Guide Culinaire in 1903, more than 5,000 recipes and techniques that working chefs still consult. His stage was the grand hotel: partnering with the hotelier César Ritz, at the Savoy in London from 1890 and then at the Ritz in Paris and the Carlton in London, Escoffier made the grand hotel's restaurant the temple of fine dining for the rich.

His most famous dessert began at a Savoy banquet in 1893, made in honour of the soprano Nellie Melba: poached peaches and ice cream set on a swan carved from ice, a nod to Lohengrin, the Wagner opera Melba was singing, whose hero arrives in a boat drawn by a swan. Years later, opening the Ritz Carlton in London with César Ritz, Escoffier finished the dish with a sweetened raspberry purée, renamed it Pêche Melba, peach Melba, and declared the recipe perfect as it stood. Melba, ill and fussy, also complained that her toast was too thick, so Escoffier toasted a slice, split the warm slice through its edge into two thin halves, and toasted the cut sides, making a crisp, delicate toast half the usual thickness that never scorched. Melba toast, named around 1897, still carries her name.

every-spice-is-a-plant-part-in-disguise.context_blurb:
Open a spice drawer and you see jars of brown and red powders and shrivelled bits. Every one is a particular part of a particular plant, dried: a fruit, a bark, a seed pod, a lacy web around a seed. Some of those plant parts were once worth more than gold, and men killed for them.

Black pepper looks like a hard seed, but each peppercorn is a dried fruit, a shrivelled little berry from Piper nigrum, a tropical vine from India that climbs trees and poles up to about four metres high. White pepper comes from the very same berry, picked fully ripe and soaked in water for about a week, until its flesh rots away and leaves only the pale seed inside. Black pepper is the unripe berry, boiled and then sun-dried until dark and wrinkled, and green pepper is the unripe berry kept green.

Cinnamon is the inner bark of the cinnamon tree: in Sri Lanka, harvesters scrape off the outer bark, hammer the branch to loosen what lies beneath, and pry off strips no thicker than half a millimetre, throwing the woody core away. No one rolls those strips, because as the long, wet ribbons of bark dry, in just four to six hours, they coil up all by themselves into the hollow scrolls called quills.

Vanilla comes from an orchid, a climbing vine whose long seed pods first grew in Mexico's southern rainforests, where its flowers are pollinated by Melipona, a tiny bee with no sting. Anywhere else in the world that bee is missing, so every vanilla flower must be pollinated by hand, one at a time, which makes vanilla one of the most labour-intensive spices on Earth. Even a ripe pod smells of almost nothing when it is picked; the famous vanilla scent appears only after months of curing, as the pods are blanched, sweated and dried.

The hand trick was found in 1841 on Réunion, a French sugar colony, by Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy of twelve: with a thin sliver of bamboo he lifted the flap that separates the flower's male and female parts, then pressed the two together with his thumb. A vanilla flower opens for just one morning, and his method still runs the world's vanilla trade, including on Madagascar, which now grows most of it. France never paid him, and after France abolished slavery in 1848 he drifted into poverty and was jailed for theft, but officials released him early in honour of what he had done for vanilla. He died poor in 1880.

The nutmeg tree gives two spices from one fruit: the hard brown pit is nutmeg, and the bright red, lacy web wrapped around it, called an aril, dries into a second spice, mace, fading to orange as it dries. The tree grew wild almost only on Indonesia's tiny Banda Islands, which made them a prize that empires fought over. In 1621 Jan Pieterszoon Coen, at the head of the Dutch East India Company, seized the islands to take the nutmeg monopoly, and his men killed or enslaved almost all of the Bandanese, cutting a people of about 15,000 to roughly 1,000. England clung to one nutmeg island, a speck called Run, until the Treaty of Breda in 1667, when the Dutch kept Run and England kept a swampy Dutch trading post called New Amsterdam, on the island of Manhattan, which grew into New York. In effect, nutmeg was traded for New York.

falafel-the-fried-bean-fritter.context_blurb:
Falafel is one of the great street foods of the Middle East, sold from carts and stalls from Cairo to Beirut: crisp brown balls, fried to order and stuffed into warm flatbread with salad, pickles and sesame tahini sauce. It needs no meat, no egg and no flour, only beans, herbs and a pot of hot oil.

A falafel ball is made almost entirely of ground beans, which is why it became the beloved vegetarian street food of the whole region, eaten in pita, laffa or samoon bread. The secret is that the beans are never cooked first: dried chickpeas soak for about a day until they at least double in size, and then the swollen beans are ground raw into a paste, shaped and deep-fried at about 190°C. Raw, soaked beans hold a sticky natural starch that glues the paste together like Velcro, but boiling or canning bursts that starch, so a cook who grinds canned chickpeas finds the balls fall apart into mush in the oil. One cook compared it to trying to fry hummus.

Cut a fresh falafel open and the inside glows mossy green, though chickpeas are pale gold, because the cook blends fistfuls of fresh green herbs into the raw paste: parsley and cilantro, sometimes mint, whose chlorophyll dyes the whole batter green and gives falafel its fresh flavour.

Egypt makes its own version, ta'ameya, from fava beans instead of chickpeas, which gives it an earthier taste and an even greener inside, and many food historians believe this fava-bean falafel is the original; some say Coptic Christians first made it for meatless fast days.

Ancient pharaohs never ate falafel, and one reason is the oil: deep-frying swallows a great deal of cooking oil, which was a costly luxury in the ancient world, so a fried bean fritter made no sense then. Falafel probably arose in the port city of Alexandria and turns up in written Egyptian sources only after the British occupation of 1882.

fannie-farmer-makes-recipes-work.context_blurb:
In the 1890s a recipe might call for "a lump of butter" and "a teacup of flour", and the cake came out differently in every kitchen, since every lump and every cup was different. A Boston cooking teacher named Fannie Farmer changed that, and her 1896 cookbook taught American cooks to measure.

Farmer's rule for a cupful was to fill the cup, rounding it slightly, and then scrape the top flat with the straight edge of a knife, taking care never to shake the cup, so that every cook measured exactly the same amount. With every ingredient measured in level cups and level spoons, her recipes could make a promise no cookbook had made before: a novice and a master cook following the same recipe would turn out the same food, and cooking became something you could repeat instead of guess.

Her publisher, Little, Brown, doubted the book and, as the story goes, risked a first run of just 3,000 copies, which Farmer had to pay for herself, yet The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book sold more than four million copies in her lifetime, and she became known as America's Mother of Level Measurements.

Her book also explains why Americans still scoop flour into cups while most of the world weighs it in grams: in the late 1800s kitchen scales were expensive and unreliable, while a cheap standard cup, scraped level, gave the same amount every time.

farmed-vs-wild-where-your-fish-comes-fro.context_blurb:
For all of human history, people caught their seafood wild, with nets, lines and spears. Today a fillet of salmon or a bag of shrimp has probably never seen the open sea. Farmed and wild fish differ in colour, fat and what they eat, and the honest story of fish farming is more surprising than either its fans or its critics tend to say.

In 2022 the balance flipped for the first time: fish farming, called aquaculture, produced about 51 percent of all the aquatic animals people raised or caught, and about 57 percent of the seafood bound for people's plates, overtaking the wild catch after half a century as the fastest-growing kind of food production on Earth. About 70 percent of the world's salmon is now farm-raised, grown by the thousand in big net pens anchored in sheltered coastal water. Wild shrimp are even harder to find, because nearly all the shrimp sold today is farmed and reaches the shops frozen, shipped from farms in Asia and Ecuador.

A farmed Atlantic salmon follows the same pattern as a wild one, fresh water first and salt water later: it hatches and spends about its first year in tanks of fresh water at a hatchery on land, then moves to a net pen in the sea and is harvested at about two years old.

The most-farmed animal on the planet by sheer numbers is probably not the chicken but the whiteleg shrimp, farmed in shallow ponds along the coasts of Ecuador, India, Thailand and Vietnam at an estimated 300 to 620 billion a year, close to nine-tenths of all farmed shrimp. Salmon are hunters, so they cannot live on grain, and their feed pellets have long been made from small wild fish such as anchovies, sardines and herring, ground up and pressed, since those little forage fish supply about 70 percent of the world's fishmeal and fish oil. Mussels and oysters need no feed at all, because they pump seawater through their bodies and strain out the tiny food drifting in it, so no wild fish are caught to feed them and they rank among the greenest seafood a farm can grow.

Crowding brings disease, and the biggest health problem on salmon farms is the sea louse, a tiny parasite that clamps onto the fish and feeds on its mucus, skin and blood, costing the industry well over a billion dollars a year. Farmers even stock cleaner fish, wrasse and lumpfish, which pick the lice off the salmon.

Wild salmon turn pink by eating krill and shrimp rich in a pigment called astaxanthin, but farmed salmon would be grey or beige, so farmers mix that same pigment into the feed. The more pigment goes in, the deeper the colour, and feed companies sell farmers the SalmoFan, a fan of swatches like a paint-shop colour card, so they can pick the exact shade a buyer has ordered, most often a number between 24 and 28.

A farmed fillet carries nearly twice the fat of a wild one, about 27 grams against 13, because a penned salmon never swims hard against the currents, and you can see that fat before cooking in the wide, creamy-white stripes that marble the raw flesh. Wild salmon is leaner, firmer and deeper in colour.

Critics long complained that it took several pounds of wild fish to grow one pound of farmed fish, but counting all aquaculture together, fish, shellfish and seaweed, farms now use about half a ton of wild fish to grow a full ton of seafood, so farming produces more seafood than the wild fish it consumes. Even in Norwegian salmon farming, the wild fish needed for each kilogram of salmon fell from about 7.2 kilograms around 1990 to about 1.5 by 2013.
