fat-carries-the-vitamins-why-you-butter-.context_blurb:
Some vitamins dissolve in water, and some dissolve only in fat. That simple split explains why grandmothers buttered their carrots, why a tomato sauce simmered in olive oil beats a raw slice, and why you need vitamin C daily while vitamin A can wait for weeks.

Of the thirteen vitamins, the four fat-soluble ones are A, D, E and K, easy to remember because together they spell ADEK, and because they ride in fat, the body can only absorb them from a meal that has some fat in it. The other nine, the B vitamins and vitamin C, dissolve in water instead. That is why vitamin C cannot be stockpiled: it dissolves in water, so the body keeps no reserve and simply flushes any extra out in urine, and you need a fresh supply from citrus, peppers or berries every day.

Carrots, sweet potatoes and pumpkins are all orange for the same reason, a pigment called beta-carotene, which is not yet a vitamin: the gut uses an enzyme to split each beta-carotene molecule and build vitamin A from it, the vitamin your eyes depend on to see in poor light. A raw carrot gives up only about 11 percent of its beta-carotene, but sauté the same carrot in a little oil or butter and you absorb about 74 percent, more than six times as much, because the fat dissolves the pigment and ferries it across the gut wall.

Tomatoes break the "raw is best" rule too, because their red pigment, lycopene, is also fat-soluble, and gentle cooking in olive oil ruptures the tomato's tough cell walls so the oil can carry the freed lycopene into you. In a tomato paste simmered in oil, lycopene can be up to four times easier to absorb than in a raw tomato.

The fat-soluble vitamins can also be banked: more than 90 percent of your vitamin A reserve sits in your liver, often close to a year's supply, which is why liver and cod-liver oil are so rich in it. The catch is that stored vitamins A and D can build up to harmful levels if someone takes far too much of them.

fat-is-not-the-enemy-what-fat-actually-d.context_blurb:
For much of the twentieth century, Americans were told that dietary fat was the enemy. Nutrition science has since walked much of that back. Fat is fuel, insulation, flavour and building material, and the body cannot run, think or grow without it. Here is what fat actually does.

Gram for gram, fat is the densest fuel in food, so a spoonful of olive oil carries more than twice the energy of the same weight of sugar, rice or egg white: nutritionists sum it up as four calories per gram for carbohydrate and protein, nine for fat. The layer of fat just under your skin, called subcutaneous fat, is more than spare fuel, because it keeps you warm by insulating your body and cushions your organs against knocks and shocks. It is also the body's long-term battery: about 80 to 85 percent of a healthy adult's stored energy is body fat, enough for days or even weeks, while the fast sugar store, glycogen, runs low after an hour and a half to two hours of hard exercise.

Fat also carries taste, which is easy to miss. Many of the compounds that give food its flavour and smell dissolve in fat but barely in water, so fat dissolves them and carries them across your tongue, which is why a chef finishes a pan sauce with a knob of cold butter, the French trick called monter au beurre.

Fat is building material, too. Every one of your roughly thirty trillion cells is wrapped in a cell membrane, a thin skin built from two sheets of fat molecules, called a phospholipid bilayer, that keeps the cell's insides in and decides what passes through. The brain is the fattiest organ of all, about 60 percent fat by dry weight, because the fat there is not fuel but the very material its cells are built from. Long nerve fibres are wrapped in myelin, a sheath that is 60 to 75 percent fat and works like the plastic coating on a wire, and it lets each nerve signal leap from gap to gap instead of creeping steadily along, so signals travel far faster.

Even cholesterol, the most feared word on a label, is a raw material the body cannot live without. The body builds its steroid hormones from it, including cortisol and the sex hormones testosterone, estrogen and progesterone, which drive growth and puberty. Sunlight works on it as well: ultraviolet rays hitting the skin convert a close relative of cholesterol into vitamin D. Your liver and intestines make about a gram of cholesterol a day, far more than the 300 milligrams or so a typical person eats, and after a big breakfast of fried eggs, rich in cholesterol, the body simply makes less of its own to balance out.

Fat keeps you full, because when it reaches the small intestine it slows the stomach from emptying and sets off gut hormones that quiet your appetite, so a rice cake with peanut butter holds hunger off far longer than a plain one.

Fat became the villain through real science. The physiologist Ancel Keys argued through the 1950s that eating fat led to heart disease, and the first official American diet goals, issued in 1977, told people to cut their fat. Later critics argued that Keys, fixed on fat, overlooked sugar, which they suspect may itself drive heart disease. There were honest reasons for the low-fat advice, but many experts now argue that fat was over-blamed.

fat-shortening-and-flakiness.context_blurb:
A flaky pie crust, a crumbly shortbread and a tall, soft cookie all come down to what fat does inside a dough. Bakers have a whole word built on that job, shortening, and a few rules about temperature and lump size that decide whether pastry flakes, crumbles or turns hard and greasy.

Work butter or oil into flour and the fat coats every grain in a greasy film that keeps water out, and without water the flour's proteins cannot link up and toughen the dough, which is why a rich, buttery dough bakes soft and tender while a lean bread dough turns chewy. Those proteins, given water and kneading, form gluten, the stretchy network that gives bread its chew, and fat stops them from growing into long strands, cutting the gluten short. That is where solid baking fat got its name, shortening, and why shortbread and shortcake are "short".

How the fat goes in matters as much as how much. Rub butter fully into flour and the dough bakes evenly crumbly, the sandy texture of shortbread; leave cold butter in pea-sized lumps and you get pie crust. In the oven each of those lumps melts away and leaves a flat gap in the dough, and the dough above the gap lifts into a thin, separate layer, so a crust full of lumps bakes into a crust full of flakes. The lumps must still be cold and solid when the pan goes in, because butter is only about 80 percent fat and the rest is mostly water, which flashes into steam in the heat and pushes the layers apart. Let the butter soften and soak into the flour in a warm kitchen, and there is no water pocket to steam and no gap to lift, so the crust bakes greasy, hard and flat.

Before 1911 most American cooks relied on lard for solid fat, porky in flavour and in need of a cold larder, until Procter & Gamble launched Crisco, a white, shelf-stable fat made by hardening oil pressed from cotton seeds; the name comes from crystallized cottonseed oil. Vegetable shortening is almost all fat, with no water, and it stays firm until about 44 to 47°C, while butter melts near 38°C, so shortening stays solid longer in the oven and the cookie sets before the fat can spread, baking up tall and puffy, while a butter cookie spreads thin. Shortening has less flavour, though, and no water to make steam.

fat-soluble-vitamins-need-fat-eat-the-bu.context_blurb:
Vitamins A, D, E and K are the odd ones out. Unlike vitamin C and the B vitamins, they will not dissolve in water, only in fat, so a plate of vegetables delivers far more of them when it comes with butter, olive oil or another fat.

At Iowa State University, volunteers ate big mixed salads of greens, carrots and tomatoes with fat-free dressing, and blood tests afterward found almost none of the vegetables' carotenoids, the pigments the body turns into vitamin A, had reached their blood.

The reason lies in bile, a yellow-green juice from the liver that the gallbladder squirts into the gut when fatty food arrives: bile bundles fats and the fat-soluble vitamins into tiny droplets called micelles, which the gut wall can absorb. That is why people with a blocked bile duct run short of all four vitamins even when their food is full of them.

The kind of fat matters too: in feeding trials at Purdue, the food scientist Mario Ferruzzi found that olive oil and canola oil, both monounsaturated fats, delivered the vegetables' vitamins with just three grams of fat, while other fats needed more to do the same job.

Because the body stores these vitamins instead of flushing them out, too much can poison: in 1913 Douglas Mawson and his fellow explorer Xavier Mertz, starving on the Antarctic ice, ate the livers of their sled dogs, and the classic explanation for their peeling skin and Mertz's death is a poisonous excess of vitamin A. Some animal livers hold so much of it that about 500 grams of polar bear liver is a toxic dose, which is why the Inuit refuse to eat it.

fat-the-sixth-basic-taste.context_blurb:
Everyone agrees on five basic tastes: salty, sweet, bitter, sour and umami. Butter, cream and marbled steak taste "rich", and most people assume that richness is only texture, the way fat feels in the mouth. Some food scientists now argue that the tongue tastes fat itself.

In 2015 Richard Mattes and his team at Purdue University argued that fat deserves a place on the list as a sixth basic taste in its own right, something the tongue detects through its own receptors, separate from the slippery feel of grease. They named it oleogustus, from the Latin oleo, "oily", and gustus, "taste".

When volunteers tasted fat on its own, stripped of its smell and silky texture, it was not delicious at all, because it tasted rancid, like spoiled oil, and Mattes described it as a warning signal. The idea is that the tongue senses the free fatty acids of fat that has gone off, so you can catch food that has spoiled.

In that way fat behaves like bitterness, which repels us in a strong dose but pleases us in a faint one, the touch that makes coffee and dark chocolate so good. Fat-taste is off-putting when strong and appealing when faint.

Japanese food science has another word for richness, kokumi, "mouthfulness", the deep, lingering fullness of aged Parmesan, garlic, onions and broth simmered for hours. Kokumi compounds such as glutathione taste of almost nothing alone, but they switch on a sensor in the taste cells that turns up the salty, sweet and savoury tastes already in the food.

fats-what-they-do-and-the-seed-oil-debat.context_blurb:
Fats come in many shapes. Some sit solid on the counter and some pour, some keep for months and some go rancid. Your body depends on fat to think, grow and absorb vitamins, and nutritionists still argue hard about which fats serve it best, with the fight over industrial seed oils as the hottest front of all.

The brain is the body's fattiest organ, about 60 percent fat once its water is set aside, and one omega-3 fat, DHA, is the most common fatty acid in it, keeping the membranes of nerve cells fluid enough to fire. Fat also carries a set of vitamins: vitamins A and D, along with E and K, pack into tiny fat droplets and ride through the gut wall with dietary fat, so a salad with no fat at all gives up far less of them, while vitamin C and the B group dissolve in water. The body can build almost every fat it needs, but not two, alpha-linolenic acid, the parent of the omega-3 family, and linoleic acid, the parent of the omega-6 family, so these essential fatty acids must come from food.

The shape of a fat's molecules decides how it behaves. Butter, beef tallow, lard and coconut oil are saturated fats: their straight, unkinked chains pack tightly together, so they stay solid at room temperature. Olive oil is mostly monounsaturated fat, whose single double bond puts one kink in each chain, enough to keep it liquid on the counter but not in the fridge, where it turns cloudy and thick like slush. Polyunsaturated fats have several double bonds and several kinks, so their molecules cannot pack at all and stay pourable even when chilled; fish oils rich in omega-3 and corn and other seed oils rich in omega-6 all belong to this family.

Chefs fry in refined oils and save extra-virgin olive oil for pouring over finished food, because the chlorophyll and aroma compounds that give it its peppery flavour are the same ones that burn easily, giving it a low smoke point of roughly 160 to 210°C. Refining strips them out, which raises the smoke point but takes the flavour too.

The modern Western diet carries roughly fifteen times as much omega-6 fat as omega-3, against a proposed ancestral balance of about one to one, and the fix nutritionists suggest is not fearing fat but eating more oily fish like salmon, sardines and mackerel, two or three servings a week.

Fear of fat has a history. When President Dwight Eisenhower suffered a heart attack in the autumn of 1955, his physician, Paul Dudley White, appeared on live television to tell Americans to eat less saturated fat and cholesterol, following the researcher Ancel Keys's diet-heart idea, and so began decades of low-fat eating, which critics say filled the gap with sugar.

Cooks who favour traditional fats such as butter, tallow and olive oil note that seed oils are not simply pressed: factories flake soybeans or corn and wash them with hexane, a solvent refined from petroleum, then refine, bleach and deodorize the oil into a clear, flavourless liquid. They argue that this heavy processing, and the fragile omega-6 fat these oils carry, are reasons to prefer traditional fats; the harm they claim is contested, not settled. Stripped of slogans, the honest seed-oil debate does not turn on fat being bad; it turns on the heavy processing, about whether heating fragile omega-6 oils again and again turns them into reactive compounds, and about the lopsided omega-6 balance of modern diets. The trials disagree: the Minnesota Coronary Experiment and the Sydney Diet Heart Study found no benefit, or worse outcomes, from swapping saturated fat for omega-6 oil, while the American Heart Association points to trials showing about 30 percent less heart disease.

feijoada-brazils-black-bean-and-pork-ste.context_blurb:
Feijoada is Brazil's national dish, a dark, smoky stew that simmers for hours in a big black pot and brings families together on Saturdays. It has a famous origin story that Brazilian historians now reject, and its ingredients come from three continents.

The heart of feijoada is black beans and pork: a full feijoada completa slow-cooks the beans all day with salted pig's ears, tail and feet, smoked ribs, bacon, sausage and dried beef, until the broth turns a deep purplish brown. It always comes with the same companions, white rice, sautéed collard greens called couve, and farofa, toasted cassava flour scattered on top, plus slices of fresh orange, whose sharp acid cuts the rich pork and is said to help digestion.

A romantic legend credits enslaved Africans with creating the dish out of scraps the masters discarded, but historians such as Carlos Augusto Ditadi call that story modern folklore: the stew descends from cozido, the pork-and-bean stew of northern Portugal. Two facts sink the myth. Europeans prized pig's feet and ears as good food, and the African cultures that enslaved people came from did not traditionally cook beans with pork, while Latin Europe did. Feijoada belongs to a whole family of beans simmered slowly with salted and smoked pork, along with France's cassoulet and Spain's fabada, and food historians trace that family back to the meat-and-bean stews of the ancient Romans.

The plate is a meeting of continents: black beans are a crop of the Americas, first grown in Mesoamerica over 7,000 years ago, but pigs were unknown there until Europeans brought the first ones on Columbus's second voyage, 1493.

Even the farofa hides a danger, because bitter cassava root holds a compound called linamarin, and when the root is grated or crushed, an enzyme breaks it down and releases cyanide. Grating, soaking, fermenting and drying the root remove up to 99 percent of that poison, which is why properly made farofa is harmless.

fermentation-rot-you-can-eat-on-purpose.context_blurb:
Bread, cheese, yogurt, sauerkraut, soy sauce and chocolate are all made with the help of microbes, in a process that looks from the outside like spoiling on purpose. People learned to steer it thousands of years before microscopes revealed the tiny workers, and they used it above all to make food last.

Sauerkraut, the traditional German pickle, needs only shredded cabbage and salt, packed tight into a crock and left somewhere cool for several weeks, with no vinegar at all, and it comes out tangy and sour and keeps all winter; the German name means simply "sour cabbage". Nobody adds bacteria, because the lactic-acid bacteria that sour the cabbage already live on the raw leaves. The salt and the airless brine simply let those salt-tolerant microbes take over while spoilage microbes are held back, so the cook selects the culture rather than adding it.

Cheese is milk made to last. A cheesemaker adds rennet to warm milk so it clumps into curds, then drains away the watery whey, which carries off most of the milk's water, so roughly ten pounds of milk shrink down into a single pound of cheese. The hard cheeses, such as cheddar and parmesan, have lost the most water and keep the longest of all, for months or even years.

In Korea, families made a winter's worth of kimchi each autumn in a great communal effort called gimjang, packed it into brown earthenware jars called onggi, and buried the jars in the ground, where the steady cool earth kept the kimchi fermenting slowly for months. For most of its history kimchi was pale, cabbage simply salted and white rather than red, because chili peppers came from the Americas and reached Korea only around 1600; the first Korean mention of chili appears in 1614, and red kimchi spread only in the 1800s.

Ancient Romans poured garum, a pungent fermented sauce, over almost everything, and they made it by packing small fish and fish guts in salt and leaving them to break down for weeks before straining it. Its savoury punch makes it an ancestor of today's fish sauces. The finest garum, made from mackerel near Cartagena in Spain, was so costly that a couple of gallons could fetch about a Roman legionary's whole year of pay, and the writer Pliny the Elder said hardly any liquid but perfume cost more.

The word fermentation comes from the Latin fervere, "to boil", because a fermenting vat of grapes fizzes with bubbles of gas and looks exactly as if it were boiling, though nothing in it is hot. The name stuck for centuries before anyone discovered that tiny living things were making that gas.

ferran-adria-reinvents-the-dish.context_blurb:
Ferran Adrià is the Spanish chef who turned his restaurant, elBulli, on the coast of Catalonia, into the most famous kitchen in the world. From the 1990s onward he served diners spheres that burst, clouds of flavour and familiar dishes rebuilt beyond recognition, and he kept asking what a dish could be.

His first spherified dish, melon caviar in 2003, was a spoonful of shining orange pearls that could pass for fish eggs but tasted of sweet ripe melon, because each bead was melon juice wrapped in a skin that holds until it pops in the mouth. The technique is called spherification. In 2005 Ferran and his brother Albert went further with the liquid olive, which looked like a shiny green olive but was pure olive juice inside a skin so thin it burst the moment the diner closed his mouth on it, flooding the tongue with olive juice.

Adrià also invented culinary foam, espuma, in 1994, whipping the pure flavour of a single food into a weightless cloud with a cream siphon, and one of his strangest, smoke foam from 1997, was a glass holding only a trembling cloud made from smoked water that tasted of pure smoke.

His boldest idea was deconstruction: keeping a familiar dish's flavours but rebuilding its form. He served the Spanish potato omelette as layers in a glass, confited onion, liquid egg and warm potato foam, spooned up from the bottom so the flavours combine only as you eat; he said the tortilla is finished inside the diner's mouth.

To keep inventing, Adrià closed elBulli for about six months of every year so that his team could experiment full time at a workshop in Barcelona, elBulliTaller, creating hundreds of new dishes before each season. That is how one dinner could run to more than 40 tiny courses. In 2011, when some two million people a year were asking for about 8,000 seats a season, Adrià shut elBulli for good, not because it had failed but to turn it into a food-research laboratory, later the elBulliFoundation, saying that what he lived for was creating, not repeating.

fiber-the-food-you-cant-digest.context_blurb:
Fibre is the tough, stringy stuff that holds a plant together, and beans, oats, whole grains and apple peel are full of it. Fibre is the food your body cannot digest, and that is exactly why it matters: it shapes how full you feel, how fast sugar reaches your blood, and what the trillions of bacteria in your gut get to eat.

Your digestive enzymes cannot break fibre down, so while sugar and protein from the same meal pass into your blood, the fibre travels through you largely undigested, and that toughness is the point. Fibre comes in two kinds with two jobs. Soluble fibre, found in oats, barley, beans and psyllium, dissolves in water and swells into a thick gel in your stomach, which slows the stomach from emptying, so a bowl of oatmeal keeps hunger away until lunch. Insoluble fibre, in wheat bran and the skins of whole grains, soaks up water without dissolving and adds bulk, which keeps everything in your gut moving along regularly. The champion is corn bran, the papery outer coat of the corn kernel, at about 79 grams of fibre in every 100 grams, almost twice as much as wheat bran.

That is why doctors steer people with diabetes toward oatmeal and beans rather than white bread: the gel of soluble fibre thickens the meal, slowing both the stomach and the absorption of glucose, so the carbohydrates turn into blood sugar slowly, in a gentle rise instead of a spike.

Fibre is not wasted when it reaches the large intestine, because there your gut bacteria feast on it, fermenting what your own enzymes could not touch, which is what the word prebiotic means. In return the bacteria release short-chain fatty acids, and one of them, butyrate, is the main fuel of the cells that line the wall of your colon, supplying about 70 percent of their energy, so fibre feeds your own gut through a bacterial middleman.

Some starch acts like fibre too. An unripe green banana is full of resistant starch, which slips past digestion to feed the gut bacteria, but as the banana ripens soft and sweet, or is baked, that starch turns into ordinary starch that the body digests into sugar. The change can also run the other way: cook a potato and then let it cool in the fridge, and some of its starch re-crystallizes into resistant starch, nearly three times as much after a night at 4°C, so cold potato salad feeds your gut bacteria more than a hot baked potato.

Oats also lower blood cholesterol by a sneaky route: their soluble fibre, beta-glucan, traps bile acids, which the liver makes from cholesterol, and carries them out of the body, so the liver pulls cholesterol out of the blood to make replacement bile. About three grams a day of beta-glucan from oats or barley does the job.

fish-and-chips-britains-national-dish.context_blurb:
Fish and chips is Britain's national dish: a slab of white fish, almost always cod or haddock, dipped in batter and fried, served with thick-cut fried potatoes from a chip shop wrapped in paper. It became the hot, cheap meal of Britain's working families in the 1800s, but the fried fish half of it arrived with refugees centuries earlier.

In the fryer, the hot oil browns and crisps the batter into a golden jacket, but it barely touches the fish inside, which cooks gently in the steam of its own trapped juices, so it stays soft and flaky while the coating crunches. Many chip-shop cooks make the batter with cold beer, because beer is full of dissolved carbon dioxide, and when the cold batter hits the hot oil the gas rushes out into thousands of tiny bubbles that set into a light, lacy crust.

Battered fried fish came to England with Sephardic Jews, families driven out of Spain and Portugal in the 1490s. They fried fish on Friday so that it could be eaten cold on Saturday, the Sabbath, when Jewish law forbids lighting a fire to cook, and for a long time the English called fried fish fish cooked "in the Jewish manner". In Spain and Portugal they fried in olive oil, the everyday oil of Iberia, which stays light and crisp even stone cold, while hard animal fats turn waxy and unpleasant as they cool.

Fried fish became cheap enough for factory towns in the 1800s thanks to two new machines: steam-powered trawlers that dragged huge nets and landed vast catches, and railways that raced the fish inland to the cities. Cheap fish plus cheap potatoes made the perfect working-class meal.

In the Second World War, when Britain rationed meat, butter, sugar and eggs, fish and chips was never put on the ration at all, because the government protected the supply to keep up the nation's morale. Winston Churchill called the pair "the good companions", and legend says some British soldiers on D-Day used "fish" and "chips" as a password in the dark.

fish-sauce-the-fermented-bottle-that-mak.context_blurb:
Fish sauce is the thin, amber, salty liquid that cooks in Thailand and Vietnam splash into nearly every dish, much as other cooks reach for salt. It smells alarming in the bottle and tastes wonderful in the pot, and it has a twin from the far side of the ancient world.

Thai nam pla and Vietnamese nuoc mam can look like soy sauce, but there is no soybean in them: they are made from nothing but small salted fish. The fish are almost always anchovies, packed whole into coarse salt, bones and all, about two or three parts fish to one part salt, and left in barrels for a year or more without any cooking.

Nothing is added to break them down, because the fish's own enzymes slowly digest their proteins into free glutamate, the molecule behind umami, the deep savoury taste that makes food seem rich and complete, so a bottle of fish sauce is umami in liquid form. Straight from the bottle it smells sharp enough to make you wince, but stirred into a curry or a stir-fry the smell mellows into a gentle, round savouriness, adding a depth plain salt cannot give without making the dish taste fishy.

Fish sauce never really vanished from Western tables. Worcestershire sauce, created in 1837 by the English chemists Lea and Perrins in the city of Worcester, is the tangy brown sauce shaken over steaks and into Caesar salads, and fermented anchovies hidden in the recipe give it its savoury kick. Italy still makes colatura di alici, an anchovy sauce with ancient roots.

Those roots belong to the Romans, who made their own fish sauce, garum, by fermenting salted fish in the sun, on the other side of the world from Southeast Asia and with no known contact between the two. It is a striking case of two peoples finding the same shortcut to savoury taste, not a recipe handed down. Garum stank so badly while it fermented that its factories were pushed to the edges of town.

flowers-on-the-plate-the-buds-and-blooms.context_blurb:
Most people eat flowers every week without noticing. Broccoli, cauliflower, artichokes, capers, cloves and saffron are all flowers, or parts of flowers, caught at just the right moment. Sometimes we eat the unopened bud, sometimes a single thread from inside the bloom, and knowing which part is on your plate changes the way you see the vegetable aisle.

A head of broccoli is a mass of closed flower buds, so you eat the plant before it can bloom; left in the garden, the buds loosen and open into small, four-petalled yellow flowers. Its name comes from the Italian broccolo, "the flowering crest of a cabbage". A cauliflower's white head, called the curd, is also a mass of unopened buds, and because sunlight brings out a red-purple pigment in it, farmers have long folded the plant's own big leaves over the head to shade it and keep it white. One cousin, Romanesco, a lime-green variety of cauliflower, builds its head from spiral cones that each copy the whole, a rare fractal pattern in food often said to follow the golden ratio.

An artichoke is a giant flower bud too, the young bud of a cultivated thistle, picked before it opens; you eat the soft base of each scale and the tender heart. The thistle that grows it can stand about two metres tall. Left on its stalk, the bud bursts open into a big, feathery thistle flower in vivid purple, and the fuzzy choke that cooks scoop out of an artichoke is a cluster of those flowers before they bloom.

A caper is the unopened flower bud of a Mediterranean bush, pickled in brine, but a bud left to bloom and set fruit gives a second pickle from the same plant, the caper berry, plump, olive-sized and full of soft seeds. Nobody sells the caper flower itself, white petals around long violet stamens, because it opens at dawn and withers by sunset, lasting a single day, so pickers gather the tight buds every morning.

Even a whole clove from the spice rack is a flower bud: the dried, unopened bud of a tropical evergreen, Syzygium aromaticum, picked as it turns from green to red, its little round head made of four folded petals. Its name comes from the Latin clavus, "nail", for its shape. For centuries every clove in the world came from a handful of little volcanic islands in today's Indonesia, and the Dutch East India Company kept them rare and costly by chopping down every clove tree it did not control. One ancient tree on Ternate survived, and in 1770 the Frenchman Pierre Poivre smuggled clove seeds out and broke the monopoly.

Saffron, which costs more per gram than any other spice, is a single part of a flower: the dried red stigma, the thread at the heart of the purple saffron crocus. Each crocus gives only three threads, so it takes about 150 hand-picked flowers to make one gram.

foams-and-spherification-edible-illusion.context_blurb:
Modernist cooks use chemistry to make food that looks like one thing and behaves like another: juice served as glistening caviar, a broth served as a weightless cloud. The tricks sound like laboratory magic, but some of them began in food factories and some are sold at the mall.

The best known is spherification. The cook mixes sodium alginate, an extract of seaweed, into fruit juice and drips it into a bath rich in calcium. Each drop instantly grows a thin gel skin on the outside while staying liquid inside, because the calcium locks the alginate's long chains together only where the drop touches the bath. The result is a fragile sphere that bursts in your mouth. The same trick makes popping boba, the bursting fruit-juice beads sold cheaply as a topping at bubble-tea counters.

Spherification was not born in a restaurant: in the 1940s the inventor William Peschardt patented it for the food company Unilever as a factory way to seal a skin around a liquid, and it went into artificial cherries and the red pimento paste stuffed into pitted green olives. It sat in factories for about sixty years before chefs took it up.

The chef who made it famous was Ferran Adrià, whose restaurant elBulli, on Spain's Catalan coast, served its first spherified dish around 2003: dozens of tiny orange spheres that looked exactly like fish roe but burst with the sweet juice of cantaloupe melon.

Adrià's foams, which he called espumas, needed no lab gear at all, just an ordinary whipped-cream siphon charged with nitrous-oxide cartridges to force air into a flavoured liquid. Its maker, iSi of Vienna, even built him a siphon that could handle hot liquids, so he could serve warm foams, something cold whipped cream could never do.

folate-the-leaf-vitamin.context_blurb:
Folate, vitamin B9, helps the body build new cells, and it matters most at the very start of life, when a baby's spine is forming. Its name carries a clue to where it is found, and its story includes a cheap breakfast spread that saved lives in India before anyone knew the vitamin existed.

The name comes from the Latin folium, "leaf", the same root as "foliage", because scientists in the 1940s first isolated the vitamin from dark-green leafy vegetables such as spinach. Leaves are not the richest source, though: chicken liver carries about 578 micrograms of folate in every 100 grams, roughly four times as much as spinach's 146, and more than lentils and beans.

In 1931 the doctor Lucy Wills was studying a deadly anaemia among poor pregnant women working in the textile mills of Bombay, in India, and she cured it with Marmite, a cheap yeast-extract spread packed with B vitamins. The mystery nutrient was called the Wills factor until the 1940s, when it was identified as folate.

The tube that becomes a baby's spine closes within about four weeks of conception, often before a woman even knows she is expecting, so many countries now add folic acid to bread and flour by law; after the United States began doing so in 1998, birth defects of the spine fell by about 35 percent.

Heat and water are folate's enemies: after twenty minutes at the boil, as much as 89 percent of spinach's folate has leached into water that goes down the sink, but steaming, which keeps the leaves out of the water, loses almost none. Lightly steamed or raw greens keep far more than boiled ones.

fond-deglaze-and-the-pan-sauce.context_blurb:
Sear a steak or a chop in a hot pan, lift it out to rest, and sticky brown bits cover the floor of the pan. A beginner reaches for the scrubbing brush. A chef reaches for a bottle of wine or stock, because those bits are the start of a sauce, and the whole trick takes about a minute.

That stuck-on crust is not burnt mess but concentrated flavour, the very same browning that gives the seared meat its tasty crust, only glued to the metal instead of the meat, so scrubbing it away sends good flavour down the drain. French cooks call those browned bits the fond, a word meaning "bottom", "base" or "foundation", which is also their word for stock, the simmered backbone of French cooking.

To rescue the fond, the cook sets the hot pan back on the heat, splashes in wine, stock or even plain water, and scrapes with a wooden spoon while the liquid hisses and bubbles, so the fond dissolves off the metal into the liquid; this is called deglazing. Fond that is golden or a rich deep brown is worth saving, but fond that has gone jet black is burnt and would only make the sauce bitter, so it goes in the bin. Keep the brown, throw out the black. Milk and cream are the wrong liquids for the job, because dairy hitting a scorching pan can curdle at once into grainy little lumps that ruin a smooth sauce.

The deglazed liquid becomes the cook's pan sauce or gravy, rich with everything the meat left behind, which is the whole reason to deglaze: chefs often simmer it down to concentrate the flavour and then swirl in a knob of cold butter to make it glossy and smooth. Nothing from the pan is wasted.

food-is-information-tailoring-the-diet-t.context_blurb:
Some nutrition scientists say that food is information: a meal is not only a number of calories but a set of signals your body reads. Two meals with the same calories can tell the body very different stories, and researchers still argue about which signals drive overeating.

When volunteers ate breakfasts with the same calories built mostly from different nutrients, the protein breakfast sent the strongest fullness signal, raising the gut's fullness hormones and quieting the hunger hormone ghrelin more than the fat or carbohydrate breakfasts did. A fast hit of sugar, such as a can of soda, floods the blood with sugar and makes the body overshoot with insulin, so two hours later blood sugar has often dipped below where it began, a rebound called reactive hypoglycaemia, and you feel hungry again while a friend who ate eggs still feels full.

Two biologists in Sydney, David Raubenheimer and Stephen Simpson, noticed that locusts fed watered-down, protein-poor food ate more of it. In 2005 they proposed that human appetite works the same way, keeping us eating until we reach a set protein target, about 15 percent of calories, so protein-poor junk food makes people overshoot on calories. They call it protein leverage, a well-supported idea that is still debated.

In 2019 the researcher Kevin Hall let volunteers eat as much as they liked of ultra-processed or unprocessed meals matched on calories and on sugar, fat, salt and fibre, and on the ultra-processed food they ate roughly 500 extra calories every day. Hall's leading explanation was speed: the soft processed meals went down faster, so people finished eating before the gut's fullness hormone had time to signal stop. Protein intake was the same on both diets.

David Ludwig and Cara Ebbeling propose a rival model, the carbohydrate-insulin model, in which fast carbohydrates raise insulin, insulin makes fat cells hoard energy, and with less fuel left in the blood the body answers with hunger, so overeating is partly a result of storing fat, not only its cause. It is a serious hypothesis that other scientists still contest.

foods-that-are-secretly-made-from-animal.context_blurb:
A vegetarian scanning the shelves might never guess how many everyday foods hide an animal inside. Cheese, honey, red sweets, gummy bears, clear beer and a favourite steak sauce all owe something to a calf, a bee, an insect, a pig or a fish, and a few of those secrets have changed in recent years.

Cheese begins with rennet, an enzyme that gathers milk proteins into curds, and for centuries cheesemakers took it from the fourth stomach chamber of a calf still drinking its mother's milk, where the enzyme chymosin makes milk curdle into solid curds and watery whey. Today most American and British cheese uses chymosin that no calf ever made: microbes such as the fungus Aspergillus niger carry a copy of the calf's chymosin gene and brew the identical enzyme. Approved in America in 1990, this fermentation-made chymosin now sets roughly 80 to 90 percent of their cheese.

Honey is made inside the bee, in its honey stomach, a pouch called the crop that holds about 40 milligrams of nectar; back at the hive the bee brings the load up and passes it mouth to mouth to other bees, which add enzymes and fan it dry with their wings. That is why honey keeps for years: the bees dry it until it is only about 15 to 18 percent water, and one of their enzymes makes it mildly acidic, with a pH of about 3.4 to 4.5, while also releasing a trace of hydrogen peroxide, so microbes find no room to grow.

Many red sweets, strawberry yogurts and maraschino cherries are coloured with carmine, also called cochineal, a dye crushed from insects: tiny scale bugs raised on prickly-pear cactus in Peru and Mexico, about 70,000 of them for every pound of dye, and only the females are used. The Aztecs and Maya dyed with them long before the Spanish came. After Spain conquered Mexico, cochineal became one of the colony's most valuable exports, a red rivalling silver itself in worth. In 2012, when a vegan barista revealed that a Starbucks strawberry drink was tinted with crushed insects, a petition pushed the company to change its red to one from a plant: lycopene, the pigment extracted from tomatoes.

Gummy bears, marshmallows and jelly owe their wobble to gelatin, which is collagen boiled out of pork skin and the bones and hides of cattle, leftovers from the butcher, so vegetarians often swap in agar, made from seaweed. Many beers and wines are cleared with isinglass, a form of collagen made from the dried swim bladders of fish, the gas-filled organs fish use to float, which clumps leftover yeast so it sinks. Guinness used isinglass for nearly 200 years, until a new filtering system made its beer free of it by 2018.

Worcestershire sauce tastes of nothing fishy, yet its savoury depth comes from anchovies fermented in it for months. As the story goes, the chemists Lea and Perrins judged their first 1837 batch inedible and left the barrel in a cellar, then found it delicious a year and a half later.

foods-that-dont-grow-the-way-youd-think.context_blurb:
Ask people to picture how a pineapple, a banana or a fig grows and most will picture it wrong. Familiar fruits hide strange lives: some are clusters of flowers fused together, some grow on giant herbs rather than trees, and one cannot even make seeds without a tiny wasp that dies inside it.

A pineapple does not hang from a tall tree: it grows one fruit at a time, sitting in the centre of a low, spiky plant only about one to one and a half metres tall, a bromeliad related to Spanish moss. Each fruit is many fruits in one, because the plant raises a head of 50 to 200 small flowers whose berries swell and fuse around a central core, and every six-sided eye on the rind marks the place where one of those flowers once grew. Shop-bought pineapples have no seeds, because growers raise every plant as a clone, and you can do the same at home by twisting off the spiky, leafy crown, letting it dry and rooting it in a pot of soil to grow a whole new plant.

A banana plant may tower over a grown man, yet it has no wood at all: its trunk is a tight bundle of overlapping leaf stalks, which makes the banana plant the largest herb on Earth, and botanically the banana itself is a berry. Until the 1950s, the banana in lunchboxes was a sweeter variety called the Gros Michel, until Panama disease, a fungus that spreads through the soil, wiped out the plantations, and by the 1960s exporters had switched to the resistant Cavendish. Every Cavendish is a seedless clone, and a new strain of the same fungus now threatens it too.

A fig is stranger still, because it is not really one fruit but a fleshy pouch lined inside with hundreds of tiny flowers, a bloom turned outside-in, and the crunchy specks you bite are the true seeds that grow from those hidden flowers. The flowers can only be pollinated by a tiny fig wasp, and the hole at the tip of the fig is so tight that the female wasp tears off her own wings and most of her antennae squeezing through. Inside she pollinates the flowers, lays her eggs and dies; neither fig nor wasp can reproduce without the other.

Dates kept desert caravans going for months with no ice or cellar, because a date dries and grows intensely sweet while still hanging on the palm, reaching about 63 percent sugar, too sugary for spoilage to take hold. People in Arabia have grown date palms since about 6000 BCE.

french-kitchen-words-on-a-menu.context_blurb:
A fancy menu is sprinkled with French words, because French chefs shaped the modern restaurant kitchen and named its techniques. Each phrase is a short promise about how a dish is made, and a diner who knows a handful can read the menu like a cook.

"En croûte" means "in a crust": the food comes to the table sealed inside a shell of pastry and baked, and the most famous example is filet de boeuf en croûte, which English speakers call Beef Wellington, a beef fillet coated in mushroom paste and baked in puff pastry until crisp. "À la" means "in the style of", and sole à la meunière is fish in the style of the miller's wife: since a miller works with flour, the cook first dusts the whole sole in flour, then fries it in browned butter and finishes it with lemon and parsley. "Au gratin" promises a browned crust on top, usually of cheese or breadcrumbs crisped in the oven or under a grill; the name comes from the French gratter, "to scrape", for the crust you scrape from the dish.

"Flambé" means "flamed": at the table, the cook splashes a spirit such as brandy into a hot pan and lights it, so a burst of blue flame leaps up, the whole show of dishes like crêpes Suzette. Only strong spirits of about 40 percent alcohol, such as brandy, cognac or dark rum, will do, because wine and beer hold too little alcohol to catch fire, while much stronger spirits are too dangerous to use.

Many people believe the flames burn all the alcohol away, but when food scientists tested flamed dishes afterward, roughly three-quarters of the alcohol was still there, because the quick flame barely touches the liquid below it.

from-milk-to-butter-the-cream-emulsion.context_blurb:
Butter is cream turned inside out. For thousands of years people skimmed cream off milk and churned it until it suddenly split into yellow grains and a thin, watery liquid. The whole story turns on tiny globules of fat floating in milk: how they rise, how a machine can fling them apart, and how churning breaks them open.

Leave fresh, whole farm milk standing overnight and a rich layer of cream gathers at the top, because butterfat is lighter than the watery part of milk and slowly floats up, which is what people skimmed off for centuries to make butter. Shop milk never separates, because it is homogenized: forced through tiny openings under high pressure, which smashes the fat globules into specks so small they can no longer rise, so the fat stays spread evenly through the carton.

Skimming once took a day of waiting, until Gustaf de Laval, an engineer from Sweden, invented a cream separator in 1878 that spun milk at high speed, flinging the heavier skim milk out to the wall while the lighter cream gathered in the centre, doing in minutes what standing had done in a day.

Gentle stirring will never make butter, because every droplet of milk fat is wrapped in a thin, three-layered skin, the milk fat globule membrane, that keeps the droplets apart, and only long, hard churning batters the droplets until those skins tear and the freed fat can clump into butter grains. Churning turns one emulsion into its opposite: cream is tiny drops of fat floating in water, but butter is the reverse, tiny drops of water trapped inside a solid mass of fat, a flip called phase inversion. The thin, slightly sour liquid left behind in the churn, with under half a percent of fat, is true buttermilk. Fresh butter grains still hold pockets of that liquid, so the butter-maker works the butter, pressing and kneading it with flat wooden paddles called Scotch hands, to squeeze out the last of the watery liquid before shaping the block.

The tangy buttermilk sold in cartons today only borrows the name: dairies make it from ordinary fresh milk by adding bacteria such as Lactococcus lactis, which sour it and thicken it.

The colour of butter tells you what the cow ate, because fresh green grass is rich in beta-carotene, the orange pigment of carrots, and a grazing cow stores it in her fat, so butter from grass-fed cows is deep golden while butter from cows fed on grain is pale. Butter holds its shape on a warm counter while olive oil runs, because about 70 percent of milk fat is saturated, made of straight molecules that stack together tightly into a solid, while the kinked molecules of olive oil cannot pack close.

By law butter is only about four-fifths fat, and roughly 16 percent of it is water, so when a pat hits a very hot pan the hidden water flashes into steam and bursts up through the melting fat, which is why butter hisses, foams and spatters before it browns.

fugu-the-fish-that-can-kill-the-diner.context_blurb:
Few meals in Japan cost more than fugu, and none is more dangerous. A single fish holds enough poison to kill about thirty adults, there is no antidote, and only cooks with years of training and a government licence may prepare it. Diners order it anyway.

Fugu is the pufferfish, and its poison, tetrodotoxin, is far deadlier than cyanide: it paralyses the diaphragm, the muscle you breathe with, so a poisoned diner cannot draw breath. In Osaka and the rest of the Kansai region, people nicknamed the fish teppō, the gun, because of a pun: the same word means both to be hit and to be poisoned, so, like a bullet, if fugu hits you, you die. That is why fugu sashimi there is called tessa and fugu hotpot tecchiri.

The flesh people eat is safe; the poison gathers in the ovaries, the skin and above all the liver, which a chef must cut away perfectly, because a single nick of the knife can spread poison into the meat. That is why Japan has required a government licence for fugu chefs since 1958: a cook trains for two or three years as an apprentice, then sits an exam with written, fish-identification and knife-skill parts that only about a third of candidates pass.

Tetrodotoxin paralyses every muscle, yet victims stay conscious and often completely clear-headed, fully aware of what is happening but unable to move or call for help. With no antidote, doctors can only keep them breathing on a machine until the poison wears off, which usually takes some hours.

For generations fugu lovers prized the liver, fugu-kimo, as the tastiest bite of the fish, though it was also the most poisonous part, and in 1984 Japan made it illegal for any restaurant to serve it.

fugu-the-fish-that-trains-its-chef-for-y.context_blurb:
Japanese chefs who serve fugu must train for years before the law lets them near a customer. Their whole craft is a knife skill: knowing exactly where a deadly natural poison lies inside the fish and removing every trace of it, then turning the safe flesh into a work of art on the plate.

Fugu is the Japanese name for the pufferfish, a prized and costly delicacy served most famously as delicate raw slices, and notorious as a meal that can kill, though careful preparation means deaths are now rare. The chef cuts the raw flesh so thin that the plate's painted pattern shows through, a style called usuzukuri, and fans the overlapping slices across a round dish in the shape of a chrysanthemum blossom, its petals spreading from the centre.

The poison, tetrodotoxin, pools hardest in the liver: in 1975 the celebrated kabuki actor Bandō Mitsugorō VIII, a Living National Treasure, insisted in a Kyoto restaurant that he could resist it, ate four servings of fugu liver and died about eight hours later. Japan banned the serving of fugu liver in 1984.

Cooking cannot make fugu safe, because the poison survives heat and cannot be boiled or fried away, so the licence exam tests a chef's knife work, cutting out every poisonous part. Japan has licensed fugu chefs since 1958, and only about 35 percent of candidates pass.

Strangest of all, pufferfish do not make their poison themselves: wild puffers take it in from bacteria in the food they eat, and it builds up in their organs, so tiger pufferfish raised in tanks on a clean, controlled diet grow up almost free of poison. The tiger pufferfish, torafugu, is both the most prized fugu and, in the wild, the most poisonous.

garum-romes-fermented-fish-sauce.context_blurb:
In ancient Rome one brown, salty sauce stood on every kitchen shelf. Cooks splashed it into stews, over roast pork and even into honey desserts, the way people today reach for ketchup or soy sauce. It was called garum, and its story runs from sunny vats on the coast to a celebrity sauce-maker of Pompeii.

Garum was a fermented sauce made from small fish, the Romans' all-purpose seasoning, and it turns up all through the Roman cookbook Apicius, even mixed with wine for a dessert of pears and honey. Makers layered whole little fish, such as sardines and anchovies, with plenty of coarse salt in big vats and left them in the sun for two or three months with no fire at all. The heavy salt kept the sauce safe, holding off foul bacteria while the fish's own gut enzymes broke the flesh down into a clear amber liquid. The clear liquid drawn off the top was the prized garum, while the thick, cheap fish paste left at the bottom of the vat, called allec, went to poorer families to flavour porridge and everyday meals.

Fermenting the fish freed glutamate, the source of the deep savoury taste called umami, the same compound that ageing frees in parmesan and brewing frees in soy sauce, so garum was Rome's soy sauce, the all-purpose savoury bottle. In Pompeii a freed slave named Aulus Umbricius Scaurus grew rich on garum and paved his floor with mosaics of his sauce jars, like ancient advertisements, one of which boasts of his "flower of garum" made from mackerel.

The finest and costliest garum, garum sociorum, "the garum of the allies", came not from Italy but from Roman Spain, from the colonies at Cartagena and Gades, today's Cádiz, and Pliny the Elder wrote that hardly any liquid but perfume cost more, about 1,000 sesterces for a few quarts. Researchers in Cádiz have since recreated it.

After Rome fell the fashion faded, but the method lived on in Cetara, a fishing village on Italy's Amalfi Coast, where people still layer anchovies with salt in small wooden barrels and collect the amber liquid that drips from the bottom, a sauce called colatura. The fish sauces of Southeast Asia are cousins by coincidence, invented separately.

ginger-and-turmeric-the-underground-rhiz.context_blurb:
In the produce aisle, knobbly "ginger root" and "turmeric root" sit side by side. Neither one is a root. Both are a thick underground stem that the plant uses as a pantry, and the two plants are close cousins whose colours and flavours have spiced food and dyed cloth across Asia for thousands of years.

A lump of ginger is a stem, a kind called a rhizome that grows underground: unlike a true root, it is dotted with buds that push green shoots up toward the light and send fresh roots down into the soil. That is why a leftover knob from the shop can be planted to grow a whole new ginger plant. Irises and turmeric grow from rhizomes too, and so does bamboo, a giant grass that creeps sideways underground and throws up new canes metres away, which is how one clump can quietly take over a whole garden.

From the outside, turmeric looks like a smaller, browner piece of ginger, but cut it open and the inside is a bright orange so strong it stains fingers, knives and chopping boards for days. The colour comes from a pigment called curcumin, and the dried, ground rhizome gives curry powder its golden yellow. In medieval Europe, where real saffron was so costly that only the rich could colour their food with it, thrifty cooks used cheap turmeric to tint dishes almost the same gold and nicknamed it Indian saffron.

Ginger and turmeric belong to the same plant family, the ginger family, called Zingiberaceae, and another favourite spice belongs to it too: cardamom, which grows from an aromatic rhizome like its cousins, as does galangal.

The hot bite of raw ginger comes from an oil called gingerol, and cooking does not simply tame it: heat turns some gingerol into shogaol, which is even more pungent, so gently cooked ginger can bite harder than raw. Drying does the opposite, turning gingerol into zingerone, a milder, sweeter compound, which is why ground baking ginger tastes warm and mellow.

At a sushi counter, the curls of pickled ginger, gari, are a soft pink without any dye, because traditional gari is made from young ginger whose tender tips are naturally blushed pink, and the sour pickling vinegar draws that pink pigment out through every slice. Older ginger is tan, so cheap gari is often dyed to fake the look.

gluten-and-flour-strength-bread-vs-cake.context_blurb:
Flour is not all the same. Bakers choose it by how much gluten it can build, the stretchy wheat protein that gives bread its chew. A chewy loaf or a bagel needs strong flour, a tender cake needs weak flour, and a few people cannot eat gluten at all. Here is what gluten is and where it comes from.

Kneading is more than mixing: pushing and folding dough for ten minutes works the flour's proteins until they link up into a stretchy, springy network, so the baker is building a protein web inside the dough that lets it stretch and spring back. That network is gluten, a Latin word that meant "glue", a fitting name for the sticky protein that holds dough together. Dry flour holds the makings of gluten but no gluten at all, because gluten forms only when water is worked into wheat flour, letting a protein called glutenin link into a network joined to a second protein, gliadin. The two proteins split the work: glutenin makes the dough strong and springy, so it snaps back when poked, while gliadin gives it stretch, so pizza dough can be pulled long and thin without tearing.

The white powders sold as bread flour and as cake flour look alike, but they differ in their protein content: bread flour comes from wheat with more protein, about 12.7 percent, which builds plenty of gluten for a chewy loaf, while cake flour comes from wheat with about 10 percent and makes a tender crumb. Millers call the high-protein wheat for bread "hard" wheat and the low-protein wheat for cakes and pastry "soft" wheat, since a wheat's hardness really means its protein and gluten potential. The dense, tear-with-your-teeth chew of a New York bagel comes from high-gluten flour, about 14 percent protein, even stronger than ordinary bread flour. Strongest of all is durum, the hardest wheat there is, Latin for "hard", which is why dried spaghetti made from it keeps for months and still boils up firm.

Wheat is not the only grain with gluten, because barley and rye contain it too, which is why people who must avoid gluten also watch out for beer, rye bread and many cereals. Glutinous rice, the sticky rice of Japanese mochi, is safe for them despite its name, because its stickiness comes from a starch called amylopectin, not from gluten, and it is called glutinous only because it is glue-like.

Gluten does not dissolve in water, so if you rinse a lump of kneaded wheat dough under the tap, the starch rinses out as cloudy water and leaves a stretchy lump of almost pure gluten, which Buddhist monks, by tradition, turned into a chewy meat substitute called seitan, or "wheat meat".

About one or two people in every hundred have celiac disease, an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten makes their own immune system attack the lining of the small intestine, so they must avoid gluten completely. For everyone else, gluten is just the protein in wheat that gives bread its structure, nothing to fear.

gluten-wheat-and-the-fructan-twist.context_blurb:
Gluten is the protein that gives wheat bread its chew, and it has become one of the most feared words on a food label. For a few people it is truly dangerous. For many others who feel sick after eating wheat, the science points to a different culprit hiding in the same grain.

The word gluten comes straight from the Latin for glue, a good name for the sticky binder that holds dough together in one springy mass. Kneading links its strands into a stretchy web that traps the gas from yeast, and foods meant to be chewy, like bagels and pizza, need plenty of gluten and a long, vigorous knead, while pastry and pie crust are barely worked so they stay tender.

For people with celiac disease, about one in a hundred, gluten makes the immune system attack the small intestine, flattening the villi, the tiny finger-like bumps that absorb food, so the body can no longer take in nutrients properly. Doctors screen for it with a blood test, and for these people avoiding gluten is a medical necessity.

Many more people say wheat leaves them bloated and sore though they have neither celiac disease nor an allergy to wheat, and doctors call this non-celiac gluten sensitivity. It is hard to prove because no blood test or biological marker can detect it, so doctors can only name it after ruling out the other two. The symptoms are real; the cause is what scientists debate.

In a 2018 trial in Oslo, 59 people convinced that gluten made them ill ate muesli bars without knowing what was in them, and the bars with gluten caused no more trouble than plain ones, while bars with fructans, a carbohydrate found in wheat, caused the most bloating and stomach pain of all. Fructans, also found in onions and garlic, slip past the small intestine undigested, and bacteria in the colon ferment them into gas.

That helps explain why some people who struggle with quick-risen bread manage slow-fermented sourdough better: over its long, slow rise, the starter's microbes digest part of the fructans, about half in some studies, and part of the gluten as well. Real sourdough is still not safe for anyone with celiac disease.

gluten-why-you-knead-bread-but-barely-st.context_blurb:
A bread baker pushes, folds and stretches dough for many minutes. A muffin baker stirs the batter a few strokes and stops while it is still lumpy. The two habits look like opposites, but they come from the same rule about one wheat protein, gluten: build it up for chew, keep it down for tenderness.

There is no gluten in a bag of flour: it forms only when water or another watery liquid soaks into the flour and the flour's proteins link together, so gluten is built, not poured in. It is two wheat proteins working as a team: glutenin, which makes dough snap back when it is pulled, and gliadin, which lets it stretch out, and worked together in wet dough they cross-link into a network that stretches without tearing. Corn and rice flour cannot make a loaf rise, because their storage proteins are different and will not link into a stretchy web that traps gas, while gluten makes up 75 to 85 percent of the protein in bread wheat.

Kneading lines the proteins up into long, elastic strands woven all through the dough, and that gluten net traps the carbon dioxide the yeast breathes out, so the loaf holds the gas, rises and springs back instead of baking flat. A baker checks the dough with the windowpane test, pulling a small piece gently between the hands: fully developed dough stretches into a film so thin that light shows through, without tearing, while dough that rips early needs more kneading. A shortcut called autolyse saves effort: the baker mixes flour and water and lets it rest for 20 to 60 minutes, and in that time the flour soaks up the water and gluten bonds start forming on their own. The heavy chew of a bagel comes from kneading its dough long and hard, far more than soft bread ever gets, usually with high-gluten flour.

Muffins, pancakes and cakes want the opposite. Stir muffin batter until it is smooth and glossy and the extra work builds too much gluten, so the muffins bake tough and rubbery, chewy like bread instead of tender like cake. Over-mixed muffins also grow long, wormy tunnels inside, because the extra gluten traps too much gas, and as the crust sets firm while the inside keeps expanding, the gas is forced upward through the crumb. Cake flour helps, because its low protein, about 10 percent, can build only a little gluten, which keeps the crumb soft and fine, while bread flour, at about 12.7 percent, builds a strong, chewy web. Fat helps too, which is why bakers call solid fat shortening: it coats the flour so the proteins cannot take up water and link into long chains, shortening the gluten strands and giving pie crust and cookies a tender, crumbly bite.

Gluten-free bakers have no wheat web at all, so they most often stir in a little xanthan gum, which forms a flexible, sticky network that mimics gluten's stretch and holds the crumb together. It works well for cakes and muffins but struggles most with bread.

gnocchi-the-potato-newcomer.context_blurb:
Potato gnocchi, soft little dumplings served with butter or tomato sauce, feel like an ancient Italian peasant food. The dumplings are old, but the potato is a newcomer to Italy, and the oldest gnocchi were made from something else entirely.

The potato was first farmed thousands of years ago high in the Andes of South America, around Lake Titicaca in today's Peru and Bolivia, and Spanish explorers carried it to Europe only in the second half of the 1500s, so potato gnocchi could not have existed in Italy before Columbus. Italian cooks shaped gnocchi for centuries before any potato arrived, making them from semolina and breadcrumbs, or flour or bread: one ancient Roman recipe was a baked porridge of semolina and eggs, and in fifteenth-century Lombardy, dumplings called zanzarelli were bound with bread, milk, cheese and ground almonds.

The old semolina style survives in gnocchi alla romana, Roman gnocchi, a porridge of coarse semolina, milk, butter, egg and Parmesan that is spread flat to firm up and cut into discs. The cook overlaps the discs in a buttered dish with more butter and cheese and bakes them in the oven until golden and crisp on top.

The secret of light, pillowy potato gnocchi is to use as little flour as possible, often only about a third as much flour as potato, because extra flour and hard kneading build gluten that turns the dumplings tough and gummy. Expert cooks bake the potatoes instead of boiling them, so they stay dry and need even less flour.

Italian cooks often press each gnocco against a fork or roll it over a ridged wooden board just before it goes in the pot, marking it with little grooves, and those grooves grab and hold the sauce, just like the ridges on penne or rigatoni, so every bite comes coated.

grain-into-beer-why-barley-needs-an-extr.context_blurb:
Wine and beer are both made by yeast turning sugar into alcohol, but they start from very different places. Grapes arrive ready to ferment. Grain does not, so beer needs an extra step that wine skips. That step, and the drink it made possible, runs through the whole history of civilisation, from the first written records to the medieval tavern.

Crush ripe grapes and they begin to turn into wine on their own, because wild yeast rides along on the dusty skin, in the pale film called the bloom, and the fruit is already full of ready-to-eat sugar. Beer uses no fruit at all: its classic base is barley, a cereal grain, though brewers also use wheat, rye and others. Barley fresh from the field is useless to yeast, because its energy is locked up as starch, over 60 percent of the kernel against only about 2 percent sugar, and yeast can eat sugar but not starch.

The extra step is malting: the barley soaks until the seeds just begin to sprout and warm air then dries them; sprouting switches on the grain's own enzyme, amylase, which chops the long starch chains into sugars the yeast can finally eat. Malting ends in a kiln, and how far the maltster roasts the grain, from pale gold to nearly black, sets the colour and much of the flavour of the beer, so a near-black stout simply uses malt roasted darker than a golden lager.

Most beer is flavoured with hops, the papery green cones of a climbing vine, Humulus lupulus, which belongs to the same small plant family as cannabis, making the two close botanical cousins. Hops add a bitter edge, and boiled in the brew they also act as a mild antibacterial, a natural preservative that kept beer from spoiling in the centuries before refrigeration. Hops are latecomers, taking over European brewing only from the 1200s to the 1500s, and before them brewers flavoured their ale with gruit, a blend of wild herbs such as sweet gale, yarrow, mugwort and heather.

Beer is as old as writing. A clay tablet found at Uruk, in today's Iraq, about 5,000 years old and now in the British Museum, records the wages of a gang of workers, and they were paid in beer, drawn as a cone-shaped jar beside the sign for a ration. The Sumerians praised beer in a hymn written down around 1800 BCE to Ninkasi, their goddess of brewing, whose name translates roughly as a lady who fills the mouth, though the hymn is a song of praise, not a proven recipe.

Medieval working people drank small beer all day, often only about 1 percent alcohol, too weak to make anyone drunk, and they valued it as a cheap and filling "liquid bread", a way to drink their grain and its calories. The popular claim that they drank it because the water was unsafe is a myth, historians say: medieval towns prized clean water, London began piping free spring water into the city through its Great Conduit in 1237, and people drank water freely.

grain-legume-a-complete-protein.context_blurb:
All over the world, in places that never traded recipes, cooks landed on the same plate: a grain with a legume. Rice with beans, bread with hummus, corn with limas, lentils over rice. They were solving a protein puzzle long before anyone knew what an amino acid was.

Of the twenty or so amino acids that make up protein, nine, among them lysine, methionine and tryptophan, are called essential not because they matter more but because your body cannot make them itself, so they must come from food. The everyday staples of those kitchens, rice, wheat, corn and most beans, each fall short on one essential amino acid or another when eaten alone, but a grain and a legume eaten together make up for each other's gaps, a trick called protein complementation, which is why peoples with no contact all invented the same pairing.

The most widespread version on Earth is rice and beans: Costa Rica's gallo pinto, Cuba's moros, New Orleans red beans and rice, and countless West African plates. In the Middle East the legume is the chickpea, mashed with garlic into the smooth dip called hummus and scooped up with wheat pita bread. In New England, succotash simmers sweet corn kernels with lima beans, a pairing Native cooks made for centuries; its name comes from the Narragansett word msickquatash, "boiled whole kernels of corn".

Even a peanut butter sandwich follows the rule, because the peanut is no nut but a legume, a cousin of peas, beans and lentils, whose pods ripen underground. Spread on bread, it gives the same grain-plus-legume combination as rice and beans.

grains-the-seed-that-built-civilization.context_blurb:
A field of wheat, a rice paddy and a stand of corn could hardly look more different, but every grain is the same thing: the seed of a grass, packed with starch. When people learned to plant, harvest, store and grind those seeds, villages, cities and empires followed, along with some hidden dangers in the way we prepare them.

Wheat, oats, rice and corn are all grasses, members of one plant family, and the grain we harvest is simply the grass's seed. The starch crammed into each grain is a packed lunch for the baby plant that will sprout from it, fuelling the sprout until it grows leaves and can feed itself by sunlight, and we simply eat the lunch. That starchy store, the big middle of the seed, is called the endosperm, and white flour is almost pure endosperm, because milling strips off the outer bran, which carries most of the fibre, and the germ, which carries vitamins and healthy fats.

The world's biggest grain crop by weight is not wheat or rice but corn, or maize, at roughly 1.1 billion tonnes a year, feeding people and billions of farm animals. Corn is a human creation: farmers in Mexico's Balsas River valley bred it about 9,000 years ago from a scraggly wild grass called teosinte. A teosinte ear held only five to ten tiny kernels, each sealed in a shell so stony it could crack a tooth. When doubters claimed nobody could ever have lived on such kernels, the geneticist George Beadle, as the story goes, popped them like popcorn and ate them, and his experiments showed that only a few genes separate teosinte from modern corn. Thousands of years of breeding also made corn helpless: a ripe cob keeps its kernels locked tight instead of dropping them to sow the next crop, as wild grasses do, so without farmers to plant it, maize would vanish within a few seasons.

Milling and cooking can change what a grain gives the body. Polishing rice white scours away its bran and germ, taking with them thiamine, vitamin B1, and in 1700s Japan whole cities that lived on polished rice suffered beriberi, a disease that attacks the nerves and the heart. The Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman found the cause in 1897, using chickens fed only polished rice, which grew too weak to stand until he fed them the discarded bran and they recovered, proof that a disease could come not from a germ but from something missing in the food. It was the first clue to vitamins, and it earned him a share of the 1929 Nobel Prize.

Mesoamerican cooks had solved a corn problem thousands of years earlier: before grinding dried corn into tortilla dough, they steeped it in limewater or in water with wood ashes, a step called nixtamalization, which frees niacin, vitamin B3, that raw corn keeps locked away. When corn travelled to Europe and the southern United States without that step, people who lived mostly on corn fell ill with pellagra, the disease of too little niacin, which had never troubled the Native peoples who soaked their corn.

grapes-into-wine-the-oldest-accident-in-.context_blurb:
Wine was almost certainly discovered by accident. Leave crushed grapes in a jar and, with nothing added, the sweet juice starts to bubble and change, thousands of years before anyone knew why. The cause is a tiny living worker that was riding on the grapes all along, and the same worker later gave the world Champagne.

The worker is yeast, and fermentation is its meal: yeast cells eat the grape sugar and, with no oxygen around, split each sugar molecule into carbon dioxide gas, the bubbles, and ethanol, the alcohol that turns juice into wine. Nobody needs to add it, because wild yeast lives in the powdery, dusty coating on the skin of every grape, called the bloom, a few hundred to tens of thousands of cells on a single berry, so fermentation can begin the moment the grapes are crushed. Many wild yeasts start the work and die out, and the one that usually finishes it is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the very same species bakers use to make bread dough rise, which is why many winemakers now add a measured dose of it.

Even dark purple grapes give pale, greyish juice, so red wine gets its colour only by fermenting with the dark grape skins soaking in it, as red pigments and tannins seep out of the skins; pull the skins out early and you get rosé. Fermentation stops when the yeast eats all the sugar or when the alcohol it has made builds up and poisons it, attacking the yeast cells' own membranes, so common wine yeast dies off at around 15 percent alcohol and a wine can be left a little sweet. Stronger drinks must be distilled.

Legend says the monk Dom Pérignon invented Champagne's bubbles, but the truth runs the other way: the gas trapped in his cold abbey's bottles kept making them burst, and his job was to get the bubbles out of the wine. The English scientist Christopher Merret had already described making wine sparkle on purpose in 1662. Champagne makers do it on purpose now, with no gas pumped in: they add a little sugar and fresh yeast to still wine and seal the bottle, so it ferments a second time inside, and the new carbon dioxide, with nowhere to escape, dissolves into the wine until the bottle is opened. That gas pushes on the glass with five or six times the pressure of the air around us, over double what a car tyre holds, so the fat, mushroom-shaped cork is pinned down by a little cage of twisted wire called the muselet, invented in 1844.

guacamole-and-the-strange-avocado.context_blurb:
Guacamole is far older than the tortilla chips it is served with. The Aztecs of Mexico mashed it in stone bowls centuries before the Spanish arrived, and its main ingredient is one of the strangest fruits in the market, built from fat rather than sugar and water.

Guacamole is at heart ripe avocado, mashed with salt and chili, a recipe that goes back to the Aztecs; the lime juice, onion and cilantro that brighten it today came later, Old World foods that the Spanish brought to the Americas after 1519. The Aztecs called it ahuacamolli, from ahuacatl, avocado, and molli, the Nahuatl word for sauce, so the name simply means avocado sauce, and the same molli hides inside the name of the Mexican dish mole.

Most fruits are mostly sugar and water, but an avocado's flesh is about 15 percent fat, mostly the same oleic acid found in olive oil, with hardly any sugar, so fat supplies about 75 percent of its calories.

Leave guacamole on the counter and its bright green surface turns grey-brown within an hour, because mashing exposes the flesh to oxygen in the air, and an enzyme in the avocado drives a reaction that builds brown pigment, the same one that browns a cut apple. The guacamole has changed colour, not spoiled.

The traditional tool for mashing it is still found in Mexican kitchens: the molcajete, a mortar carved from a single block of volcanic basalt and used with a stone pestle called a tejolote. The Aztecs and the Maya both used it.

gumbo-and-the-roux-three-cultures-in-one.context_blurb:
Gumbo is Louisiana in a bowl: a thick, spicy stew of meat or seafood that cooks simmer all afternoon. Food historians say three peoples each gave it something essential, West Africans, the French and the Native peoples of the Gulf South, and each of their gifts is a different way to thicken the pot.

Nearly every Cajun and Creole gumbo begins with the same chopped base, which Louisiana cooks call the holy trinity: onion, bell pepper and celery. It is Louisiana's answer to the French mirepoix, with green pepper taking the place of carrot because it grew better and cheaper in the heat; the chef Paul Prudhomme made the name famous, and cooks joke that adding garlic is adding the Pope. A bowl of gumbo is always built the same way, with the stew ladled over a mound of white rice placed first in the empty bowl and never stirred in, so the grains soak up the broth spoonful by spoonful.

The dish's name came with okra, the green, ridged pod that enslaved West Africans brought to Louisiana in the 1700s and called ki ngombo, which Louisiana cooks softened to gumbo; as the sliced pods simmer they release a slippery sap that thickens the stew without any flour. From the French side comes the roux, flour and fat cooked together slowly and stirred without a break as they darken through gold and tan toward deep chocolate brown, thickening the stew and lending it a deep, nutty flavour. Oddly, the darker a roux gets, the more flavour it gives but the less it thickens, because the long heat breaks down its starch, so a chocolate-brown roux has only about a quarter of a pale roux's thickening power. Cooks make dark roux with oil rather than butter, since oil survives the long cooking without burning.

The third thickener is filé, a green powder made from nothing but the dried, ground leaves of the sassafras tree, which grows across the American South. It was a gift of the Choctaw, Native people of the Gulf region, who were the first to grind sassafras leaves into a seasoning, long before the French arrived; their word for it was kombo. Filé goes in last, off the heat, because if the gumbo keeps boiling after it is added, the stew turns stringy and ropey, and the name itself comes from the French filer, "to make threads".

The smoky backbone of a Cajun gumbo is usually andouille, a coarse, heavily peppered pork sausage smoked over pecan or sugarcane wood, and the town of LaPlace, near New Orleans, calls itself the Andouille Capital of the World. Two styles split over one red ingredient: city Creole gumbo from New Orleans often includes tomatoes and leans toward seafood, while country Cajun gumbo uses no tomato at all and a darker roux.
