hakarl-the-shark-you-must-rot-before-you.context_blurb:
In Iceland, people have eaten hákarl since Norse times: small, pale cubes of shark meat that has been buried for weeks and then hung in the wind for months. Famous chefs have gagged on it in front of the camera. The long, smelly cure exists for a simple reason: the fish it comes from is poisonous when fresh.

Hákarl is made from the Greenland shark, a huge, slow fish of the deep, freezing Arctic whose fresh meat really is poisonous, and instead of wasting the catch, Icelanders learned to make it safe by letting it rot on purpose. The shark keeps its body's waste, urea, the same waste chemical found in urine, stored right in its flesh, along with a related compound called TMAO, and those chemicals help it float and survive in cold, salty, deep water. Eaten raw, the flesh poisons the eater, because TMAO turns into a toxin in the gut that leaves a person staggering as if drunk, and Icelanders call that state "shark drunk"; sled dogs that gulp the raw meat get too sick to stand.

The cure has two stages. First the shark, gutted and beheaded, goes into a shallow gravel pit under heavy stones, which press the poisonous fluids out of the meat while it ferments for six to twelve weeks. Then the drained shark is cut into strips and hung up in a wooden drying shed for several months, until a brown crust forms on the outside, which is trimmed away before the meat is cut into small cubes.

The finished hákarl tastes milder than its reputation, but it reeks of ammonia, like cleaning fluid, because ammonia is what remains when the urea and related chemicals that once made the meat poisonous break down, so newcomers often hold their noses as they take a bite.

heat-transfer-how-the-heat-actually-reac.context_blurb:
Heat does not simply appear inside a steak. It travels into food by one of three physical routes: direct contact with something hot, a hot liquid or gas flowing past, or invisible rays crossing open space. Every pan, pot, oven and campfire uses one or more of them, and knowing which one explains why food browns, burns or stays pale.

A steak in a hot cast-iron pan cooks by conduction, the heat passing directly from the hot metal into whatever touches it, so the side pressed against the pan browns first and the meat cooks from the outside in. Pans are made of metal because metal is superb at carrying heat fast into food: copper and aluminium pass heat along hundreds of times faster than water and thousands of times faster than air, which is why nobody makes a frying pan of wood or glass.

Boiling pasta, steaming dumplings in a basket and deep-frying in oil look like three different methods, but all three cook by convection, a swirling, moving hot fluid, water, steam or oil, that sweeps heat onto the food. Water has a hard ceiling, though: at 100°C it boils away as steam, so however high the burner goes, boiling or steaming can never give food a browned, crisp crust, since the browning reactions need about 140°C and more. Yet a splash of boiling water scalds far worse than the air of a 100°C oven, because, weight for weight, water holds about four times as much heat energy as air and dumps far more of it into your skin. That is also why wet cooking works faster than dry oven air at the same temperature.

A marshmallow held above glowing embers, touching neither flame nor coal, still browns because of radiation, invisible infrared rays crossing open air to heat its surface with no contact and no fluid in between. An overhead grill colours a gratin from above in the same way.

herb-vs-spice-which-part-of-the-plant.context_blurb:
Is it an herb or a spice? The answer depends on which part of the plant ends up in your food. Herbs are leaves. Spices are everything else: a seed, a strip of bark, a dried fruit, a flower bud, an underground stem, the thread at the heart of a bloom. Some plants give us both.

Basil, mint, oregano and sage, like thyme and bay, are called herbs for one simple reason: the part we eat is the leaf. One plant, Coriandrum sativum, fills two jars: its fresh, citrusy leaves are the herb cilantro, while its dried seeds, ground, are the warm spice coriander. Dill does the same, with feathery dill weed as the herb and dill seed as the spice.

Cinnamon is bark, the soft inner bark of the Cinnamomum tree: workers strip it off in long pieces that curl into quills as they dry, keeping a layer only about half a millimetre thick and scraping away and throwing out the rest. A peppercorn is a dried fruit, the berry of the climbing vine Piper nigrum, a fruit with a single hard stone like a tiny cherry, which darkens and wrinkles as it dries. A clove is an unopened flower bud of the tree Syzygium aromaticum, snapped off just as it flushes red, before its four little petals can open, and dried hard and brown.

Saffron, the most expensive spice in the world by weight, often more than five thousand dollars a kilogram, comes from the crocus, Crocus sativus, and because each flower gives just three red threads, a single kilogram takes about 150,000 hand-picked blooms. Every autumn in Spain and Iran, workers hurry into the fields at dawn to pluck those threads, which are the stigmas, the female, pollen-catching tips at the centre of each crocus flower.

Ginger, though everyone calls it ginger root, is not a root at all but an underground stem of the plant Zingiber officinale, a kind of stem called a rhizome. The proof is in its little pale bumps, called nodes, the joints of a stem: bury a knob of ginger with a node facing up and it pushes a green shoot up and new roots down, something a true root, which has no nodes, can never do. Turmeric, ginger's cousin, works the same way.

The nutmeg fruit gives two spices from two parts: the hard brown seed is nutmeg, and the lacy red covering that wraps it, called an aril, is peeled off and dried into a separate spice, mace. For centuries both grew only on the tiny Banda Islands, and European empires fought bloody wars to control them.

honey-how-bees-make-it-and-why-it-never-.context_blurb:
Honey is one of the hardest-won foods on Earth and one of the longest-lasting. By common estimates, a single pound takes some 55,000 miles of flying and visits to about two million flowers, and the finished honey can keep for years in a sealed jar. Its long life comes from chemistry the bees build into it.

Bees gather nectar, the sweet juice that flowers make, which is about 70 to 80 percent water, as thin as sugar-water. Back in the warm hive, at about 35°C, worker bees fan the nectar hard with their wings, evaporating the water until the honey is only about 17 percent water. A bee enzyme also turns some of the sugar into gluconic acid plus tiny amounts of hydrogen peroxide, the same antiseptic that fizzes on a scraped knee, so honey is both acidic and mildly germ-killing.

Honey also soaks up moisture straight from the air around it, which is why bakers love it: honey keeps a cake moist and tender for days after a sugar cake goes stale. The same power means an open jar can pull in enough water, above about 20 to 25 percent, for yeast to grow and ferment it, so honey only keeps while it stays sealed and dry.

Even good honey is unsafe for one group, babies under one year old, because raw honey can carry rare spores of Clostridium botulinum, the germ behind botulism. An older child's or adult's gut handles the spores easily, but a baby's immature gut cannot, so doctors say no honey before the first birthday.

honey-the-first-sweetener.context_blurb:
Long before anyone grew sugar cane, honey was the sweetest food people could find, and they risked their lives to get it. Wild honey hunters climbed cliffs and trees, and later the Egyptians kept bees in clay hives and sealed honey in their tombs.

In the Spider Caves at Bicorp, near Valencia in eastern Spain, a rock painting some eight thousand years old shows a figure on rope ladders reaching into a wild bees' nest for its honey while bees swarm around him, the earliest known picture of people gathering honey.

Honey resists spoiling because it is only about 17 or 18 percent water, and its tightly packed sugar pulls the water out of any mould spore or germ that falls into it, so the microbe dries up and dies. Stories of honey from Egyptian tombs still being edible rest on reports of unspoiled pots rather than settled proof, but the chemistry behind them is sound.

Egyptian beekeepers housed their colonies in walls of stacked clay-and-mud tubes, and by traditional accounts they floated the hives along the Nile on rafts, following the flowers as they bloomed from one stretch of the river to the next.

how-a-kitchen-earns-michelin-stars.context_blurb:
The Michelin star is the highest honour in restaurant cooking, and chefs have wept over winning and losing them. Yet the famous red guide that awards the stars was started by two brothers who knew nothing about cooking, as a clever way to sell their real product.

André and Édouard Michelin, the brothers who started the guide in 1900, ran a company that made car tyres, in Clermont-Ferrand, at a time when France had fewer than 3,000 cars. Their first guide was a survival manual for motorists, filled mostly with maps of the roads and lists of where to buy petrol, along with how to change a tyre and where to find mechanics and hotels, and the brothers printed 35,000 copies and gave every one away. The plan was simple: the more people drove, the faster they wore out their tyres, and the more new Michelin tyres they would buy.

The guide began awarding stars in 1926, and it insists that they depend only on the food that reaches the plate, not the decor or even the service, which is why a small bistro with plain chairs can outrank a glittering palace. Michelin rates comfort and luxury separately, with symbols of crossed forks and spoons, from one for "quite comfortable" up to five, so a grand five-fork dining room can still hold no stars at all. One star means high-quality cooking, worth a stop; two stars mean excellent cooking, worth a detour; and three stars mean exceptional cuisine, "worth a special journey", a meal worth crossing the whole country to eat.

To stop kitchens from cooking a special meal for the critic, Michelin's inspectors book under false names and pay the bill like any other diner, so no chef can spot them. An inspector may eat around 250 restaurant meals a year and is told not to reveal the job even to close friends.

how-cheese-is-made-curds-whey-and-aging.context_blurb:
Cheddar from England, paneer from India, brie from France: the world makes thousands of cheeses, and each one is a way of turning milk, which spoils in days, into a food that keeps for months or years. The tools are few and very old: acid, an enzyme, salt, microbes, heat and time.

Every cheese begins with the same move: the cheesemaker splits the milk into solid curds and a thin liquid called whey, the same parting you see when milk sours into pale lumps. The curds become the cheese. The simplest way to split milk is with acid. An Indian cook making paneer at home needs only lemon juice, squeezed into a pot of hot milk: the acid alone curdles it, and the curds drain in a cloth and press into a block. Paneer is never aged, so it stays firm in a hot pan and never melts, which is why it can be fried or simmered in a curry.

Acid makes soft, fragile curds, good for paneer but too weak to press and age, so for firmer cheese the cheesemaker reaches for rennet, an enzyme that sets the milk into a firm, springy gel that can be cut, pressed and kept for years. Nearly every hard cheese on Earth depends on it. Even the leftovers become cheese: Italian cheesemakers heat the runny whey a second time until soft new curds float up, then skim them off as ricotta, a name that means 'recooked'. Mozzarella is made by a method called pasta filata, 'spun paste': once the curd is acidic enough, it is plunged into very hot water, which loosens its proteins so they slide past one another, and then pulled and folded by hand until the strands line up into that famous stretch.

For thousands of years rennet came from one place, the stomach of a young calf still drinking its mother's milk: the enzyme works in the fourth stomach, the organ that breaks that milk down, and it was collected as a byproduct of veal. An old legend says cheese was found by accident, when a traveller carried milk in a pouch of stomach lining and found it curdled by nightfall. Some cheeses keep changing in the cellar. In a wheel of Swiss Emmental, a bacterium feeds on the cheese's lactic acid and gives off carbon dioxide gas, and the gas, trapped in the firm paste, gathers into round bubbles: the holes the Swiss call eyes. Aging is a slow digestion. Nothing new goes in, yet over months and years enzymes and microbes break the cheese's mild proteins and milkfat into savory, tangy and nutty compounds, and that breakdown is what turns a bland young block sharp and complex.

Calf rennet has nearly disappeared. Since the 1990s most cheese has been set with chymosin brewed by microbes in huge fermentation tanks: the microbes carry a copy of the calf's own gene and make the identical enzyme, the first genetically engineered enzyme the FDA ever approved. Blue cheese needs a different kind of help. Its veins are Penicillium roqueforti, a safe mold the cheesemaker adds on purpose, but mold cannot grow without oxygen, so workers drive long steel needles through each wheel to open air channels deep inside, and the blue spreads along those tunnels, which is why it runs in streaks.

Under a microscope the rennet set is a precise piece of chemistry. Milk's casein proteins float in tiny bundles, each wrapped in a hairy, negatively charged coat called kappa-casein that pushes its neighbours away; chymosin makes one exact cut that clips that coat off, and the bare bundles stop repelling each other and bond into curd. Long aging leaves crystals behind. The little white grains that crunch in a Parmigiano-Reggiano aged two years or more are tyrosine, an amino acid set free as the cheese's proteins slowly break apart; once enough of it gathers, it hardens into crunchy specks that a young wheel never has. The Emmental eyes held one last surprise. When Swiss cheesemakers saw their holes shrinking and even vanishing, researchers at the Swiss agency Agroscope showed in 2015 that each gas bubble needs a microscopic speck of hay dust to grow around: old open-bucket milking let hay dust drift into the milk, and spotless modern milking machines had taken it away.

hummus-and-tahini-chickpeas-meet-sesame.context_blurb:
Hummus is the creamy dip of the eastern Mediterranean, eaten from Beirut to Cairo with warm flatbread. Its base is simple: boiled chickpeas, one of the oldest crops people ever farmed, blended with a pale seed paste, lemon and garlic. Simple food can still start fights, and several nations insist that hummus belongs to them.

The seed paste is tahini, and it is nothing but sesame seeds, hulled, toasted and ground into an oily paste that tastes a little like peanut butter. Chickpeas and tahini alone make a bland, pasty mush; what turns them into hummus is a bright, sharp finish of lemon juice and garlic. The dish is often served with a pool of olive oil and a few whole chickpeas on top.

The name is no fancy title: 'hummus' is simply the everyday Arabic word for chickpea, the word a shopper writes on a list. The dish's full name, hummus bi tahina, means 'chickpeas with tahini'. A new jar of tahini often looks spoiled, with clear oil floating over a stiff paste, but nothing is wrong: real tahini is only sesame and its own oil, and the oil rises the way it does in natural peanut butter, so the cook simply stirs it back in until smooth.

The chickpea is ancient. Farmers in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East domesticated it roughly ten thousand years ago, alongside the first grains, peas and lentils that people ever planted, and the oldest chickpea remains ever dug up, from Syria, are more than nine thousand years old. Its scientific name, Cicer arietinum, means 'ram-like', because botanists thought the little pointed beak on the seed looked like a ram's head. Restaurant hummus is silky while homemade hummus is often gritty, and the difference is labour: good cooks peel the thin papery skin off every single cooked chickpea, because those skins are what make cheap hummus grainy.

There is a shortcut. A pinch of baking soda in the simmering pot makes the water alkaline, which breaks down the tough chickpea skins so they loosen and float away, and it softens the beans in half the time.

The earliest surviving recipe that mashes chickpeas with sesame comes from a cookbook of thirteenth-century Aleppo, in Syria, attributed to the historian Ibn al-Adim, and it did not say 'hummus' at all: it called the dish kisa, the Arabic for a garment or cloak. That old purée used chickpeas, lemon, sesame and olive oil, but no garlic. Today Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Syria and Egypt all claim the dish, a feud nicknamed the Hummus Wars. In 2010 some three hundred cooks near Beirut built a single bowl weighing about 10,450 kilograms, more than double the record Israel had set only weeks earlier, and Lebanon took the Guinness title.

hydration-water-electrolytes-and-the-myt.context_blurb:
Water is the body's most basic need, and the advice about it is full of myths. The truth is less about a magic number of glasses and more about replacing what sweat, breath and urine carry away, including the salt minerals called electrolytes. A surprising share of that water arrives in food, not in a cup.

Some foods are practically drinks. A cucumber is about 95 percent water wrapped in a thin skin you can eat, which is why a cold slice feels so refreshing on a hot day; celery and romaine lettuce are just as watery. Even meat is mostly water: fresh beef muscle is roughly 65 to 75 percent water, so a dense red steak is more water than protein, and cooking drives that moisture out, which is why meat shrinks in the pan.

The famous rule of eight glasses a day has no solid science behind it. In 2002 Heinz Valtin, a kidney scientist at Dartmouth, searched the evidence and found no proof. The rule seems to come from a 1945 report by the Food and Nutrition Board that advised about two and a half quarts of water daily, and the sentence right after that advice said most of it is already contained in prepared foods; people remembered the number and forgot the food.

Hard exercise changes the picture. An athlete can sweat more than a liter an hour, and the mineral lost in the largest amount is sodium, about a gram in every liter of sweat, which is why sweat tastes salty and stings the eyes; potassium comes a distant second. That loss explains a danger sports doctors have documented: a runner who sweats for hours and refills only with plain water can thin the sodium in the blood to a dangerously low level, a condition called hyponatremia. One study found about 13 percent of Boston Marathon runners had it, mostly mildly, and at least eight endurance athletes have died of it since 1985, so after heavy sweating athletes replace salt as well as water.

injera-and-teff-the-bread-that-is-the-pl.context_blurb:
In Ethiopia and Eritrea, dinner arrives on a bread. Injera is a huge, round, spongy flatbread with a sour tang, spread across a tray like a tablecloth, and the family's stews are spooned on top in bright mounds. There are no plates and no forks: the bread does the work of both.

To eat, you rip a strip from the edge of the injera with your right hand and use it to pinch up a bite of stew, so the bread is the spoon as well as the platter. By the end of the meal the bottom sheet has soaked up all the juices, and it is not thrown away: that gravy-soaked bread is eaten last, the prized final bite of the dinner.

Injera's flour comes from teff, the smallest grain in the world: a hundred teff seeds together weigh about the same as one grain of wheat. The meal is shared, too: one great round of injera usually feeds two or three people at once, all reaching into the same bread.

The stews on top are called wat, and the most famous is doro wat, chicken simmered for hours with onions, spiced clarified butter and chili, with a whole hard-boiled egg tucked into the sauce. Teff also has no gluten, the protein in wheat, barley and rye that harms people with celiac disease, so injera is safe for them to eat every day. Wat gets its rusty red colour and slow, building heat from berbere, an Ethiopian blend of dried chillies with warm spices such as fenugreek, ginger and cardamom.

The tiny grain is a nutritional heavyweight: teff holds about 7.6 milligrams of iron in every 100 grams, among the highest of any grain, so a plate of injera is a strong source of iron. Injera takes days to make. The cook stirs teff flour into water and leaves the batter out for two or three days while wild yeasts and bacteria feed on it, releasing gas and acid, and that fermentation gives the bread its sour bite, much like sourdough. When the batter hits the hot griddle, steam bubbles up and pops open hundreds of tiny holes across the top, and Ethiopians call those holes the bread's eyes; they are what let a torn piece grip and soak up stew.

At an Ethiopian table, food can also say 'I love you'. Using injera, you scoop up a bite and place it by hand straight into a friend's or relative's mouth, a custom called gursha, the Amharic word for 'mouthful', and the bigger the bite, the deeper the affection.

iodine-iodized-salt-and-the-end-of-the-g.context_blurb:
A century ago, in the Swiss Alps and the American Midwest, whole villages had people with huge swollen lumps on their necks, called goiters. Doctors traced the problem to a trace mineral missing from the local food. The cure turned out to be one of the cheapest health fixes in history, and it sits on nearly every kitchen table.

The goiter is a swollen thyroid, the little gland low in the throat that helps set the body's energy use. The thyroid builds its hormones out of iodine, which makes up about 65 percent of the weight of the hormone T4, so a gland starved of iodine swells as it struggles to keep up. Iodine slowly washes off the land and collects in the sea, so sea vegetables are its richest natural source, above all kelp, dulse and the dark-green nori seaweed sheets that wrap sushi rolls. People who ate seafood rarely fell short.

That same washing explains the goiter belts. Around the Great Lakes, in the Appalachians and in the Swiss Alps, glaciers and mountains had left poor soil with almost no iodine, so the crops grown there and the animals grazing on it carried almost none either, and the families who lived on local food went short. Surveys in the 1920s found goiters in 70 to 100 percent of schoolchildren in parts of Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin. A Michigan doctor, David Cowie, pushed a cheap fix: put the iodine into table salt, which nearly everyone eats in small amounts every day of the year. The first American iodized salt went on sale in Michigan on 1 May 1924, and Morton Salt carried it across the country the same year.

Iodized salt did more than shrink necks. A baby's brain needs iodine to develop in the womb, and the economists Feyrer, Politi and Weil found that for the quarter of Americans who had been most iodine-starved, iodization raised intelligence by about 15 IQ points.

The worst harm came before birth. A baby badly short of iodine in the womb grew up stunted and with lifelong intellectual disability, a condition once called cretinism, a name doctors no longer use. Even today, no other cause of intellectual disability that could be prevented harms as many children worldwide, though a mere trace of iodine prevents it.

iron-heme-meat-vs-non-heme-plants.context_blurb:
Iron is the mineral that lets your blood carry oxygen, and running short of it leaves a person tired, pale, weak and foggy-headed. It is also the most common nutrient shortfall on Earth. Food holds iron in two quite different forms, and which form you eat matters far more than how many milligrams the label lists.

Iron sits at the core of hemoglobin, the protein inside red blood cells that picks up oxygen in the lungs and ferries it to every corner of the body. With too little iron the blood carries less oxygen, which is the tiredness and cold hands of iron-deficiency anemia. Over a billion and a half people worldwide are short of iron, and a doctor's simplest advice is to eat red meat, which carries the richest and most easily absorbed iron of any common food, with seafood close behind.

The reason is the form of the iron. Heme iron, found in meat, fish and poultry, is taken up easily, about a quarter of it, and food around it barely gets in the way; non-heme iron, the kind in beans, lentils, greens and grains, is absorbed poorly, often under a fifth and sometimes as little as a twentieth on an all-plant diet.

Plant iron can be helped. Eaten with vitamin C, from a squeeze of citrus, bell peppers or tomatoes, plant iron stays in a soluble form, and one meal's absorption can rise two- or threefold, though the gain over a whole day turns out to be modest. Other drinks work the other way: the tannins in tea and coffee lock iron into compounds the gut cannot take up, and in one classic study a cup of tea with a hamburger cut the iron absorbed by about 64 percent, and coffee by about 39.

Spinach is the famous trap. Popeye swallowed it for strength, and raw spinach really does hold iron, but it is packed with oxalates that bind that iron so tightly the body takes in only about one or two percent of it. An old pan can do better than a leaf. In 1986 John Brittin and Charlene Nossaman simmered tomato sauce in a bare cast-iron pan and found it held nearly ten times the iron of the same sauce cooked in other pots, because acidic, watery food pulls real, usable iron out of the metal, and a new unseasoned skillet gives up the most.

Meat's advantage comes down to packaging: heme iron arrives already held inside a porphyrin ring, part of the hemoglobin and myoglobin in the muscle, so the blockers in the gut cannot grab it, while plant iron floats loose and is easily caught. That is why heme iron makes up only 10 to 15 percent of the iron in a Western diet yet supplies about 40 percent of the iron absorbed. People who eat no meat can still get enough, but they are advised to eat nearly twice as much iron, pair it with vitamin C and keep tea away from meals.

jambalaya-vs-paella-the-saffron-that-was.context_blurb:
Spain's paella and Louisiana's jambalaya look like cousins: both are rice cooked in one pot with meat, and in the popular telling one grew from the other. Each has its own rules, its own fights over what is authentic, and its own trick for colour and crunch, and the difference between them starts with a famous golden spice.

Paella began as a dish cooked outdoors in the fields of Valencia, and its name comes from the Latin patella, a shallow pan: it first meant the wide, two-handled steel pan itself, and only later the rice cooked in it. Valencians say the real thing is a farmland dish with no seafood at all, made with rabbit, chicken and snails along with beans; a 2022 study found rabbit in 89 percent of traditional versions.

The best bite is the socarrat, the crisp golden crust of rice on the bottom of the pan. Near the end the cook turns up the heat and listens, and when a light crackling rises from the pan, the crust is forming; a moment more and it would burn. The other rule is never to stir once the broth is in, because stirring knocks starch out of the grains and turns paella gummy; the creaminess that stirring gives an Italian risotto is exactly what paella must avoid, so the short-grain bomba rice drinks the broth while each grain stays separate.

The popular story of jambalaya says Spanish settlers in New Orleans tried to cook paella but could not afford saffron, the costly golden spice, so they used tomatoes in its place. Historians add that Louisiana's rice cooking owes just as much to enslaved West Africans brought from rice-growing Senegal.

Louisiana now has two jambalayas. Creole cooks in New Orleans add tomatoes for a red version, while Cajun cooks leave the tomato out and still get a deep brown pot, because they sear the meat dark in a cast-iron pot first and the caramelized bits stuck to the bottom colour the rice.

japanese-blades-the-single-bevel-edge-an.context_blurb:
Japanese kitchen knives are among the sharpest in the world, and many are built for one job alone. A sushi chef needs to cut raw fish without tearing it, and centuries of that careful cutting shaped blades unlike the European chef's knife, above all in one odd detail: many are sharpened on only one side.

The everyday home knife is the santoku, whose name means 'three virtues' or 'three uses': created in the 1940s, its short, flat blade with a rounded tip handles meat, fish and vegetables alike, so one knife does the work of several. Many santoku blades carry rows of shallow oval dimples just above the edge, called a Granton edge, and the little pockets of air they make keep sticky slices of potato or cucumber from clinging, so the slices drop cleanly away.

The traditional professional knives go further. They are single-bevel blades, ground on only one face while the back is left flat apart from a shallow hollow, and that lopsided shape lets the edge come to a far finer point than a knife ground in a V from both sides, sharp enough to slice a tomato nearly see-through. The sushi chef's slicer is the yanagiba, the 'willow blade', long and slender like a willow leaf, and he cuts with a single long, smooth pull from the heel of the blade to its tip, a stroke called hiki-giri. A professional yanagiba runs about 270 millimetres precisely so that a whole slice comes off in one draw.

Sawing back and forth would ruin the fish: it leaves a jagged face and tears and bruises the delicate flesh, so the slice turns mushy and loses its glossy shine. The deba, the 'fish-preparer', is a heavy, thick-spined knife made to chop through the spine and rib bones of a fish, and though it looks like a small cleaver, it is the wrong tool for a pork or beef bone, because hard butcher's bone would chip its keen one-sided edge.

The one-sided grind makes a famous trick possible. With the usuba, the 'thin blade', a chef performs katsuramuki: he turns a thick cylinder of daikon radish slowly against the edge and peels away a single unbroken sheet so thin you could read print through it, and because the single bevel follows the radish's curve, the sheet stays perfectly even. The same shape is built into the steel, so a left-handed chef cannot just turn a right-handed yanagiba around; he has to special-order a mirror-image knife, ground on the opposite side for the left hand.

jollof-rice-west-africas-one-pot-and-the.context_blurb:
Jollof rice is West Africa's great party dish: rice cooked in a deep-red sauce of tomato, pepper and onion until every grain is stained with flavour. From Senegal to Nigeria to Ghana, families serve it at weddings, birthdays and holidays, and neighbouring nations argue, loudly and happily, over whose version is best.

What makes jollof is that the rice cooks inside the sauce: the cook pours the rice in raw, straight into a simmering purée of tomato, onion and red pepper, so the grains drink up the colour and taste instead of being served plain beside it. The dish takes its name from the Wolof people of Senegal and The Gambia, whose medieval Jolof Empire stood in inland Senegal, and from there it spread east across West Africa.

The most fought-over spoonful is the 'bottom pot', the layer pressed against the hot metal, which comes out charred, crunchy and a little bitter, and Nigerian guests jostle to scrape it up. Other rice cultures prize the same scorched crust, which Persian cooks call tahdig.

Fans say the finest version is 'party jollof', cooked outdoors in giant cast-iron pots over an open wood fire, and the wood smoke soaks into the rice and gives it a flavour no kitchen stove can match. Since the 2010s, Nigeria and Ghana have fought the 'Jollof Wars', a friendly rivalry over which nation cooks it better, waged only with cook-offs, jokes and memes.

Yet the red sauce is younger than the dish. Tomatoes and chili peppers are native to the Americas and reached West Africa only after Columbus crossed the Atlantic, so the old Jolof cooks never had them; the idea of rice cooked in sauce is old, but its red base arrived much later. West Africans guard the recipe fiercely. In 2014 the British TV chef Jamie Oliver published a 'jollof' that used lemon, parsley, cilantro and cherry tomatoes, and in the online storm called jollofgate one rallying cry warned that West African plates would not be colonized, until the recipe was pulled.

julia-child-brings-france-home.context_blurb:
Julia Child was a tall, cheerful American who fell in love with French food in Paris and then taught a whole nation to cook it. Through her cookbook and her television show in the 1960s, she convinced ordinary home cooks that the grand dishes of France were within their reach, and she made cooking on camera look like fun.

Her show was called The French Chef, and it first aired on 11 February 1963 from WGBH, the public-television station in Boston, one of the very first cooking shows on American television. Every episode closed the same cheerful way: she gave her name to the camera and then sang out 'Bon appétit!', French for 'enjoy your meal'.

Her promise was that every recipe would work in an ordinary American kitchen, so she checked that each ingredient could be found in American grocery stores and even had French products flown over to test whether the American substitutes really tasted right. She treated mistakes as lessons. When a potato pancake she flipped landed half on the stovetop, she scooped it back into the pan and kept cooking. She told viewers that a cook must have the courage of his or her convictions, and that if you are alone in the kitchen, nobody will see; the famous story that she dropped a whole turkey is a myth.

It had started in Paris. Her husband was posted there as a diplomat in 1948, a plate of sole meunière won her heart, and in 1949 she enrolled at Le Cordon Bleu, the best-known cookery school in Paris, where she was the lone woman among American former soldiers. Working with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle, two Frenchwomen she had befriended, she then spent nearly ten years writing Mastering the Art of French Cooking, published in 1961 with 524 recipes in its first volume, two years before the television show.

For the very first episode she chose boeuf bourguignon, beef browned and then braised for hours in red wine, because a slow beef stew showed viewers that French technique was something they could truly manage at home, and, as she promised them, it was a perfectly delicious dish.

ketchup-started-out-as-a-fish-sauce.context_blurb:
Ketchup seems as American as the hamburger, but its name and its idea travelled a long way to reach the bottle. The word began in Southeast Asia, crossed to England with sailors, and named several very different sauces before an American finally made it red. Its oldest ancestors were salty, savory and made from the sea.

In Hokkien Chinese, ke-tsiap was the salty brine of pickled fish or shellfish, a fermented fish sauce without a single tomato, and English sailors in Southeast Asia carried the word home. In the 1600s British cooks tried to copy the savory taste with whatever they had, using walnuts, oysters, anchovies and above all mushrooms, and dark mushroom ketchup became a British staple that the novelist Jane Austen was famously fond of.

Tomato ketchup was an American invention. In 1812 James Mease, a scientist in Philadelphia, printed the first known recipe for it, made from tomato pulp, spices and brandy, and he called the tomatoes by their old nickname, love apples. Early bottled ketchups spoiled quickly, so makers filled them with chemical preservatives that one critic in 1866 called filthy and putrid. Henry Heinz found a cleaner answer: his recipe used ripe tomatoes and plenty of vinegar and sugar, with salt, so the ketchup kept without the chemicals.

The family of fish sauces is older still. Two thousand years ago the Romans loved garum, made by packing fish guts with salt and leaving the mix to rot gently under the sun for months, and they splashed its salty, savory juice over almost every dish, the way Thai and Vietnamese cooks use fish sauce today.

kimchi-koreas-living-fermenting-dish.context_blurb:
Kimchi is Korea's national side dish: napa cabbage and radish packed with chili, garlic, ginger and a little salted seafood, then left to sour in a jar. It appears at nearly every Korean meal, and it is alive, quietly changing in the jar from the day it is made until the last leaf is eaten.

Kimchi shares its secret with Turkish yogurt and German sauerkraut, foods invented far apart by people who never met: all three are made by fermentation, letting lactic-acid bacteria preserve the food without heat or canning, which is how kimchi keeps for months without a fridge. The first step is salt. Cooks rub coarse salt into the cabbage until the leaves wilt and weep water, and the salty brine shuts out dangerous microbes while the salt-loving lactic-acid bacteria survive to do the souring.

Those bacteria never stop. They eat the cabbage's sugars and give off acid and a little fizzy carbon dioxide, and as long as they keep feeding the acid builds up, so a jar of kimchi grows steadily more sour in the fridge with nothing added.

Kimchi's fiery red is surprisingly new. The chili pepper is a plant of the Americas, first recorded in Korea in an encyclopedia of 1614, and red chili did not become a standard kimchi ingredient until the 1800s; for most of its long history, kimchi was not red at all.

Long before the fridge, Korean families made a winter's worth of kimchi each autumn, a tradition called kimjang, and packed it into brown earthenware jars called onggi. They sank the jars into the earth as far as their necks because the ground stayed cool and steady all winter, so the kimchi fermented slowly and never froze, and the porous clay let gas escape while holding the brine in. Today many Korean homes keep a special kimchi refrigerator instead.

koji-the-mold-behind-soy-sauce-and-miso.context_blurb:
Japan's most savory foods depend on a mold. Koji, a pale-green fungus grown on steamed rice or soybeans in warm, damp rooms, is the hidden worker behind miso, sake and soy sauce. It turns plain beans and grain into deep, rich flavour, and over many centuries Japanese brewers have tamed it into a safe and precise tool.

The savory depth of a bowl of miso soup was built long before the cook heated it: miso ripens for six months to a year in wooden tubs and soy sauce for months, and their flavour comes from that slow fermentation, not from cooking. The recipe for miso is tiny: steamed soybeans, salt and a grain, usually cooked rice and sometimes barley, mixed and left to age together.

Koji, whose scientific name is Aspergillus oryzae, matters so much that in October 2006 Japan's brewing society officially named it the national fungus, kokkin, at the suggestion of the scientist Eiji Ichishima.

Koji works with two kinds of chemical scissors. One family of enzymes cuts proteins into savory amino acids, the taste of miso, while the other, the amylases, breaks starch down into sugar, and that sugar is what lets brewers turn plain rice into sake.

Traditional Japanese soy sauce needs more than beans: brewers mix the beans with roughly the same amount of roasted wheat, grow koji on the mix and leave the salty mash, called moromi, to ferment for months. Koji also has a dangerous relative, the wild mold Aspergillus flavus, which poisons stored crops with aflatoxin, among the deadliest toxins found in nature. About two thousand years of careful breeding by brewers left koji unable to make that poison, turning a toxic wild mold into a safe enzyme factory.

The savory taste koji builds has a famous name. In 1908 the chemist Kikunae Ikeda pulled glutamate out of dashi made from kombu, which is dried kelp, and named the fifth basic taste umami, a 'pleasant savory taste'; a spoon of miso delivers the same molecule.

korean-bbq-banchan-ssam-and-the-grill-ta.context_blurb:
Korean barbecue turns dinner into a game. Instead of a chef cooking in a back kitchen, the waiter brings raw meat to the table, and the diners grill it themselves, wrap it up and eat it hot, surrounded by little dishes. Every part of the meal, from the meat to the side plates, has its own name and its own rules.

The cooking happens on a grill built right into the centre of the tabletop, burning charcoal or gas, and diners grill their own strips of meat as they eat, sliding pieces to the cooler outer edge so they do not burn. Around the grill come banchan, small shared side dishes such as kimchi and seasoned greens, and when one is emptied the staff refill it for free, as often as the table wants. Korean meals were even ranked by their number of side dishes, and the royal court's grandest spread had twelve.

The favourite cut is samgyeopsal, 'three-layer meat', named for the stripes of lean and fat in every slice; it is pork belly, the very cut bacon is made from, left uncured and sliced thick for the grill.

The meat is eaten as ssam, a word meaning 'wrapped': the diner lays hot grilled meat, a little rice, raw garlic and some paste on a raw lettuce leaf, often with a minty perilla leaf too, and folds it into one bite. The paste, ssamjang, mixes two fermented pastes, soybean doenjang and chili gochujang.

Bulgogi, 'fire meat', is thin-sliced beef steeped in garlic, sugar, soy sauce and sesame oil, and cooks grate Asian pear into the marinade, because the fruit's natural enzymes break down the beef's proteins and make it tender, though a day too long turns the meat mushy.

The heat in Korean food is younger than it seems. The chili pepper is a plant of the Americas that Portuguese traders brought to Korea around 1600, part of the great swap of crops that followed Columbus, so Korea's fiery cooking is only about four hundred years old.

lamination-the-croissants-hundred-layers.context_blurb:
Tear open a good croissant and it shatters into dozens of crisp, paper-thin flakes. That is the work of lamination, a baker's technique of folding cold fat into dough again and again until the pastry becomes a stack of many separate sheets. The oven then turns the stack into a light, crackling honeycomb.

The second ingredient is butter: a laminated pastry is a true stack of alternating layers of thin dough and thin solid butter, often more than eighty of them, and a croissant sliced straight across shows the stripes. The baker wraps a cold slab of butter in dough, rolls it out and folds it in thirds like a letter, and every such fold triples the number of layers, so four folds reach 81 and a fifth makes 243. The croissant's ancestor is the kipferl, a crescent roll baked in Austria since at least the 1200s. The tale that bakers invented the crescent to mock the Ottoman army after a siege of Vienna is folklore with little evidence behind it.

Butter is not pure fat. About a sixth of every block is water, and in the oven that water flashes into steam that pushes each sheet of dough up off the one below, which is what lifts the layers; puff pastry has no yeast at all and rises on steam alone. Meanwhile the melting butterfat fries each thin sheet of dough crisp, which is why a croissant shatters into flakes instead of turning soft like a roll.

Professionals choose European-style butter, about 82 to 86 percent fat instead of about 80, because the extra fat makes the butter firmer and more pliable, so it rolls out into one unbroken paper-thin sheet without melting into the dough. Temperature is everything, and the dough is chilled between every fold: butter that grows too warm and soft soaks into the dough, the sheets fuse together, and the layers disappear.

More folds are not always better. King Arthur's test bakers found that past about 160 layers the butter is pressed so thin that it holds too little water to steam the sheets apart, and the pastry bakes up tight and dense; when they cut the folds in one recipe, the crumb came out more open.

leavening-what-actually-makes-bread-rise.context_blurb:
A loaf of bread is full of holes, and every hole was once a bubble of gas. Bakers call anything that fills dough with gas a leavener, and there are several: a living fungus, a jar of wild microbes, a fizzing chemical reaction. Each makes bread in its own way, and people have argued, prayed and experimented over them for thousands of years.

Leave a bowl of bread dough in a warm corner and within an hour it can double in size before it ever sees an oven, because countless tiny bubbles of gas are forming inside it and inflating it like a balloon. Flatbreads such as the corn tortilla, the Indian roti and matzo stay thin and dense for a simple reason: their dough goes into the heat before it has any time to rise, so it never fills with bubbles, and bakers call such bread unleavened.

The gas in those bubbles is carbon dioxide, the same gas that hisses out of a soda can when you open it. Many home bakers tend a sourdough starter, a bubbling living culture they feed with fresh flour and water every day, saving a spoonful from each batch, and some starters have been kept alive and handed down for generations.

The carbon dioxide in most bread comes from yeast, a single-celled fungus and so a cousin of the mushroom, named Saccharomyces cerevisiae; it eats the sugars in the flour and gives off the gas as it feeds. Yeast can sleep a very long time. In 2019 Seamus Blackley, one of the creators of the Xbox, revived dormant yeast scraped from Egyptian pottery about 4,500 years old, and then used it to bake a real loaf of bread that people could eat. Unleavened bread carries a story, too: for Passover, Jewish bakers must get matzo from first wetting to fully baked in under eighteen minutes, before it can begin to rise, so that the flat bread recalls the Exodus, when the Israelites fled Egypt with no time to let their bread rise.

Yeast makes a little alcohol as well as gas, the same ethanol found in beer, but the heat of the oven drives it off as vapour while the loaf bakes, so fresh bread smells wonderful and never makes anyone tipsy. Sourdough, the most ancient method of raising a loaf, uses no packet of yeast at all: its wild yeasts and tangy Lactobacillus bacteria drift into the wet mix from the flour and from the air itself, and it was the usual way of making bread until packaged baker's yeast took over after the 1870s. Pancakes, banana bread, muffins and cornbread have no time to wait for a microbe. These quick breads rise in minutes because a fast chemical reaction in the batter fizzes out gas as soon as it is mixed and heated.

Gas alone would leak out of dough as easily as bubbles leave a glass of soda. It stays because wheat dough is laced with gluten, a stretchy protein web that catches each bubble and holds it, so the trapped gas can only push the dough upward: yeast makes the gas, and gluten keeps it. The chemistry of quick breads is acid meeting base. Baking soda is a base that does almost nothing alone, but paired with an acid such as buttermilk, yogurt or lemon juice it instantly fizzes off carbon dioxide, and baking powder is simply soda with the acid already mixed in.

leaves-on-the-plate-greens-herbs-and-one.context_blurb:
A great deal of what we eat is leaves. Salad greens, cabbage, kale, fresh herbs and even the tea in a teapot are the flat green parts of plants, built to catch sunlight. Knowing which part of a plant you are eating explains why lettuce turns bitter, why herbs differ from spices and why a cook dunks greens in ice.

Lettuce, spinach, kale and cabbage look like four different vegetables, but in every case you are eating leaves, a plant's solar panels: thin, broad and packed with green pigment to soak up sunlight and turn it into food. Lettuce likes cool weather, and when summer heat arrives it bolts, shooting up a tall stalk and throwing all its energy into making flowers and seeds before the heat kills it, so gardeners pick it first.

The difference between herbs and spices comes down to the part of the plant: herbs are the leaves, like basil, mint and parsley, while spices come from every other part, such as the bark of cinnamon, the berries of pepper, the flower buds of cloves and the root of ginger.

A bolted lettuce turns bitter on purpose. As it bolts the plant pumps a milky sap through the veins of its leaves, loaded with bitter compounds that make the leaves unpleasant to insects and grazing animals, so it is defending its leaves while its seeds ripen. The Romans named the plant Lactuca after their word for milk, and that name wore down into 'lettuce'.

One plant crosses the line. Coriander gives us both: its fresh leaves are the herb sold as cilantro, and its dried round seeds are the warm spice called coriander, one plant with two foods from two different parts; dill plays the same trick. Green tea and black tea seem like different drinks, but both are the leaves of one evergreen shrub, Camellia sinensis, handled in two ways: black tea's leaves are bruised and left to darken, while green tea's are heated quickly to keep them green.

Boiling dulls green vegetables because heat knocks the magnesium atom out of each chlorophyll molecule, turning bright green into drab olive. Restaurant cooks stop it by plunging the greens straight into ice water the moment they leave the pot, which halts the cooking at once and locks in the colour. A splash of acid such as vinegar would do the opposite and make them fade faster.

listeria-the-germ-that-grows-in-your-fri.context_blurb:
Most food-poisoning germs give up in the cold, which is why the refrigerator feels like a safe place. Listeria monocytogenes is the exception. It turns up in deli meats, soft cheeses and other ready-to-eat foods, it is especially dangerous during pregnancy, and it explains several of the food rules doctors give expectant mothers.

Most food germs stall at ordinary fridge temperature, about 4°C or 40°F, but listeria keeps on slowly multiplying in the cold and can grow even close to freezing, so a week in the fridge gives it time to build up rather than die off.

Listeria is cruel in pregnancy because the mother often feels only a mild, passing flu that is easy to ignore, while the germ crosses the placenta and can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or a deadly infection in the newborn. Pregnant women are about ten times likelier than other healthy adults to catch it, and in about a fifth of pregnancy cases the baby is lost, which is why they are told to skip cold deli meat and soft cheese, or to heat deli meat until it steams.

Dairies kill listeria with pasteurization, heating milk to 161°F, or about 72°C, for just fifteen seconds, which destroys it and other dangerous germs. Raw-milk cheese skips that step, so American rules require it to age at least sixty days before sale, though researchers note that aging alone may not make soft cheeses fully safe.

live-bugs-vs-their-food-probiotics-and-p.context_blurb:
Your gut is home to trillions of bacteria, and many of them help you digest food and stay well. Some foods add new living helpers to that crowd; others feed the ones already there. The two kinds have nearly identical names, probiotic and prebiotic, but they do quite different jobs.

Yogurt, kefir and raw sauerkraut each deliver live helpful bacteria, and nutrition scientists call any food carrying such living, beneficial microbes a probiotic; the key word is live. The name means 'for life', and it was coined as the mirror image of antibiotic, 'against life', the medicine that kills germs: an antibiotic wipes bacteria out, and a probiotic adds living ones.

Those bacteria must stay alive to count. Heating sauerkraut on the stove for a sandwich kills its bacteria, so cooked kraut has no live cultures left, and only raw, unpasteurized kraut still carries them. That is why yogurt tubs print a seal promising live and active cultures.

A prebiotic is not a living thing at all: it is fiber that your stomach cannot digest, which travels down to the colon and feeds the helpful microbes already living there. The scientist Marcel Roberfroid named it in 1995. The best-known prebiotic fiber, inulin, is packed into two plain kitchen vegetables, onions and garlic, along with leeks and asparagus; chicory root is the champion, about two-thirds inulin by weight.

Cooling can make food more prebiotic. When boiled potatoes are chilled overnight, some of their soft starch re-forms into resistant starch that the stomach cannot digest, nearly tripling the amount, so cold potato salad feeds gut bacteria more than hot potatoes do; the bacteria turn that starch into butyrate, a fuel for the cells lining the colon.

low-and-slow-collagen-melts-to-gelatin.context_blurb:
Barbecue cooks seek out the cheap, tough cuts of the animal, such as brisket, pork shoulder and shank, and cook them for eight or ten hours over gentle smoke until a fork pulls them apart. The secret is a tough protein that holds the meat together, and the patience to let heat transform it.

The same treatment would ruin an expensive steak. A tender filet mignon has very little of that tough protein to melt, so hours of gentle heat would only dry it out and leave it tough; a tender cut wants a quick, hot sear instead. The cuts that reward slow cooking are the muscles that worked hardest in the living animal, the chest, shoulder, leg and tail, because constant work builds up thick connective tissue, while the barely used loin stays tender.

That tissue is collagen, protein strands wound into a tight triple twist, and long, gentle heat unwinds the strands and lets water in, turning collagen into gelatin, the wobbly stuff of gummy bears and jelly. The change takes time: collagen begins to dissolve around 160°F, but it keeps converting for hours and melts most fully when the meat is held near 180 to 200°F, so pulling a brisket off the moment it reaches 160 leaves it chewy. Rushing with fierce heat backfires, too, because hot muscle fibers seize and squeeze out their water before the collagen has time to melt, so the meat turns dry and stringy, and a slab can lose a fifth of its weight. Brisket is the toughest cut of all because a cow has no collarbone, so its chest muscle braces about 60 percent of the standing animal's weight, day and night, and packs in collagen.

Collagen also makes a great stock. A stock that sets into a firm wobble when chilled is full of gelatin, and the cheap parts of a chicken richest in connective tissue are its feet, skin and joints, so tossing them into the pot gives the stock its jiggle; lean meat, fat and organs do not gel.

Pitmasters know a strange pause called the stall, when a brisket's temperature sticks near 150°F for hours. The cause is evaporation: moisture sweating out of the meat cools the surface as fast as the fire heats it, just as sweat cools you, and Professor Greg Blonder showed it by smoking a wet sponge, which stalled the same way. The cure is the Texas crutch, wrapping the brisket tightly in aluminum foil, which traps the moisture so evaporation stops and the temperature climbs again; wrapped, a brisket can hit 180°F within roughly six hours, while an unwrapped one may still not get there after ten. Gelatin's last trick happens in the mouth: it melts at about 95°F, very close to the temperature of your body, so a cold, firm spoonful of stock turns to warm liquid on the tongue, and it sets again when cooled.

mac-and-cheese-and-the-mother-sauce.context_blurb:
Macaroni and cheese looks like the simplest food in the world, but a real baked version is classic French sauce-making in disguise. Its creamy coat starts as a cooked paste of flour and butter, becomes one of France's famous mother sauces, and only then meets the cheese. The dish also has a surprising American history.

Every good cheese sauce begins with a roux: equal parts flour and butter stirred together over the heat and cooked until it smells nutty, the thickener that lets a sauce cling to pasta. Whisk milk slowly into that roux and it thickens into béchamel, the classic French white sauce, often seasoned with a little onion or nutmeg.

In 1937, during the Great Depression, Kraft put boxed mac and cheese on store shelves that needed no icebox, because the real cheese had been dried into a powder that kept for months in a packet, and families bought about eight million boxes in the first year.

Add grated cheese to béchamel and it gets a new name: Mornay, which is exactly what hides inside a baked mac and cheese. The French make Mornay with nutty Gruyère and Parmesan, but the American dinner-table version melts in cheddar instead.

Béchamel belongs to the five 'mother sauces' that Auguste Escoffier listed in 1903, but the idea was older: in 1833 the French chef Marie-Antoine Carême had already organized four grand sauces, béchamel among them, and Escoffier reworked Carême's list, dropping one and adding two, tomato sauce among them.

The roux also protects the cheese. Melted straight into hot milk, cheese often breaks: its proteins clump and squeeze out the fat, and the sauce turns greasy and grainy. In a béchamel, the flour's starch granules wrap every little drop of fat, so the fat cannot gather into pools and the proteins cannot knot into rubbery lumps. Thomas Jefferson fell in love with baked macaroni in Europe and in 1802 he offered presidential dinner guests a baked 'pie called macaroni', helping to make it famous in America, but the cook who actually made it was James Hemings, a man Jefferson held in slavery and had trained in French cooking.

magellan-cloves-and-the-first-lap-of-the.context_blurb:
In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan led five Spanish ships west into the unknown, and three years later one battered ship limped home after the first voyage all the way around the world. Schoolbooks remember a feat of geography, but the expedition was a business trip, and its prize was a spice.

Spain sent Magellan west to reach the Spice Islands, the Moluccas, by a route the Portuguese did not control, and to buy cloves, the most sought-after spice of the age, right where they grew; the trip was never meant to show that the world is a globe.

The Pacific nearly killed them all. The crossing lasted about ninety-nine days with no fresh food, and Antonio Pigafetta, who kept the voyage's record, wrote that the starving men ate biscuit crumbs full of grubs, chewed leather and paid half a crown apiece for rats; scurvy and starvation killed far more men than battle.

In 1522 only the Victoria came home, carrying just 18 survivors out of some 240 sailors, but her hold carried some 26 tons of cloves. Because cloves grew almost nowhere but a few islands in the Moluccas, that one cargo was worth more than all five ships put together, and the voyage made a profit.

maillard-reaction-why-a-sear-smells-and-.context_blurb:
Put a steak into a very hot, dry pan and two things happen: its outside darkens to a rich brown, and a smell no raw steak ever had drifts through the house. That is the Maillard reaction, the browning chemistry behind toast, roasted coffee, fried onions and bread crust, and it explains much of why cooked food tastes so good.

The browning starts when two things already in the food react under dry heat: its proteins, through their building blocks the amino acids, and its sugars. It is not burning, which would be charring, and it is not sugar simply melting. The same reaction browns many foods: toast, fried onions, the malt in dark beer, and coffee, whose dark colour and rich roasted flavour come from Maillard browning as the green beans roast.

Not every browning is Maillard. A cut apple browns on the counter with no heat at all, because a natural enzyme in the fruit reacts with oxygen in the air, and a squeeze of lemon slows it down; toast browns only when heat drives the Maillard reaction.

The sear's smell is brand new. Raw steak smells of almost nothing, but the Maillard reaction builds hundreds of fresh aroma molecules from scratch, with names like pyrazines and furans, which smell roasty, nutty and meaty and did not exist in the raw meat at all. The colour is new as well: as the reaction runs, it builds large brown pigment molecules called melanoidins, so the brown of toast or a steak crust is fresh pigment made during cooking, not soot or scorching. Cooks can speed the reaction up. Onions that need about 45 minutes to caramelize can get there in about 15 with a tiny pinch of baking soda, which makes them more alkaline and supercharges the browning, though too much leaves them tasting soapy.

Most of a sear's flavour is actually smell. As you chew, the aroma rises up the passage at the back of your throat into your nose, a route called retronasal smell, so pinching your nose closes the path and the roasted flavour almost disappears. The browning takes its name from Louis-Camille Maillard, a French doctor and chemist who described it in 1912, but he was not cooking: he was studying how the human body puts proteins to use, and the browning turned up along the way.

maize-from-a-wild-grass-to-corn.context_blurb:
Corn is one of the greatest inventions in history, and it was invented by farmers. Thousands of years ago in Mexico, Native farmers took a scraggly wild grass and, generation after generation, bred it into the fat golden cob. Science has since uncovered how few changes it took, and how corn learned to work in a team.

Native farmers grew squash, beans and corn side by side in a single mound and called them the Three Sisters, because each helped the others: the tall corn stalk served as a living pole for the bean vines to climb, so the beans grew upward instead of sprawling on the ground.

Corn's wild ancestor, teosinte, sealed each seed inside a fruitcase as hard as stone, tough enough to crack a tooth, and a change in a single gene, called tga1, is thought to have stripped that case away and left the bare kernel we eat.

In 2002 geneticists compared corn DNA from around the world and found that every corn plant on Earth traces back to a single taming of a single grass in one region, southern Mexico, at one time, so all the world's corn is really one enormous family.

The beans had a secret role underground. Bacteria living on the bean roots pull nitrogen out of the air and fix it into the soil, replacing what the hungry corn drains, so the patch keeps feeding itself; corn and beans also form a complete protein when eaten together. The geneticist George Beadle grew some 50,000 corn and teosinte hybrids and worked out from their ratios that only about four or five genes stand between the wild weed and the cob, few enough for ancient farmers to manage by saving rare plants.

Corn hides a nutritional trap. Corn's niacin, vitamin B3, is chemically locked away where the body cannot use it, and Mesoamerican cooks freed it by soaking the corn in water with wood ash or lime, a process called nixtamalization. When corn spread around the world after 1492, many people adopted it without that soak, and in the American South between about 1906 and 1940 the result was pellagra, a niacin-deficiency disease that struck some three million people and killed more than a hundred thousand, until the doctor Joseph Goldberger showed it came from diet, not infection.

maize-goes-global-and-the-pellagra-trap.context_blurb:
Corn feeds the world today, but it came from a single homeland and carried a hidden danger on its travels. Ancient cooks in that homeland knew a trick that made it safe and workable; many of the people who adopted corn after 1492 skipped it, and they paid with a terrible disease.

Corn's wild ancestor is teosinte, a scrawny, branching grass whose few tiny seeds sit in hard cases. Farmers domesticated it about nine thousand years ago in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico, and after Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, corn spread from there to the whole world.

Thousands of years of breeding left corn helpless. Teosinte scatters its seeds to replant itself, but corn's kernels stay fixed on the cob, so a fallen ear never sows a new field, and the plant depends completely on people to strip and replant it.

Ground dried corn will not bind into smooth dough on its own. Mesoamerican cooks first simmered and soaked the kernels in water mixed with mineral lime or wood ash, a step called nixtamalization, from the Nahuatl words for ashes and corn dough; the alkali loosens the hulls and turns the corn into masa, the soft dough of tortillas and tamales.

Pellagra brought the 'four Ds', dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia and death, and killed more than a hundred thousand people in the American South, where poor families lived on cornmeal, fatback and molasses. The South never took up the lime soak, and cornbread stayed, yet by the mid-1940s the disease had nearly vanished, because millers began putting niacin back into white flour.

maizes-journey-the-columbian-exchange-gr.context_blurb:
Before 1492, nobody in Europe, Africa or Asia had ever seen an ear of corn. It was an American grain, bred by Native farmers over thousands of years from a weedy wild plant. Then Columbus's voyages opened the great swap of foods between the hemispheres, and corn sailed east to change what half the world ate.

After Columbus reached the Americas in 1492, corn crossed the Atlantic in the two-way food swap historians call the Columbian Exchange, and it took root so well that it became a daily food from Italy to central Africa; every corn plant in the Old World grew from seed carried over after that date.

Corn's wild ancestor is a grass, a scrawny, branching plant whose whole 'ear' is just five to ten hard kernels in two rows. That grass is teosinte, and it still grows wild in the highlands of Mexico; DNA studies show that every kind of corn on Earth, from sweet corn to rainbow corn, was bred from it, and crossing the two proved how close they are. The fat modern ear, with up to about 1,200 kernels in as many as 32 rows, never grew wild: Native farmers built it over thousands of years by saving and replanting the seed from their best, biggest ears, generation after generation.

Farming began in the Balsas River valley of south-central Mexico, where corn was grown and milled about nine thousand years ago; grinding stones still crusted with maize from near Iguala are some of the oldest farming evidence anywhere. In Italy corn took over an old name. Polenta had once meant a peasant mush of chestnut flour, millet or chickpeas, and after maize arrived in the 1500s the word passed to a stiff yellow mush of cornmeal simmered in water, the staple food of northern Italy's poor.

Teosinte's stony seed case was armour with a purpose: a seed could be swallowed by a grazing animal, travel through its gut and still sprout wherever it landed, spreading the plant, and farmers slowly bred that armour away to leave the soft kernel. In Africa, Portuguese ships brought maize in the 1500s, and its big harvests pushed aside sorghum, the grain Africans had grown for thousands of years; today stiff cornmeal porridge, called ugali, nsima, sadza or pap, is the daily meal in a great swath of Africa's east and south.

Corn's journey also carried a disease. In the early 1900s pellagra was killing poor families who lived on corn in the southern United States, and many doctors blamed a germ. From 1915 the doctor Joseph Goldberger fed sufferers in orphanages and asylums fresh meat, milk, eggs and beans, and the disease vanished, proving that a poor diet lacking niacin was the cause. The lesson of maize's journey is that a food's know-how must travel with its seeds.

mal-sichuans-numbing-pepper.context_blurb:
The food of Sichuan, in western China, is famous for a double hit. One part is the burn of chili, the other is a strange buzzing numbness that no jalapeño can deliver, and cooks there pair the two on purpose. The numbing spice behind it is not what its English name says, and science has only recently explained it.

A bite of Sichuan hotpot brings the chili burn first, and then a second feeling, a tingling that leaves the lips buzzing and numb; Sichuan cooks call the chili heat là, 'spicy', and the numbing má, so the pairing is málà, 'numbing-and-spicy'.

The numbing spice is called Sichuan peppercorn, but it is neither a chili nor a relative of black pepper. Its plant belongs to the citrus family, the same botanical family as the orange and the lemon. The part you eat is the dried outer husk of a tiny berry-like fruit: cooks split the dried fruits open, throw away the gritty black seeds and keep only the fragrant reddish husks.

One famous Sichuan dish carries a nickname. Mapo tofu, soft tofu in a fiery red sauce, is said to come from a Chengdu cook around 1862 called Chen Mapo, and 'mapo' means a pockmarked old woman, so the dish is named for pockmarked Grandma Chen; the tale is local legend, though a real woman is remembered behind it.

Chongqing hotpot has a humble origin story. In the late 1800s, it is said, poor dock workers along the Yangtze pooled cheap scraps, often offal nobody else wanted, into one shared pot, and loaded it with chili and Sichuan pepper partly to hide the strong smell of that cheap offal.

Scientists now know why the two spices feel so different. Chili's capsaicin fires the nerves for heat and pain, but the numbing molecule in Sichuan pepper, hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, fools your touch nerves, the ones that feel light contact, so the lips seem to vibrate. In 2013 researchers at UCL found people matched the buzz to a vibration of about fifty taps a second, like a phone set to vibrate.

maple-syrup-forty-gallons-of-sap-to-make.context_blurb:
Maple syrup starts as clear, watery sap dripping from a tapped tree in the cold of late winter. In New England and Canada, sugar-makers collect it in buckets or tubing and boil it all day in a shed full of steam, the sugarhouse. What comes out is a small amount of thick, amber syrup, and almost everything about it is made in the pan.

The sap runs only in late winter and early spring, during freeze-thaw weather: a hard freeze at night followed by a thaw by day builds pressure inside the trunk that pushes the sap out of the tap. With no freezing nights there is no flow, so the season lasts only four to eight weeks.

Fresh sap is only about two percent sugar; the rest is water. Hours of boiling drive almost all of that water off the pan as steam, which is why roughly 40 gallons of sap shrink down to a single gallon of syrup.

The sap starts almost colourless and barely sweet, and the colour and rich, toasted flavour are made during the long boil, as the heat browns and caramelizes the sugars; the flavour is created in the pan, not carried up from the tree.

Bottles are graded by colour, from Golden through Amber and Dark to Very Dark, but all are pure maple syrup. The grade tells you when in the season the sap was collected: early sap boils into lighter, milder syrup and late sap into darker, bolder syrup, so a dark bottle is not a lesser one.

The Anishinaabe tell a legend about why syrup takes so much work. Once, the story goes, maples dripped ready-made syrup all year, and people grew so lazy that they lay beneath the trees with their mouths open, so the culture-hero Nanabozho poured water into the maples to thin the sap, and ever since, people have had to boil it down to earn their sweetness.

marbling-the-fat-inside-the-muscle.context_blurb:
Study a fine raw steak and you will see thin, creamy-white streaks of fat running through the red meat. That fat inside the muscle is called marbling, and it decides how juicy a steak will be, how it is graded in the shop and why some beef costs a fortune.

The streaks reminded people of the veins in polished marble, the stone sculptors carve, so since about 1770 fat-veined meat has been called marbled. Not all fat counts. The thick pale ring around the outside of a steak is the fat cap, fat that grew under the animal's skin, while true marbling is the fine fat laced between the muscle fibres themselves.

In a hot pan those inner flecks melt and baste the steak from the inside as it cooks, keeping it juicy and carrying much of its flavour; a steak needs only about three to seven percent of this inside fat to taste rich, and a lean steak tastes dry however carefully it is cooked.

That is why American grades turn on marbling: USDA inspectors judge how much fat is threaded through the muscle and stamp the beef Prime, Choice or Select, and Prime, with the most and evenest flecking, costs the most. The grader does not inspect the whole animal; he cuts between the twelfth and thirteenth ribs to expose the face of the ribeye muscle and scores the marbling on that single surface for the entire carcass.

The most marbled beef on Earth is Wagyu, and its name is plain Japanese: 'wa' means Japan and 'gyu' means cow, so Wagyu is simply Japanese cow, cattle bred for lacy marbling far denser than Western beef. The real difference is in the fat itself. Wagyu fat melts at a far lower heat than ordinary beef fat, starting to soften below the temperature of your body, so a slice begins to dissolve on a warm tongue; it is rich in oleic acid, the same fat found in olive oil, which lowers its melting point.

menthol-the-cold-that-isnt-cold.context_blurb:
A peppermint candy can make your mouth feel like a snowstorm, and a chili pepper can make it feel like a fire, yet neither changes the temperature in your mouth by a single degree. Both are tricks played on the nerves that sense hot and cold, and the scientists who explained them won a Nobel Prize.

The chill of mint is pure sensation: menthol switches on the nerve that reports cold without removing any heat, so a thermometer under your tongue would read exactly what it did before the candy, even while your brain insists your mouth is freezing.

Menthol also leaves the cold-sensing nerves on a hair trigger, lowering the temperature at which they shout 'cold', so after a mint, ordinary cool tap water crosses the line and feels as icy as meltwater.

Chili plays the opposite trick. Its capsaicin switches on TRPV1, the body's heat-and-pain sensor, which normally fires only when something is truly scalding, above about 43°C, so a chili trips the same alarm as a hot stove although nothing in your mouth gets warmer. Menthol works on the cold sensor, TRPM8, and the two scientists who found this pair of sensors, David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian, shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.

meringue-whipping-egg-whites-into-a-clou.context_blurb:
Meringue is one of the kitchen's small miracles: clear, runny egg whites and sugar beaten into a glossy white cloud that can be piped into shapes and baked crisp. It works because of what beating does to the proteins in the white, and it can be ruined by a single drop of the wrong thing.

Whisking changes the egg-white proteins themselves. Their tightly wound coils unfold, a change called denaturation, and the loosened chains link up with one another around the air bubbles you are beating in, so the clear liquid becomes a white foam that holds its shape. Crisp meringues bake low and slow, at about 80 to 90°C for up to two hours, because the gentle heat slowly dries the moisture out of the foam without browning the meringue or cracking its surface.

Sugar, beaten in a spoonful at a time, is the stabilizer: it dissolves into the foam and thickens the watery part, so the liquid cannot drain away from between the bubbles, and a fragile froth turns glossy and stiff. A little cream of tartar, which is a gentle acid, is insurance against over-beating: without it the protein network is easily squeezed too tight, forcing water out, so the smooth foam turns grainy and curdled.

French pastry cooks have whipped whites in copper bowls for over two centuries. A few copper ions slip from the bowl into the whites and latch onto a protein called conalbumin, and the foam comes out glossier and steadier.

The great enemy is fat. Even a speck of yolk or a greasy bowl coats the proteins and stops them linking, so the whites will never whip into peaks however long you beat, which is why bakers separate eggs carefully and scrub the bowl clean.

mise-en-place-everything-in-its-place-be.context_blurb:
Watch a professional kitchen before service and you will see cooks chopping, measuring and lining up small bowls long before anything goes on the heat. That habit has a French name, and it rests on a simple truth about how fast cooking happens. The kitchen around it was organized by one famous chef.

French cooks call the routine mise en place, 'putting in place', from the verb mettre, 'to put': read the recipe, gather the tools, measure each ingredient into its own container and get all the knife work done before any heat goes on.

It works because cooking moves faster than chopping. Once food is in a hot pan there is no time to stop, and a cook who pauses to mince garlic will scorch the sauce already cooking, so every cut and measure must be done before the burner is lit.

The kitchen's chain of command comes from Georges-Auguste Escoffier, a former army officer who ran his kitchens like an army unit, with clear ranks and every cook owning one station. His system, the kitchen brigade, let restaurants feed far more guests without losing quality.
