protein-the-bodys-repair-and-build-crew.context_blurb:
Every day your body repairs itself: it heals scrapes, rebuilds muscle after work and replaces worn-out parts. Protein is the material for nearly all of it, from the scab on a knee to the defenders that fight a cold. That is why growing kids, athletes and anyone recovering from injury or illness need enough of it.

A skinned knee that heals and arms that grow thicker with exercise are built from protein, the structural stuff of skin, muscle, blood and bone, which is why meat, eggs and fish are grouped as the plate's grow-and-repair foods. Pull a roast chicken breast apart and it separates into long threads, because white meat is muscle, built from bundles of long fibres, the very tissue that once moved the bird's wings; eating meat means eating an animal's muscle.

Protein also keeps hunger away. Given breakfasts with the same calories, the kid who ate scrambled eggs stays full longest, because protein quiets hunger better than the same calories of carbohydrate or fat. Protein builds more than muscle: your fingernails, your hair and the tough outer layer of your skin are all made of keratin, a structural protein.

When you cut a finger, repair cells weave a fresh mesh of collagen, the most abundant protein in your body, which hardens into the scar; collagen is also the main material of skin, tendons, ligaments and bone, making up roughly a quarter to a third of all your protein. The steak you eat is not plugged straight into your muscles: stomach acid and enzymes cut its protein into small units called amino acids, of which there are about twenty kinds. Your cells then restring them in a new order into proteins of your own, like taking a toy-brick cow apart and rebuilding it as you.

Fighting off a cold takes protein too. Your immune system builds millions of Y-shaped proteins called antibodies, which latch onto a virus or bacterium and block it or mark it for destruction, so a poorly fed body has trouble producing all the antibodies it needs. Of the twenty amino acids, your body can make most itself, but nine, including lysine, tryptophan and leucine, it cannot make at all, so they must come from food, and that is what 'essential' means on a label.

Blood is red and carries oxygen thanks to one protein, hemoglobin: each molecule has four protein units, each holding a ring-shaped heme group with one iron atom that grabs oxygen, which is why a doctor may tell a pale, tired kid to eat red meat for its iron and protein.

quinoa-and-the-pseudocereals.context_blurb:
Quinoa, buckwheat and amaranth cook like grains and grind into flour like grains, but they are not grains at all. True cereals such as wheat and rice are grasses; these are the seeds of broad-leafed flowering plants, so nutritionists call them pseudocereals, 'false cereals'. Each has its own surprising family tree and history in the Americas or Asia.

Quinoa fluffs up like rice, but it grows on a broad-leaf plant in the amaranth family, which makes it a close botanical cousin of spinach and beets rather than of wheat. High in the Andes, in cold, thin air that defeats wheat and rice, the Inca lived on quinoa for centuries and honoured it in Quechua as chisiya mama, meaning the mother of every grain.

Buckwheat is not related to wheat and is no grass either; its name is a worn-down form of 'beech wheat', because its small three-cornered seeds look like tiny beech nuts and it was cooked like wheat. It belongs to the knotweed family, with rhubarb, and contains no gluten. Raw quinoa seeds wear a bitter, soapy coating of saponins, from the Latin sapo, 'soap', which cooks rinse off, but on the living plant the coating works as a built-in pest repellent, so bitter that birds and insects leave the seeds alone.

Quinoa is unusually nourishing too. Wheat, rice, corn and oats all run low on lysine, the essential amino acid that is their weak link, but quinoa carries about twice as much of it, enough to supply all nine essential amino acids and count as a complete protein. Amaranth, quinoa's cousin, was holy to the Aztecs, who mixed amaranth flour and honey into edible statues of their gods; after Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 the Spanish tried to suppress the crop, but it survived, and Mexicans still press popped amaranth and honey into a sweet called alegría, 'joy'.

ramen-a-chinese-import-turned-japanese-i.context_blurb:
Ramen, the steaming bowl of broth and springy noodles, feels like the soul of Japan. Yet it arrived from China a little over a century ago, and Japanese cooks spent decades turning it into something their own, down to an instant version that conquered the world. Every part of the bowl, from the noodle to the broth, has its own story.

The heart of ramen is its noodle, and it starts as a plain dough of wheat flour, salt and water, plus one special ingredient. That ingredient is kansui, a mineral-rich alkaline water. The alkali makes the dough stretchy and springy and turns the flour's own pale pigments yellow, so the faint gold is not a dye; noodles made with plain water stay soft and pale. On a ramen menu, words such as shio, shoyu, miso and tonkotsu all name the broth: shio is salt, the oldest style, shoyu is soy sauce, miso is fermented soybean paste and tonkotsu is pork bone.

Ramen came from China. In the early 1900s the Japanese called it chuka soba, 'Chinese noodles'; Chinese immigrants had sold such soups in Yokohama's Chinatown since the 1880s, and Japan's first ramen shop, Rairaiken in Tokyo in 1910, had twelve Cantonese cooks. The word ramen traces to the Chinese lamian, 'pulled noodles', stretched and swung by hand, but the hand-pulling never came to Japan with the name: Japanese ramen noodles are cut into strands by a blade, usually in a roller-and-blade machine.

Tonkotsu broth looks as white and creamy as milk yet holds no dairy at all. Pork bones simmered gently give a thin, clear soup, but boiled hard for as long as eighteen hours they release fat and collagen that break down and blend into the water, and those tiny scattered droplets turn the broth opaque white.

In 1958 Momofuku Ando, after a year of failed experiments in a shed behind his house, invented instant ramen, and by his own account the idea came while he watched his wife fry tempura: the hot oil flashed the moisture out of the batter, so he flash-fried noodles to dry them the same way. His Chikin Ramen was ready in two minutes with hot water, and in 2000 the Japanese voted instant noodles their country's greatest invention of the century.

ratatouille-and-provence.context_blurb:
Ratatouille is the great summer stew of Provence, in the warm south of France, where country cooks around Nice used it to turn a glut of garden produce into dinner. It feels ancient and rustic, but its name, its method and even its ingredients have surprising histories, and a famous animated film gave it a fancy makeover.

The star of a classic ratatouille is eggplant, called aubergine in France, cooked with zucchini, bell peppers and onion and bound together with tomato and garlic. Purists, as the great French cookbook Larousse Gastronomique notes, do not tip everything into one pot: they cook each vegetable separately first and only then combine them to simmer slowly together, so every vegetable keeps its own texture and taste.

The name comes from the Occitan word for stirring, and when French writers first used it, early in the nineteenth century, it was an insult rather than a dish name, meaning a cheap, coarse stew, closer to slop than to anything fine.

The stew is also younger than it looks, because tomatoes and bell peppers both came from the Americas and reached Europe only after Columbus, so no medieval cook in Provence could have made it; eggplant, by contrast, is an Old World vegetable that arrived earlier through Arab trade. In Pixar's film Ratatouille, the dish that wins over the stern critic is a refined spiral of paper-thin vegetable slices chosen by the film's adviser, chef Thomas Keller: confit byaldi, created by the French chef Michel Guérard in 1976, whose name winks at the Turkish stuffed-eggplant dish imam bayildi, 'the imam fainted'.

raw-milk-vs-pasteurized.context_blurb:
Almost all milk sold in shops has been pasteurized, gently heated to kill germs. Some people prefer raw milk straight from the farm, prizing its taste and what they see as its living goodness. Health agencies warn hard against it, while a major study found raw-milk children had fewer allergies, so this is a real debate with real evidence on both sides.

Pasteurization is named for Louis Pasteur, who first proved the method in 1864 on wine, gently heating it to about 50 to 60°C to kill the microbes that spoiled it; using the idea on milk came later, after the German chemist Franz von Soxhlet proposed it in 1886. Pasteurizing gently heats milk to kill germs: the standard modern method warms it to about 72°C for just fifteen seconds, enough to kill disease-causing bacteria without boiling the milk or changing its taste.

The case against raw milk rests on outbreaks. In about 200 American raw-milk outbreaks from 1998 to 2018, with some 2,645 people sickened, nearly half of those who fell ill were kids and teens under twenty, and the commonest germ was Campylobacter. Pasteurized milk still sours in time because the brief, gentle heat does not sterilize it: hardy bacterial spores survive and slowly multiply even in the fridge, which is why every carton carries a date.

The FDA warns that raw-milk germs can trigger hemolytic uremic syndrome, which destroys red blood cells and makes the kidneys fail, mostly in children. Raw-milk drinkers answer that heat changes milk's most delicate proteins: pasteurizing makes them unfold and tangle, the same change, called denaturing, that turns a runny egg white solid, and the fragile whey proteins are the first to go.

The study that keeps the debate alive is GABRIELA, which tracked some 8,000 children from farming areas of Germany, Austria and Switzerland and found that the ones given raw milk from the farm had less asthma, hay fever and allergy, with about 41 percent lower odds of asthma. Yet the same research team, led by a scientist named Loss, still concluded that people should keep avoiding raw milk, because its risk of dangerous germs such as listeria and E. coli is real. The protective proteins seem to be destroyed by heat, so boiled farm milk lost the benefit, and no milk on the shelf yet offers both safety and protection.

red-meat-and-the-cancer-scare.context_blurb:
In 2015 a World Health Organization agency announced that a category of meat causes cancer, and headlines around the world compared a breakfast of bacon to a pack of cigarettes. The real story is more careful: red meat is a rich source of nutrients, what the WHO's ranking means is widely misread, and experts still disagree about what ordinary people should do.

Beef is a complete protein: on its own it supplies all nine amino acids the body cannot make, while beans and rice must be eaten together to cover each other's gaps. Beef also delivers vitamin B12, which no plant makes at all; a three-ounce serving of lean beef gives roughly a full day's supply, which is why people who eat no animal foods are told to take a supplement. Popeye's spinach is a poor match for beef as an iron source, because meat's iron is the heme kind, which the gut absorbs far more readily, about 15 to 35 percent, against about 2 to 20 percent for the non-heme iron in plants.

On 26 October 2015 the WHO's cancer agency, IARC, placed processed meats such as bacon, ham and hot dogs in Group 1, 'carcinogenic to humans', the group that also holds tobacco and asbestos; it was meat that had been salted, cured or smoked, not fresh red meat, that got the top label. Scientists warned that the ranking measures how strong the evidence is that something can cause cancer, not how dangerous it is: smoking multiplies lung-cancer risk about twenty times, while eating bacon every day raises an already small bowel-cancer risk by about 18 percent.

In 2019 an expert panel called NutriRECS re-examined the same studies and issued a weak recommendation, based on what it called low-certainty evidence, that adults could keep eating red and processed meat at their usual amounts without cutting back. Critics were outraged, and Christopher Gardner of Stanford declared himself flabbergasted, which shows how contested the advice remains.

How meat is cooked may matter too. Grilling over flames can form two families of cancer-linked compounds: HCAs form inside very hot meat, while PAHs come from outside, when fat drips onto the fire and the flare-ups send smoke up to coat the meat, so cooks are advised to keep meat off direct flame, flip it often and trim charred bits.

red-meats-hidden-payload-heme-iron-and-b.context_blurb:
Red meat is famous for protein, but it carries two more treasures that are hard to get anywhere else in good amounts: iron the body absorbs easily and vitamin B12 for blood and nerves. Health advisers weigh those benefits against cancer risks, and one humble organ outdoes even steak.

A doctor treating a pale, weak patient with low blood may advise eating more red meat because it delivers iron, the mineral at the heart of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells, so iron really does build blood. Spinach and steak both contain iron, and the amounts are close; the difference is how much of it your gut can absorb, because meat's heme iron is taken up several times more readily than the iron in plants.

Popeye's spinach was never about iron at all: Segar, the cartoonist who created Popeye, gave him spinach for its vitamin A, and even the popular tale that a scientist misplaced a decimal point and overstated spinach's iron is itself a myth.

Plant iron can be helped. A squeeze of lemon over a bowl of lentils adds vitamin C, which turns the iron into a more soluble form and keeps it from binding to blockers in the meal, raising absorption two- to fourfold. Vitamin B12 does a double job, building red blood cells and keeping the nervous system working, and it comes naturally almost only from meat, fish, eggs and dairy, so strict vegans need fortified foods or supplements. The stomach even makes a special escort protein, intrinsic factor, to carry it through the gut.

Advisers do not deny red meat's iron and B12, but in 2015 the WHO's cancer agency, IARC, linked heavy eating of red and especially processed meat to a raised risk of bowel cancer and urged moderation. Supporters of traditional diets answer that such well-absorbed iron and B12 are hard to replace from plants; both sides have a case.

Long before vitamin pills, traditional cultures prized liver above prime steak and called it nature's multivitamin: about three ounces of beef liver, only some 175 calories, covers weeks of B12 and a month of vitamin A, along with iron the body takes up easily, riboflavin, folate and copper.
